item.title: UE6 砍掉蓝图和 Actor 框架：玩法改由 Verse + 新 Scene Graph 承担，理由是「AI 可操作性」 ｜ An update on Blueprints and the path to UE6
item.description:
一句话：Epic 用 AI 两周把 Fortnite 两万多个蓝图转成约 300 万行 Verse，于是决定不再保留兼容层。

要点：

  • 决定本身很硬：**UE6（含 Early Access）不再包含蓝图与 Actor Gameplay Framework**，玩法改由 **Verse** 与新的 **Scene Graph** 框架承担；设计目标里明写了一条「**AI 可操作性（AI operability）**」
  • 为什么敢这么做：原本计划让蓝图与 Actor 在 UE6 早期共存以便增量升级，但「近期 AI 能力的进展」让他们认为转换可以大幅自动化；作为验证，**两周内把 Fortnite Battle Royale 的 2 万多个蓝图转成约 300 万行 Verse 代码**（原估需要数年），目前在做性能、内存与架构的验证
  • 同一批 AI 工具已回移到 UE 5.9：**更广的 Python 脚本访问**（让 AI 工具能脚本化编辑器）、MCP 改进、**Web 作为目标平台**、**Unreal Canvas**（生成资产并把编辑器内容、引用与反馈并排保留）；作者直言「UE 5.9 的很大一部分是我们用 AI agent 构建的，包括大部分 Web 平台工作」

为什么值得看：这是引擎厂商第一次把「架构为 AI 而改」写成正式决定：砍掉可视化脚本、把玩法收进代码（Verse）与显式状态（Scene Graph），并用 AI 完成自家最大项目的迁移。对做 AI 原生引擎的人，这条同时给出了结论（要 AI 可操作）与代价（放弃蓝图生态）。

中文摘要：Epic 宣布 UE6（包括 Early Access）将不再包含蓝图与 Actor Gameplay Framework，玩法改由 Verse 语言与新的 Scene Graph 框架承担；官方给出的设计目标里明确包含「AI 可操作性」。原本的计划是让蓝图与 Actor 在 UE6 早期共存，以便 UE5 项目增量升级，但 Epic 认为近期 AI 能力的进展可以让转换过程大幅自动化、甚至全自动，因此决定按时交付更彻底的新架构。作为验证，他们在两周内用 AI 把 Fortnite Battle Royale 的两万多个蓝图转成约 300 万行 Verse 代码——这件事原本预计要数年——目前正在验证转换结果的性能、内存占用与架构质量。同一批为 UE6 构建的 AI 工具已经开始回移到 UE 5.9，包括更广的 Python 脚本访问、MCP 改进、把 Web 作为目标平台，以及把生成资产与编辑器内容、引用、反馈并排保留的 Unreal Canvas；官方还表示 UE 5.9 的很大一部分是用 AI agent 构建的，包括大部分 Web 平台工作。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unreal Engine（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

新闻

2026年11月20日 An update on Blueprints and the path to UE6

Fortnite

MegaJam

UE5

UE6

UEFN

Unreal Engine 5.9

Verse

游戏

蓝图

Hello, Unreal Engine community. Marcus Wassmer here. I want to update you on something I said in the Road to UE6 post, because it affects how you’ll get from UE5 to UE6. You may have already caught the news coming out of Unreal Fest Tokyo, but here’s the full picture.

What’s changing UE6, including UE6 Early Access, won’t include Blueprints or the Actor Gameplay Framework. Gameplay will be built in Verse and on the new Scene Graph framework.

In June, we said Blueprints and Actors would coexist in UE6 Early Access and 6.0, so UE5 projects could upgrade incrementally while the new Scene Graph framework matures. However, with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6, if not make that process fully automatic. That also means we can deliver UE6 on time (or sooner!) while meeting its design goals: a new data model, a Verse-first architecture, modularity, and AI operability.

What this means for your UE5 project We expect AI to make converting a UE5 game to UE6 practical and cost-efficient. We believe this for two reasons:

First, the cost of any given task with AI has been going down 13x year over year, and the complexity of converting a game remains more or less constant. We expect this trend to continue and to accelerate, which should result in modest conversion costs by the time UE 6.0 is out in the world.

Second, Fortnite has one of the largest libraries of Blueprints anywhere. Two weeks ago, we experimented with using AI to convert all of the Blueprints for Battle Royale to Verse. This project was expected to take years, but we now have a working prototype of Fortnite that is about 3 million lines of Verse code after porting more than 20,000 Blueprints. The team is hard at work iterating to validate the resulting performance, memory usage, and architecture. We’re doing this at scale now, and this conversion will help make the process as easy as possible for everyone else.

It’s up to you if you want to keep your project on UE5, and you don’t have to wait for UE6 to use more AI tools in your projects. We’ve already started to bring the AI tooling we built for UE6 back to UE5, beginning with the UE 5.9 MegaJam Preview.

Here’s what you can do with UE6’s AI tools in UE 5.9 Expanded Python scripting: Get much wider Python access to the editor, so you and your AI tools can script and automate more of Unreal Engine. Model Context Protocol (MCP) improvements: Connect the model you prefer to the editor and have it work directly in your project. Web as a target platform: Build and ship Unreal Engine projects to the browser. Unreal Canvas: Generate assets, and keep editor content, references, and feedback side by side; they stay current and controllable. You’ll also find a variety of rendering and animation updates and bug fixes. See the 5.9 Preview release notes for more details.

We built much of UE 5.9 with AI agents, including most of the web platform work. That’s the same approach we’re betting on for converting Fortnite, and your projects, to UE6.

You can expect continued development on targeted UE5 features, fixes, and support while we work on UE6.

Where this is going UE6 is about building a foundation for the future of games: larger in scale, more interconnected, and built on an interoperable economy where developers build together as peers. Making this change now gets us there faster, and AI advances mean that we can support UE5 more completely while we’re transitioning. We do know this is a lot of change to take in, particularly since the last major change was back in June. So thank you for bearing with us while we chart the course to a new, modern engine. We can’t wait to see what you’ll build with it. 获取有关行业创新和免费资产的最新消息！ 所属行业 登录订阅 通过提交您的信息，即表示您同意接收来自 Epic Games 的新闻、问卷调查和特惠推送。 隐私政策

item.title: 流式可控视频生成要同时做到高分辨率、高帧率、低延迟：Streaming-AAA 说现有方法三条里总缺一条 ｜ Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
item.description:
一句话：离真正可玩还差得远，因为画质、帧率与交互延迟三者无法同时满足。

要点：

  • 目标定得很明确：可控流式视频生成是通向交互式游戏模拟的一条路，但现有方法**离实用还有距离**
  • 失败模式是三者无法兼得：往往不能同时达到**高视觉保真度、高帧率与低交互延迟**，结果是响应迟钝、体验下降
  • Streaming-AAA 提出一种新范式，目标是对 AAA 级画质内容做**可控的无限长生成**

为什么值得看：这是把「生成式画面能不能进游戏」的验收标准写成了三项硬指标。任何做实时生成内容的团队都可以直接拿这三项对照自己的方案——缺哪一条，就不能叫可玩。

中文摘要：可控的流式视频生成被视为通往交互式游戏模拟的一条路径，但作者指出现有方法离实用还有明显距离：它们往往无法同时满足高视觉保真度、高帧率与低交互延迟这三项要求，结果就是响应迟钝、体验退化。Streaming-AAA 因此提出一种新的范式，目标是实现 AAA 级画质内容的可控无限长生成。它的价值在于把「生成式画面能不能进游戏」这件事写成了三项可验收的硬指标——缺任何一条，都谈不上可玩。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

Streaming-AAA:
Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at
High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency

Abstract

Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

††footnotetext: * Equal contribution. † Project Lead.

1 Introduction

Interactive game simulation has become an increasingly important application of generative video models, where the system must synthesize future visual observations conditioned on user controls in a streaming manner [20, 1, 39, 25, 33]. Unlike offline video generation, playable game generation imposes simultaneous requirements on visual fidelity, temporal consistency, frame rate, and interaction latency. These requirements are especially stringent for AAA-level games, where high-resolution rendering, fast motion, complex scenes, and long-horizon interactions are all essential to the user experience. In this work, we primarily target Genshin Impact, a widely played open-world action RPG whose environments are familiar enough that generation quality is easy to judge.

Despite recent progress in controllable video generation and world models [55, 4, 33, 23, 40, 50, 29], existing streaming generation systems remain far from practical gameplay. Many approaches can produce visually plausible short clips, but their quality degrades over long horizons. Others support control or interaction but operate at low resolution, low frame rate, or high latency, making the generated experience difficult to play. As a result, current methods do not jointly satisfy the key requirements of high-fidelity 1080p generation, real-time frame rates, low end-to-end latency, and stable infinite interaction.

We present Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite streaming AAA game video generation framework designed for high-resolution, high-frame-rate, and low-latency gameplay. Streaming-AAA first introduces an efficient high-resolution video VAE that compresses 1080p gameplay frames into compact spatio-temporal latents and reconstructs high-fidelity frames with low decoding overhead. On top of this representation, we build a UNet-based latent diffusion model with factorized spatial, temporal, and cross-attention modules, enabling efficient visual modeling, temporal reasoning, and multi-modal control. To support long-horizon streaming generation, we further adopt long-context pre-training, post-training alignment with distribution matching distillation, and a hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory. These designs allow Streaming-AAA to preserve long-range consistency while maintaining low interaction latency during real-time inference.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose Streaming-AAA, the first controllable infinite-horizon AAA game video generation framework that simultaneously delivers high visual fidelity, real-time throughput (43FPS at 1080p), ultra-low end-to-end latency (198ms), and stable long-rollout consistency. To our knowledge, this is the first system to achieve production-grade real-time gameplay generation at this specification.

  • •

    At its core, Streaming-AAA comprises a purpose-built causal video VAE and a factorized 3D-UNet latent diffusion backbone. The VAE compresses raw pixel inputs by 16 × spatially into compact latent representations, drastically reducing inference overhead. The 3D-UNet decouples spatial texture modeling, temporal dynamics learning, and conditional control via cross attention modules cutting computational cost, while supporting flexible integration of rich frame-aligned conditioning signals (e.g., agent actions, weather states).

  • •

    We establish a two-stage pre/post-training paradigm tailored for unbounded autoregressive streaming. In pre-training, we adopt a per-frame independent noise scheduling strategy (i.e., Diffusion Forcing) under the DDPM framework, which encodes the inductive bias of growing uncertainty for distant temporal horizons to match open-world evolution dynamics. In post-training, we apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) to align the model with 2-step generation, which further boosts rollout stability and temporal consistency without sacrificing real-time performance.

    • 2 Related Works

    2.1 Video Generation Models

    Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation. Large-scale text-to-video diffusion models [19, 17, 37, 30, 42, 45, 56, 12, 21, 34, 41, 44] have demonstrated impressive visual quality and diversity, producing photorealistic short clips from textual descriptions. However, these models typically require minutes of inference time to generate only a few seconds of video, and most of them lack the ability to produce arbitrarily long sequences in a streaming fashion.

    To address the long-horizon limitation, several methods[26, 13, 11, 49, 9, 14, 58] attempt to retrofit pre-trained text-to-video models for streaming generation. Self-Forcing [26] bridges the train-test gap in autoregressive video diffusion by aligning the training distribution with the streaming rollout. Context Forcing [11] introduces long-context conditioning to maintain consistency across extended autoregressive generation. LongLive [49] targets real-time interactive long video generation by combining efficient architectures with streaming inference. Alternatively, Diffusion Forcing [9] equips the model with streaming capability directly during pre-training by combining next-token prediction with full-sequence diffusion. Despite these advances, achieving real-time streaming inference at high resolution remains a significant challenge for playable game generation.

    2.2 World Models

    World models aim to learn predictive representations of environments for planning and interaction. Existing approaches fall into two categories.

    The first is based on 3D reconstruction [53, 54, 32], which builds explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time exploration. While achieving strong real-time performance, these methods produce mostly static worlds with limited interactivity.

    The second leverages video generation for world simulation. Early works [5, 6, 7, 15] demonstrate that video diffusion models can serve as world simulators. More recently, a growing body of research [20, 2, 8, 25, 1, 39, 47, 46, 10, 16, 22, 48, 36] has explored interactive and controllable world models, addressing challenges such as long-horizon memory, action conditioning, and real-time streaming. However, none of these methods simultaneously achieve high resolution (1080p), high frame rate, and low interaction latency—all essential for AAA-level playable game generation. Our work addresses this gap by jointly optimizing visual fidelity, streaming efficiency, and interactive responsiveness within a unified framework.

    3 Dataset Construction

    Modern AAA video games represent a convergence of cutting-edge graphics technologies, providing an almost inexhaustible source of high-fidelity visual data. Specifically, these environments feature:

  • •

    Geometrically Diverse Landscapes: Expansive terrains encompassing natural formations (mountains, rivers, oceans, forests, grassland) and intricate man-made architectures.

  • •

    Complex Human-Scene Interactions: Rich agent behaviors such as locomotion across uneven terrain, climbing trees, and swimming in dynamic fluid simulations.

  • •

    Sophisticated Lighting Conditions: Dramatic variations in illumination, including dawn, noon, and night cycles, often coupled with advanced effects like ray-traced global illumination.

  • •

    Realistic Physical Dynamics: Natural phenomena such as wind-induced vegetation swaying (wind-sway effects) and physically-based object interactions.

    • To train a generative model capable of synthesizing photorealistic videos with such intricate spatio-temporal details, it is imperative to expose the model to a massive and highly diverse dataset that encapsulates these multifaceted distributions. However, manual gameplay recording is labor-intensive and suffers from limited scalability, making it infeasible to cover the vast state space of modern AAA titles.

    To bridge this gap, we design an automated parallel data acquisition system, termed Automated Data Collection System to efficiently harvest these rich visual cues.

    3.1 Automated Data Collection System (ADCS)

    As illustrated in Figure 2, the proposed Automated Data Collection System (ADCS) comprises three integral components: an AI Agent Server, a Distributed Render Cluster, and a Centralized Storage Backend.

    AI Agent Server and Control Logic. The AI Agent Server acts as the control center, orchestrating in-game agents in Distributed Render Cluster via the LAN. It dispatches low-level actions to each PC game instance. To ensure comprehensive environmental coverage, we implement an autonomous navigation policy that samples actions to sufficiently cover the virtual terrains.

    Distributed Render Cluster. The cluster consists of a pool of high-end workstations executing game instances in parallel. Each node captures raw gameplay at 30 FPS and 1080p resolution using OBS Studio, preserving fine-grained motion details essential for learning physical dynamics and temporal coherence. Frame-aligned agent actions and real-time frame rate are recorded alongside the video stream. Weather and time-of-day are not read from the game; instead, they are estimated by a model (i.e., open-source Qwen-VL [3]) from the captured frames. Each recording task lasts 60 seconds. And when each task ends, the recorded video along with its annotations will be upload to the Centralized Storage Backend.

    Centralized Storage Backend. The backend serves as the unified data hub, ingesting asynchronously uploaded packages from all render nodes upon completion of each capture session. Each upload contains synchronized pairs of high-fidelity gameplay videos and their corresponding metadata streams extracted by the render cluster. The curated dataset is directly accessible to the training cluster for distributed training.

    Scalability and Throughput. The tight integration of the three components underpins the pipeline’s exceptional efficiency. By leveraging parallel execution across the render cluster and high-throughput asynchronous data ingestion at the storage backend, the system collects over 5 million frames daily. Within days of acquisition cycle, we successfully captured footage spanning approximately 5 KM2 of in-game terrain. This automated infrastructure ensures a steady supply of high-quality, curated data, enabling the model to effectively learn the complex distributions inherent in AAA game environments.

    3.2 Conquering Huge Map with ADCS

    Modern AAA titles are characterized by their sheer geographical scale, often featuring seamless open worlds spanning square kilometers (KM2). Naïvely employing a sequential, single-agent collection strategy (i.e., traversing the map linearly) presents a significant bottleneck: the data acquisition rate is fundamentally constrained by the agent’s movement speed and loading times. This results in prohibitively low efficiency and insufficient spatial data density, failing to meet the stringent demands of training high-fidelity video world models which require dense observations of environmental geometry and dynamics.

    To address this challenge, we leverage our proposed ADCS to achieve high-density spatial coverage. Our core strategy involves decoupling spatial navigation from data capture through parallelization and teleportation.

    Parallel Spatial Sampling Strategy. To ensure comprehensive coverage and high sampling density across expansive virtual environments, we employ a parallel spatial sampling strategy. First, we partition the game map with the teleportation waypoints in the map.

    Rather than relying on conventional pathfinding to traverse the terrain sequentially—which is time-prohibitive for large-scale maps—we leverage the game’s built-in teleportation waypoint. Specifically, the AI Agent Server dispatches specific teleportation waypoint targets to the Distributed Render Cluster, routing the in-game avatars to the designated waypoints.

    This approach allows us to distribute data collection tasks across multiple compute nodes in parallel. Each client is assigned a subset of the waypoints, recording high-frame-rate footage locally upon arrival. By decoupling spatial navigation from data capture, our strategy significantly accelerates the acquisition process and enhances the spatial density of the dataset. Consequently, the system can efficiently survey approximately 5 KM2 of terrain in several days, capturing fine-grained environmental details without the computational overhead of simulating long-distance traversal.

    3.3 Data Statistics

    Leveraging our proposed ADCS and the parallel spatial sampling strategy, we construct a large-scale, high-fidelity dataset that captures the rich visual and interactive complexity of modern AAA games. In total, we collect approximately 22,000 videos, each lasting 1 minute and recorded at 30 fps, aggregating to approximately 40 million frames. All footage is recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080, ensuring fine-grained spatial and temporal details suitable for high-capacity video generation models.

    Beyond raw pixel data, our collection pipeline provides frame-aligned annotations that are typically unavailable in real-world datasets. Specifically, each frame is annotated with:

  • •

    Agent Actions: Control signals ("W", "A", "S", "D" to move, ↑↓←→ to turn, "Space" to jump), recorded directly from the game agent.

  • •

    Environmental Context: Weather conditions and diurnal lighting cycles (time-of-day), which are estimated by a vision-language model (Qwen-VL [3]) rather than read from the game engine.

    • The data acquired through our ADCS framework exhibits richness across three distinct dimensions, each contributing to the overall fidelity and utility for training high-capacity video generation models.

    1. High-Fidelity Visual Stream. All videos are recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080 with a frame rate of 30 fps. This high-resolution, high-frame-rate capture ensures access to fine-grained visual details and temporally coherent motion dynamics—essential for modeling complex scene evolution and object interactions.

    2. Rich Metadata Annotations. Each frame is accompanied by annotations, including recorded control signals and model-estimated environmental context (weather and time-of-day). These annotations enable fine-grained controllability during training and inference, allowing the model to condition its output on specific physical or semantic states.

    3. Broad Coverage with High Density. Through parallelized spatial sampling, we achieve extensive geographic coverage (5 KM2) while maintaining high sample density. This combination ensures exposure to a diverse array of content including natural scenery and man-made architectures, enhancing the generalizability of learned representations.

    These annotations facilitate a wide range of downstream tasks, from conditional video synthesis to world model training that requires strict physical and geometric consistency. Statistics of the dataset are summarized in Table 1.

    4 Method

    4.1 Problem Formulation

    We formulate controllable AAA game video generation as an infinite streaming prediction problem. Given previous frames x_1:t, user controls a_1:t+k, and a compact memory state mₜ, the model predicts the next video segment:

    p_θ(x_t+1:t+k|x_1:t,a_1:t+k,mₜ).

    		(1)

    Unlike offline video generation, this task requires causal generation, faithful response to user inputs, and long-horizon stability under strict constraints on resolution, frame rate, and interaction latency.

    4.2 Overview of Streaming-AAA

    We propose Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite AAA game video generation framework for real-time gameplay. Streaming-AAA consists of three key components. First, an efficient high-resolution video VAE compresses 1080p frames into compact spatio-temporal latents and decodes them with low overhead. Second, a UNet-based latent diffusion model generates future video latents conditioned on player controls and historical memory. Third, long-context pre-training, post-training alignment, and hybrid KV-cache memory improve long-term consistency and reduce inference latency. Together, these designs enable high-fidelity, controllable, and low-latency streaming generation.

    4.3 Efficient High-Resolution Video VAE

    High-resolution decoding is a major bottleneck for real-time game video generation. We therefore redesign the VAE architecture to improve decoding efficiency while preserving fine visual details. The encoder compresses 1080p gameplay frames into compact spatiotemporal latents, and the decoder reconstructs high-fidelity frames with reduced computational overhead. This design allows the diffusion model to operate in latent space while enabling fast reconstruction of AAA-quality game visuals during streaming inference.

    To bridge the gap between high-resolution spatial modeling and temporal consistency, we propose an Enhanced VAE model design. Our architecture is designed to efficiently handle ultra-high-definition inputs (1792×1024) while maintaining a manageable latent space dimension with high-frequency details.

    Architecture Design. We configure an overall temporal-spatial compression factor of 4×16×16 relative to the input resolution. The encoder maps the input video clip x∈ℝ^(4N+1)×H×W×3 to a latent representation z∈ℝ^(N+1)×H/16×W/16×C, which is compatible for both single frame and multi-frame compression and decoding, similar to Wan-series. A key distinction of our model lies in the decoder’s upsampling pipeline. Unlike traditional methods relying solely on interpolation or transposed convolutions, we introduce an additional Pixel Shuffle layer at the tail of the decoding process. Specifically, the decoder consists of three sequential Conv3D upsampling blocks followed by a Pixel Shuffle operation for efficient sub-pixel upsampling in the largest upsample stage. This design mitigates checkerboard artifacts commonly induced by large-stride deconvolutions and preserves fine-grained texture details.

    Multi-Stage Curriculum Training. Training a VAE from scratch for high-resolution video is inherently unstable. To address this, we employ a three-stage curriculum learning strategy for faster convergence:

  • •

    Stage 1 (Spatial Initialization): We train the model on static images at 256×256 resolution to stabilize the reconstruction of basic color distributions and edges.

  • •

    Stage 2 (Temporal Extension): We extend the model to video data using 256×256 patches. Here, the model processes multiple frames within a clip to learn short-term temporal coherence.

  • •

    Stage 3 (Native Resolution): Finally, we fine-tune the model on full-resolution 1792×1024 videos to adapt to the aspect ratio and scale of real-world high-definition content.

    • Rolling Frame Prediction. For multi-frame training, we adopt a rolling prediction mechanism. Given a sequence of length T, the model predicts frames indexed as 4n+1 (n≥0). To balance computational cost and gradient flow, we selectively apply gradients only to the last 1 or 4 predicted frames of each sequence, preventing error accumulation in long sequences while maintaining temporal smoothness.

    4.4 Redesigning UNet-based Video Diffusion Models

    Leveraging the compact latent space provided by our VAE, we construct a 3D UNet-based diffusion model for high-fidelity video synthesis. The network follows a symmetric encoder-decoder structure, performing three downsampling and three upsampling operations, with the bottleneck resolution reduced to 1/8 of the input.

    Factorized Spatio-Temporal Blocks. To mitigate the computational overhead of dense 3D operations, each stage of the UNet is composed of three specialized modules:

  • •

    Spatial Module: Consisting primarily of convolutional layers, this module focuses on modeling intra-frame textures and structural details, ensuring high visual fidelity.

  • •

    Cross-Attention Module: Also constructed with Transformer layers, this module serves as the conditioning interface. It projects external signals into the latent space via cross-attention mechanisms in causal manner. This design allows the model to flexibly incorporate diverse control signals, such as action, weather and time-of-day conditions, enabling fine-grained controllability over the generation process.

  • •

    Temporal Module with Hybrid KV-Cache Memory: Built upon Transformer blocks, this module operates along the temporal axis to capture the dynamic evolution of each latent pixel across frames in causal manner, ensuring motion consistency. We also implement a Hybrid KV-Cache Memory mechanism. Once a frame is finalized, its corresponding keys and values in the self-attention layers are stored in memory. For subsequent frames, the model retrieves these cached key-value (KV) pairs as tokens reference instead of recomputing them, significantly reducing the computational complexity from O(T²) to O(T) per step, where T is the sequence length. We select both specific long-term and short-term KV-tokens to enhance long-term temporal consistency within only 30 tokens.

    • This factorized architecture effectively decouples spatial modeling, temporal dynamics, and conditional control, significantly reducing the complexity compared to full spatio-temporal attention while enhancing generalization across various scenarios.

    Unified Multi-Modal Conditioning. To handle heterogeneous inputs, we adopt a unified conditioning scheme. Each condition type (e.g., action, weather, time, frame-rate) is first processed by a dedicated embedding layer and tokenized into a fixed-dimensional vector. Subsequently, these tokens are concatenated into a unified condition sequence. This sequence is then injected into the model through the Cross-Attention modules at each stage. This design not only standardizes the input interface for various modalities but also allows the model to selectively attend to relevant conditions during different stages of denoising.

    Training and Convergence. By operating within the compact latent space provided by our VAE, the diffusion model achieves stable convergence. The efficient design ensures a high inference throughput, making it suitable for practical applications requiring multi-conditional control.

    4.5 Modeling Long-horizon Uncertainty with Diffusion-forcing Pre-training

    We adopt the Diffusion Forcing (DF) [9] paradigm in the pretraining stage of our streaming-AAA model pretraining, whose core innovation of per-frame independent noise scheduling aligns naturally with the requirements of long-horizon, controllable world simulation. Instead of enforcing a globally shared noise level across all frames, DF samples an independent noise step kᵢ∼p(k) (e.g., uniform or logit-normal distribution over the DDPM [24] timestep range [0,K]) for each frame i, where the per-frame noised latent follows the standard DDPM forward formulation:

    zᵢ^kᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ·zᵢ⁰+√1-ᾱ_kᵢ·εᵢ, εᵢ∼ℕ(0,I),

    		(2)

    with zᵢ⁰ denoting the clean VAE-encoded frame latent, and ᾱ_kᵢ=∏ₛ₌₁^kᵢ(1-βₛ) representing the cumulative product of noise retention coefficients under a predefined DDPM schedule (e.g., cosine schedule), where βₛ∈(0,1) is the pre-defined noise addition ratio at step s. Stacking these per-frame noised latents forms a 2D noise schedule matrix that encodes the inductive bias of growing uncertainty for farther temporal horizons—matching the intrinsic causal dynamics of open-world physical evolution. This design, combined with velocity (v-)prediction, enables stable arbitrary-length rollouts. Crucially, the per-frame noise assignment is natively compatible with the rich, frame-aligned metadata, enabling frame-level acute dynamic variation and transition modeling.

    For diffusion training, we opt for v-prediction instead of conventional ε-prediction. The velocity vᵢ for frame i is defined as the linear combination of the clean latent and noise term in the forward process:

    vᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ·εᵢ-√1-ᾱ_kᵢ·zᵢ⁰,

    		(3)

    Let zᵏ\triangleq{zᵢ^kᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ be the whole noised latent sequence, k={kᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ the per-frame noise steps, and c the control condition sequence (aggregating action, weather, time, and frame-rate signals). We denote f(·)ᵢ as the i-th frame of its output, and optimize the per-frame v-prediction objective:

    L_DF=𝔼_{zᵢ⁰},c,k,{vᵢ} 1/T∑ᵢ₌₁ᵀ∥f (zᵏ,c,k)ᵢ-vᵢ∥₂²,

    		(4)

    where T is the sequence length. This contrasts with the unified-timestep v-prediction loss that enforces a single noise level t for all frames. The per-frame independent (zᵢ^kᵢ,kᵢ,vᵢ) pairs act as an implicit curriculum, stabilizing pretraining on our heterogeneous AAA dataset and enabling continuous post-training distributions for infinite rollouts. Empirically, v-prediction mitigates error accumulation during long-horizon generation compared to ε-prediction, further reinforcing the stability of our streaming inference pipeline.

    Stage 1: Short-range Dynamics Modeling. In the initial phase, we focus on stabilizing the foundational visual and short-term motion patterns. The model is trained on short video clips consisting of 64 frames. This shorter sequence length allows for larger batch sizes and faster convergence, enabling the model to efficiently learn low-level textures, spatial structures, and plausible short-term dynamics without the interference of long-range dependencies. We train the model for 200 epochs in this stage.

    Stage 2: Long-range Contextual Understanding. Subsequently, we extend the temporal context to capture long-term consistency and memory. We increase the input sequence length from 64 to 640 frames (∼21 seconds of video content). This extension forces the Temporal Modules and Cross-Attention mechanisms to reason over extended horizons, mitigating temporal drift and maintaining spatial stability across distant frames. Although computationally intensive, training for 20 epochs on this extended context is sufficient to adapt the model from short-term generation to long-form video synthesis.

    4.6 Post-Training Alignment for Streaming Inference

    As illustrated in Figure 3, during streaming inference the model conditions on clean historical frames and control signals to generate future latents. Although diffusion-forcing pre-training already equips the model with an initial ability for streaming generation, there remains a non-negligible mismatch between pre-training and practical inference. During diffusion-forcing training, each latent token is independently assigned a random noise level and the model learns to denoise under a wide range of partially corrupted historical contexts. This large training space improves the model’s generative capacity and enables it to exploit ambiguous historical information. In actual streaming inference, however, we adopt a teacher-forcing-style rollout, where historical frames are clean observations with zero noise. Therefore, inference only corresponds to a restricted subset of the diffusion-forcing training distribution, which can lead to degraded generation quality and weaker temporal consistency.

    To reduce this gap, we further align the model with its inference-time behavior through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [51, 52]. Inspired by the second stage of self-forcing distillation [26], we optimize the generator to directly learn how to generate future latent tokens under fixed denoising timesteps and clean historical contexts. Unlike standard self-forcing and DMD settings, our pre-trained model already supports self-rollout after diffusion-forcing pre-training. We therefore initialize the generator, the real score model, and the fake score model from the same pre-trained checkpoint. This initialization provides a stable starting point for distribution matching and avoids the instability caused by training the rollout generator from scratch.

    Randomized Score-Model Perturbation for DMD. A key departure from conventional DMD in our streaming pipeline is the adoption of randomized score-model perturbation, which better preserves the stochastic training behavior of Diffusion Forcing (DF) by applying independent noise to each latent token, rather than a shared global noise level. Let ẑ⁰={ẑᵢ⁰}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ be the denoised clean latents from the streaming rollout of the student model, and let k={kᵢ}, ε={εᵢ} collect the per-frame noise steps kᵢ∼p(k) and Gaussian draws εᵢ∼ℕ(0,I). We define the DF-consistent perturbation operator frame-wise as

    (𝔼ₖ[ẑ⁰;ε])ᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ ẑᵢ⁰+√1-ᾱ_kᵢ εᵢ.

    		(5)

    The perturbed sequence z̃\triangleq𝔼ₖ[ẑ⁰;ε] is fed into the score networks together with the control condition sequence c. We denote μ(·)ᵢ as the i-th frame of the score network output. With the stop-gradient operator sg(·), the DMD objective on latent i is

    L_DMDⁱ=𝔼_ẑ⁰,c,k,ε[\tfrac12∥ẑᵢ⁰-sg(ẑᵢ⁰-(μᵣₑₐₗ(z̃,c,k)ᵢ-μ_fake^φ(z̃,c,k)ᵢ))∥₂²],

    		(6)

    where μᵣₑₐₗ denotes the fixed real score network and μ_fake^φ denotes the fake score network with parameter φ. The fake score network is trained on the streaming rollout of student network with the DF loss (Eq. 4). Empirically, this randomized perturbation yields superior generation quality over vanilla shared-noise DMD. We attribute this improvement to the alignment between the independently noised inputs and DF’s pre-training distribution, which enables the teacher to provide more informative gradients for stable long-horizon streaming generation, while the decoupled noise samples for teacher and student prevent overfitting to fixed noise patterns.

    Extended-Horizon Post-Training. Long-term playability requires the model to maintain stable memory over extended interactive rollouts. In post-training, we therefore further increase the training horizon as much as possible under hardware constraints. After extensive optimization, we train the model with sequences of 512 frames, corresponding to approximately 17 seconds of gameplay, on 96GB H20 GPUs. This extended horizon substantially improves the model’s ability to preserve scene context, action-dependent dynamics, and temporal consistency over long periods, reducing the probability of drift or collapse during continuous play.

    Hybrid KV-Cache Memory for Efficient Infinite Streaming. Extending the model’s temporal memory also requires increasing the effective length of the KV cache during inference. However, directly retaining a dense KV cache over a long horizon significantly increases computation and memory consumption, resulting in higher latency and lower frame rate. This directly conflicts with the goal of playable low-latency generation. To address this issue, we propose a hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory design that preserves long-range context while keeping the number of cached tokens small.

    Specifically, we divide the KV cache into two complementary parts. The long-term memory stores sparsely sampled historical tokens, retaining global scene context and slow-changing gameplay state over an extended period. The short-term memory stores a consecutive window of the most recent tokens, preserving local temporal continuity and fine-grained motion consistency. This hybrid design enables the model to access both distant context and recent dynamics without attending to every historical token.

    In our implementation, the KV cache stores 30 tokens in total. The first 22 tokens are used as long-term memory and are selected at an interval of 5 frames, while the last 8 tokens are used as short-term memory and are stored consecutively. With this design, the model can maintain an effective memory span of up to 16 seconds with a limited number of cached tokens. Importantly, we apply the same hybrid memory policy during both post-training distillation and streaming inference. This keeps the memory layout consistent between training and testing, preventing the generator from overfitting to a dense historical context that is unavailable at inference time. One visualization can be viewed at Figure 4.

    Parallelized Teacher-Forcing Inference. For streaming generation, we adopt teacher-forcing inference rather than shifted-window denoising. Since the model always conditions on finalized clean historical frames, teacher forcing reduces the ambiguity of historical context and improves generation quality. It also avoids repeatedly denoising overlapping windows, which is important for low-latency interactive gameplay. However, a naive implementation still suffers from limited parallelism because cache writing and next-frame denoising are executed sequentially.

    To improve inference efficiency, we fuse the KV-cache writing step with the initial denoising step of the next frame. As shown in Figure 5, instead of performing three separate forward passes with batch size 1, we execute one forward pass with batch size 2 followed by one forward pass with batch size 1. This batching strategy improves hardware utilization and reduces per-frame latency without changing the teacher-forcing rollout formulation. As a result, Streaming-AAA retains the quality benefits of clean-history conditioning while achieving higher inference throughput for real-time play.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Implementation Details

    Training. The VAE is optimized using a composite loss function combining L₂ (MSE) for pixel-wise fidelity and LPIPS for perceptual quality. We use a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁵. Our diffusion model is initialized from Stable Diffusion v1.5 [35]. To reduce computational overhead, we remove the two self-attention modules at the largest spatial resolution. For temporal modeling, we incorporate Motion Modules [18] to perform attention along the temporal axis, where we reduce the number of temporal blocks from 2 to 1 to further improve efficiency. The resulting model has a total of 1.2B parameters. Training proceeds in three stages. In Stage 1, we train the model with the diffusion-forcing strategy on short video clips of 64 frames (∼2 s). In Stage 2, to enhance long-term memory, we significantly extend the training sequence length to 640 frames (∼21 s). In Stage 3, we perform post-training alignment using a self-forcing-style distillation approach [26] combined with our hybrid short-long memory design, with a training length of 512 frames (∼17 s).

    Inference. We evaluate our model on NVIDIA A800 GPUs. To maximize throughput, the diffusion model and the VAE decoder are deployed on separate GPUs for pipelined execution. We set the number of denoising steps to 2, with specific timesteps at 999 and 666. To further reduce per-frame latency, we fuse the KV-cache writing step with the first denoising step (timestep 999) into a single batched forward pass. Additionally, we apply torch.compile to accelerate the diffusion model and convert the VAE decoder to TensorRT for optimized inference.

    5.2 Qualitative Results

    In-domain visualization. The upper eleven rows of Figure 6 show in-domain generation results. Our method synthesizes scenes across different times of day, including daytime (first and second rows) and night (third row). It also faithfully reproduces the wild monsters that populate the game world: as shown in the third row, our model generates the cryo slimes commonly encountered in Genshin Impact. Beyond running on flat ground, the avatar further supports climbing and swimming. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across diverse scenarios.

    Out-of-domain visualization. The bottom two rows of Figure 6 show generation results in out-of-domain scenes, where we use FLUX [31] to replace the background with a pyramid and a busy city street, respectively. As illustrated in the second-to-last row, the pyramid retains its shape without noticeable distortion even as the avatar moves through the scene, and the content gradually transitions back into the in-domain distribution. This indicates that our method generalizes to a certain degree beyond the training distribution.

    Comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. We compare our method against HY-World1.5 [29], Lingbot [43], Matrix Game 3.0 [38], and YUME [33] on Genshin Impact. As shown in Figure 7, our method surpasses all competing approaches in generation quality. In the first dusk scene, HY-World1.5 produces repeated shadow patterns that substantially degrade the visual result. Lingbot develops black blotchy artifacts after roughly 30 s of rollout. Matrix Game 3.0 renders both cases with a slightly overexposed appearance. YUME drifts rapidly from the cartoon style of the source domain toward photorealism, synthesizing realistic human bodies and washing the overall palette out to gray. In contrast, our method sustains high-quality generation throughout, without quality degradation as the rollout extends, which confirms the effectiveness of our design.

    Infinite-length gameplay. Our method is capable of supporting infinite-length gameplay. In our comparison with state-of-the-art approaches, we observe that most existing methods struggle to sustain long-horizon generation—typically, their outputs collapse within the first 30 seconds. In contrast, our method exhibits no signs of visual collapse even after one minute of continuous generation. To further verify the infinite-length gameplay capability of our method, we conduct a stress test by playing continuously for one hour. As shown in Figure 8, throughout the entire hour of gameplay, our method neither encounters catastrophic collapse that halts generation nor suffers from gradual visual degradation as the play duration extends. These results clearly demonstrate the infinite-length gameplay capability of our approach.

    5.3 Quantitative Results

    Following the protocol of Section 5, we evaluate all methods with VBench [27, 28, 57] in custom_input mode on subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, and imaging quality, and report in Table 2 the scores averaged over both evaluation titles.

    As shown in Table 2, our method outperforms all competing approaches—HY-World1.5 [29], Lingbot [43], Matrix Game 3.0 [38], and YUME [33]—on subject consistency, background consistency, and imaging quality, and leads by a clear margin on the average score. Compared with HY-World1.5, we are on par on subject consistency and background consistency, but substantially better on imaging quality (0.677 vs. 0.589). Figure 7 explains the gap: beyond roughly 30 s of rollout HY-World1.5 develops pronounced repetitive patterns, which severely hurt imaging quality. Our motion smoothness is marginally lower than that of the baselines. A plausible explanation is that the baselines move very slowly, so their rollouts consist of comparatively gentle frame-to-frame changes, whereas our rollouts contain fast locomotion and abrupt events such as jumping off a cliff, which naturally depress this metric. Our advantage is even more pronounced in efficiency: we run about 20× faster than HY-World1.5 while cutting latency by more than 98%, and we do so at 1080p rather than 480p–720p. Taken together, these results show that our method dominates existing state-of-the-art approaches in both generation quality and inference efficiency.

    5.4 Ablation Study

    Figure 9 presents our ablation study, comparing the pre-trained model against post-training with a short and an extended training horizon.

    Normal scenes. Case 1 and Case 2 report results from in-domain and out-of-domain starting frames, respectively. The pre-trained model degenerates within the first 5 s of rollout, with the generated content collapsing toward a monotonous appearance, whereas both post-trained models stay stable in either case. Post-training therefore yields a substantial quality gain within our framework.

    Static scenes. When the avatar is not moved, the pre-trained model already breaks down after 20 s, and post-training with a short horizon becomes blurry after 60 s. Only the extended-horizon variant preserves a sharp and stable scene throughout.

    Memory. We rotate the camera away and then turn back to the original viewpoint. With a short post-training horizon, the scene is already slightly altered after 4 s and differs substantially after 8 s; with the extended training horizon and longer training, it remains essentially unchanged even after 8 s. These comparisons show that both extending the post-training horizon and increasing training length are necessary to confer markedly stronger resistance to collapse in static scenes and a genuine degree of memory.

    5.5 Efficiency and Latency Analysis

    Frame rate and action-to-pixel latency are critical to interactive experience. End-to-end latency comprises the diffusion model (93 ms on an A800) and the VAE decoder (58 ms). Since player actions may arrive mid-execution, we budget an expected extra half-step of diffusion, giving 93×1.5+58≈198 ms; this is the theoretical computation latency, excluding network transmission and codec overhead. Deploying the diffusion model and VAE decoder on separate GPUs for pipelined execution further yields 1000/93×4≈43 fps, enabling real-time interactive gameplay. Relative to existing streaming systems, which operate at 480p–720p with single-digit frame rates and multi-second latency, our system delivers 1080p output at 43 fps with 198 ms latency; the detailed comparison is reported in Table 2.

    6 Conclusion

    We have presented Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite AAA game video generation framework that achieves high-resolution (1080p), high-frame-rate (∼43 fps), and low-latency (∼200 ms) streaming gameplay synthesis. Our framework integrates an efficient high-resolution video VAE with pixel-shuffle decoding, a factorized UNet-based latent diffusion model with unified multi-modal conditioning, and a progressive training pipeline spanning short-range dynamics modeling, long-context pre-training, and post-training alignment via distribution matching distillation. The proposed hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory, combined with parallelized teacher-forcing inference, enables stable infinite-horizon generation while maintaining real-time interactivity. Experiments on Genshin Impact demonstrate that Streaming-AAA produces visually rich and temporally consistent gameplay across diverse environments, weather conditions, and character actions.

    Limitations. Our current approach is primarily designed and optimized for playability within a specific game title. The model is trained on domain-specific data from a single game, and its generalization to unseen game environments, art styles, or game mechanics remains limited. Extending the framework to a universal game generation model that handles diverse titles without per-game fine-tuning is an important open challenge.

    Future Work. Looking ahead, we believe the core techniques developed in Streaming-AAA—efficient high-resolution VAE, controllable streaming diffusion, and long-horizon memory—can serve as building blocks for a broader range of downstream applications beyond playable generation. For instance, the framework could be adapted for game-specific visual enhancement, where the model upscales or refines low-quality rendered frames into high-fidelity outputs in real time. We hope that Streaming-AAA provides a solid foundation toward bridging generative video models and practical interactive entertainment systems.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：离真正可玩还差得远，因为画质、帧率与交互延迟三者无法同时满足。

要点：

  • 目标定得很明确：可控流式视频生成是通向交互式游戏模拟的一条路，但现有方法**离实用还有距离**
  • 失败模式是三者无法兼得：往往不能同时达到**高视觉保真度、高帧率与低交互延迟**，结果是响应迟钝、体验下降
  • Streaming-AAA 提出一种新范式，目标是对 AAA 级画质内容做**可控的无限长生成**

为什么值得看：这是把「生成式画面能不能进游戏」的验收标准写成了三项硬指标。任何做实时生成内容的团队都可以直接拿这三项对照自己的方案——缺哪一条，就不能叫可玩。

中文摘要：可控的流式视频生成被视为通往交互式游戏模拟的一条路径，但作者指出现有方法离实用还有明显距离：它们往往无法同时满足高视觉保真度、高帧率与低交互延迟这三项要求，结果就是响应迟钝、体验退化。Streaming-AAA 因此提出一种新的范式，目标是实现 AAA 级画质内容的可控无限长生成。它的价值在于把「生成式画面能不能进游戏」这件事写成了三项可验收的硬指标——缺任何一条，都谈不上可玩。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

Streaming-AAA:
Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at
High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency

Abstract

Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

1 Introduction

Interactive game simulation has become an increasingly important application of generative video models, where the system must synthesize future visual observations conditioned on user controls in a streaming manner [20, 1, 39, 25, 33]. Unlike offline video generation, playable game generation imposes simultaneous requirements on visual fidelity, temporal consistency, frame rate, and interaction latency. These requirements are especially stringent for AAA-level games, where high-resolution rendering, fast motion, complex scenes, and long-horizon interactions are all essential to the user experience. In this work, we primarily target Genshin Impact, a widely played open-world action RPG whose environments are familiar enough that generation quality is easy to judge.

Despite recent progress in controllable video generation and world models [55, 4, 33, 23, 40, 50, 29], existing streaming generation systems remain far from practical gameplay. Many approaches can produce visually plausible short clips, but their quality degrades over long horizons. Others support control or interaction but operate at low resolution, low frame rate, or high latency, making the generated experience difficult to play. As a result, current methods do not jointly satisfy the key requirements of high-fidelity 1080p generation, real-time frame rates, low end-to-end latency, and stable infinite interaction.

We present Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite streaming AAA game video generation framework designed for high-resolution, high-frame-rate, and low-latency gameplay. Streaming-AAA first introduces an efficient high-resolution video VAE that compresses 1080p gameplay frames into compact spatio-temporal latents and reconstructs high-fidelity frames with low decoding overhead. On top of this representation, we build a UNet-based latent diffusion model with factorized spatial, temporal, and cross-attention modules, enabling efficient visual modeling, temporal reasoning, and multi-modal control. To support long-horizon streaming generation, we further adopt long-context pre-training, post-training alignment with distribution matching distillation, and a hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory. These designs allow Streaming-AAA to preserve long-range consistency while maintaining low interaction latency during real-time inference.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose Streaming-AAA, the first controllable infinite-horizon AAA game video generation framework that simultaneously delivers high visual fidelity, real-time throughput (43FPS at 1080p), ultra-low end-to-end latency (198ms), and stable long-rollout consistency. To our knowledge, this is the first system to achieve production-grade real-time gameplay generation at this specification.

  • •

    At its core, Streaming-AAA comprises a purpose-built causal video VAE and a factorized 3D-UNet latent diffusion backbone. The VAE compresses raw pixel inputs by 16 × spatially into compact latent representations, drastically reducing inference overhead. The 3D-UNet decouples spatial texture modeling, temporal dynamics learning, and conditional control via cross attention modules cutting computational cost, while supporting flexible integration of rich frame-aligned conditioning signals (e.g., agent actions, weather states).

  • •

    We establish a two-stage pre/post-training paradigm tailored for unbounded autoregressive streaming. In pre-training, we adopt a per-frame independent noise scheduling strategy (i.e., Diffusion Forcing) under the DDPM framework, which encodes the inductive bias of growing uncertainty for distant temporal horizons to match open-world evolution dynamics. In post-training, we apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) to align the model with 2-step generation, which further boosts rollout stability and temporal consistency without sacrificing real-time performance.

    • 2 Related Works

    2.1 Video Generation Models

    Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation. Large-scale text-to-video diffusion models [19, 17, 37, 30, 42, 45, 56, 12, 21, 34, 41, 44] have demonstrated impressive visual quality and diversity, producing photorealistic short clips from textual descriptions. However, these models typically require minutes of inference time to generate only a few seconds of video, and most of them lack the ability to produce arbitrarily long sequences in a streaming fashion.

    To address the long-horizon limitation, several methods[26, 13, 11, 49, 9, 14, 58] attempt to retrofit pre-trained text-to-video models for streaming generation. Self-Forcing [26] bridges the train-test gap in autoregressive video diffusion by aligning the training distribution with the streaming rollout. Context Forcing [11] introduces long-context conditioning to maintain consistency across extended autoregressive generation. LongLive [49] targets real-time interactive long video generation by combining efficient architectures with streaming inference. Alternatively, Diffusion Forcing [9] equips the model with streaming capability directly during pre-training by combining next-token prediction with full-sequence diffusion. Despite these advances, achieving real-time streaming inference at high resolution remains a significant challenge for playable game generation.

    2.2 World Models

    World models aim to learn predictive representations of environments for planning and interaction. Existing approaches fall into two categories.

    The first is based on 3D reconstruction [53, 54, 32], which builds explicit representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting for real-time exploration. While achieving strong real-time performance, these methods produce mostly static worlds with limited interactivity.

    The second leverages video generation for world simulation. Early works [5, 6, 7, 15] demonstrate that video diffusion models can serve as world simulators. More recently, a growing body of research [20, 2, 8, 25, 1, 39, 47, 46, 10, 16, 22, 48, 36] has explored interactive and controllable world models, addressing challenges such as long-horizon memory, action conditioning, and real-time streaming. However, none of these methods simultaneously achieve high resolution (1080p), high frame rate, and low interaction latency—all essential for AAA-level playable game generation. Our work addresses this gap by jointly optimizing visual fidelity, streaming efficiency, and interactive responsiveness within a unified framework.

    3 Dataset Construction

    Modern AAA video games represent a convergence of cutting-edge graphics technologies, providing an almost inexhaustible source of high-fidelity visual data. Specifically, these environments feature:

  • •

    Geometrically Diverse Landscapes: Expansive terrains encompassing natural formations (mountains, rivers, oceans, forests, grassland) and intricate man-made architectures.

  • •

    Complex Human-Scene Interactions: Rich agent behaviors such as locomotion across uneven terrain, climbing trees, and swimming in dynamic fluid simulations.

  • •

    Sophisticated Lighting Conditions: Dramatic variations in illumination, including dawn, noon, and night cycles, often coupled with advanced effects like ray-traced global illumination.

  • •

    Realistic Physical Dynamics: Natural phenomena such as wind-induced vegetation swaying (wind-sway effects) and physically-based object interactions.

    • To train a generative model capable of synthesizing photorealistic videos with such intricate spatio-temporal details, it is imperative to expose the model to a massive and highly diverse dataset that encapsulates these multifaceted distributions. However, manual gameplay recording is labor-intensive and suffers from limited scalability, making it infeasible to cover the vast state space of modern AAA titles.

    To bridge this gap, we design an automated parallel data acquisition system, termed Automated Data Collection System to efficiently harvest these rich visual cues.

    3.1 Automated Data Collection System (ADCS)

    As illustrated in Figure 2, the proposed Automated Data Collection System (ADCS) comprises three integral components: an AI Agent Server, a Distributed Render Cluster, and a Centralized Storage Backend.

    AI Agent Server and Control Logic. The AI Agent Server acts as the control center, orchestrating in-game agents in Distributed Render Cluster via the LAN. It dispatches low-level actions to each PC game instance. To ensure comprehensive environmental coverage, we implement an autonomous navigation policy that samples actions to sufficiently cover the virtual terrains.

    Distributed Render Cluster. The cluster consists of a pool of high-end workstations executing game instances in parallel. Each node captures raw gameplay at 30 FPS and 1080p resolution using OBS Studio, preserving fine-grained motion details essential for learning physical dynamics and temporal coherence. Frame-aligned agent actions and real-time frame rate are recorded alongside the video stream. Weather and time-of-day are not read from the game; instead, they are estimated by a model (i.e., open-source Qwen-VL [3]) from the captured frames. Each recording task lasts 60 seconds. And when each task ends, the recorded video along with its annotations will be upload to the Centralized Storage Backend.

    Centralized Storage Backend. The backend serves as the unified data hub, ingesting asynchronously uploaded packages from all render nodes upon completion of each capture session. Each upload contains synchronized pairs of high-fidelity gameplay videos and their corresponding metadata streams extracted by the render cluster. The curated dataset is directly accessible to the training cluster for distributed training.

    Scalability and Throughput. The tight integration of the three components underpins the pipeline’s exceptional efficiency. By leveraging parallel execution across the render cluster and high-throughput asynchronous data ingestion at the storage backend, the system collects over 5 million frames daily. Within days of acquisition cycle, we successfully captured footage spanning approximately 5 KM2 of in-game terrain. This automated infrastructure ensures a steady supply of high-quality, curated data, enabling the model to effectively learn the complex distributions inherent in AAA game environments.

    3.2 Conquering Huge Map with ADCS

    Modern AAA titles are characterized by their sheer geographical scale, often featuring seamless open worlds spanning square kilometers (KM2). Naïvely employing a sequential, single-agent collection strategy (i.e., traversing the map linearly) presents a significant bottleneck: the data acquisition rate is fundamentally constrained by the agent’s movement speed and loading times. This results in prohibitively low efficiency and insufficient spatial data density, failing to meet the stringent demands of training high-fidelity video world models which require dense observations of environmental geometry and dynamics.

    To address this challenge, we leverage our proposed ADCS to achieve high-density spatial coverage. Our core strategy involves decoupling spatial navigation from data capture through parallelization and teleportation.

    Parallel Spatial Sampling Strategy. To ensure comprehensive coverage and high sampling density across expansive virtual environments, we employ a parallel spatial sampling strategy. First, we partition the game map with the teleportation waypoints in the map.

    Rather than relying on conventional pathfinding to traverse the terrain sequentially—which is time-prohibitive for large-scale maps—we leverage the game’s built-in teleportation waypoint. Specifically, the AI Agent Server dispatches specific teleportation waypoint targets to the Distributed Render Cluster, routing the in-game avatars to the designated waypoints.

    This approach allows us to distribute data collection tasks across multiple compute nodes in parallel. Each client is assigned a subset of the waypoints, recording high-frame-rate footage locally upon arrival. By decoupling spatial navigation from data capture, our strategy significantly accelerates the acquisition process and enhances the spatial density of the dataset. Consequently, the system can efficiently survey approximately 5 KM2 of terrain in several days, capturing fine-grained environmental details without the computational overhead of simulating long-distance traversal.

    3.3 Data Statistics

    Leveraging our proposed ADCS and the parallel spatial sampling strategy, we construct a large-scale, high-fidelity dataset that captures the rich visual and interactive complexity of modern AAA games. In total, we collect approximately 22,000 videos, each lasting 1 minute and recorded at 30 fps, aggregating to approximately 40 million frames. All footage is recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080, ensuring fine-grained spatial and temporal details suitable for high-capacity video generation models.

    Beyond raw pixel data, our collection pipeline provides frame-aligned annotations that are typically unavailable in real-world datasets. Specifically, each frame is annotated with:

  • •

    Agent Actions: Control signals ("W", "A", "S", "D" to move, ↑↓←→ to turn, "Space" to jump), recorded directly from the game agent.

  • •

    Environmental Context: Weather conditions and diurnal lighting cycles (time-of-day), which are estimated by a vision-language model (Qwen-VL [3]) rather than read from the game engine.

    • The data acquired through our ADCS framework exhibits richness across three distinct dimensions, each contributing to the overall fidelity and utility for training high-capacity video generation models.

    1. High-Fidelity Visual Stream. All videos are recorded at a resolution of 1920×1080 with a frame rate of 30 fps. This high-resolution, high-frame-rate capture ensures access to fine-grained visual details and temporally coherent motion dynamics—essential for modeling complex scene evolution and object interactions.

    2. Rich Metadata Annotations. Each frame is accompanied by annotations, including recorded control signals and model-estimated environmental context (weather and time-of-day). These annotations enable fine-grained controllability during training and inference, allowing the model to condition its output on specific physical or semantic states.

    3. Broad Coverage with High Density. Through parallelized spatial sampling, we achieve extensive geographic coverage (5 KM2) while maintaining high sample density. This combination ensures exposure to a diverse array of content including natural scenery and man-made architectures, enhancing the generalizability of learned representations.

    These annotations facilitate a wide range of downstream tasks, from conditional video synthesis to world model training that requires strict physical and geometric consistency. Statistics of the dataset are summarized in Table 1.

    4 Method

    4.1 Problem Formulation

    We formulate controllable AAA game video generation as an infinite streaming prediction problem. Given previous frames x_1:t, user controls a_1:t+k, and a compact memory state mₜ, the model predicts the next video segment:

    p_θ(x_t+1:t+k|x_1:t,a_1:t+k,mₜ).

    		(1)

    Unlike offline video generation, this task requires causal generation, faithful response to user inputs, and long-horizon stability under strict constraints on resolution, frame rate, and interaction latency.

    4.2 Overview of Streaming-AAA

    We propose Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite AAA game video generation framework for real-time gameplay. Streaming-AAA consists of three key components. First, an efficient high-resolution video VAE compresses 1080p frames into compact spatio-temporal latents and decodes them with low overhead. Second, a UNet-based latent diffusion model generates future video latents conditioned on player controls and historical memory. Third, long-context pre-training, post-training alignment, and hybrid KV-cache memory improve long-term consistency and reduce inference latency. Together, these designs enable high-fidelity, controllable, and low-latency streaming generation.

    4.3 Efficient High-Resolution Video VAE

    High-resolution decoding is a major bottleneck for real-time game video generation. We therefore redesign the VAE architecture to improve decoding efficiency while preserving fine visual details. The encoder compresses 1080p gameplay frames into compact spatiotemporal latents, and the decoder reconstructs high-fidelity frames with reduced computational overhead. This design allows the diffusion model to operate in latent space while enabling fast reconstruction of AAA-quality game visuals during streaming inference.

    To bridge the gap between high-resolution spatial modeling and temporal consistency, we propose an Enhanced VAE model design. Our architecture is designed to efficiently handle ultra-high-definition inputs (1792×1024) while maintaining a manageable latent space dimension with high-frequency details.

    Architecture Design. We configure an overall temporal-spatial compression factor of 4×16×16 relative to the input resolution. The encoder maps the input video clip x∈ℝ^(4N+1)×H×W×3 to a latent representation z∈ℝ^(N+1)×H/16×W/16×C, which is compatible for both single frame and multi-frame compression and decoding, similar to Wan-series. A key distinction of our model lies in the decoder’s upsampling pipeline. Unlike traditional methods relying solely on interpolation or transposed convolutions, we introduce an additional Pixel Shuffle layer at the tail of the decoding process. Specifically, the decoder consists of three sequential Conv3D upsampling blocks followed by a Pixel Shuffle operation for efficient sub-pixel upsampling in the largest upsample stage. This design mitigates checkerboard artifacts commonly induced by large-stride deconvolutions and preserves fine-grained texture details.

    Multi-Stage Curriculum Training. Training a VAE from scratch for high-resolution video is inherently unstable. To address this, we employ a three-stage curriculum learning strategy for faster convergence:

  • •

    Stage 1 (Spatial Initialization): We train the model on static images at 256×256 resolution to stabilize the reconstruction of basic color distributions and edges.

  • •

    Stage 2 (Temporal Extension): We extend the model to video data using 256×256 patches. Here, the model processes multiple frames within a clip to learn short-term temporal coherence.

  • •

    Stage 3 (Native Resolution): Finally, we fine-tune the model on full-resolution 1792×1024 videos to adapt to the aspect ratio and scale of real-world high-definition content.

    • Rolling Frame Prediction. For multi-frame training, we adopt a rolling prediction mechanism. Given a sequence of length T, the model predicts frames indexed as 4n+1 (n≥0). To balance computational cost and gradient flow, we selectively apply gradients only to the last 1 or 4 predicted frames of each sequence, preventing error accumulation in long sequences while maintaining temporal smoothness.

    4.4 Redesigning UNet-based Video Diffusion Models

    Leveraging the compact latent space provided by our VAE, we construct a 3D UNet-based diffusion model for high-fidelity video synthesis. The network follows a symmetric encoder-decoder structure, performing three downsampling and three upsampling operations, with the bottleneck resolution reduced to 1/8 of the input.

    Factorized Spatio-Temporal Blocks. To mitigate the computational overhead of dense 3D operations, each stage of the UNet is composed of three specialized modules:

  • •

    Spatial Module: Consisting primarily of convolutional layers, this module focuses on modeling intra-frame textures and structural details, ensuring high visual fidelity.

  • •

    Cross-Attention Module: Also constructed with Transformer layers, this module serves as the conditioning interface. It projects external signals into the latent space via cross-attention mechanisms in causal manner. This design allows the model to flexibly incorporate diverse control signals, such as action, weather and time-of-day conditions, enabling fine-grained controllability over the generation process.

  • •

    Temporal Module with Hybrid KV-Cache Memory: Built upon Transformer blocks, this module operates along the temporal axis to capture the dynamic evolution of each latent pixel across frames in causal manner, ensuring motion consistency. We also implement a Hybrid KV-Cache Memory mechanism. Once a frame is finalized, its corresponding keys and values in the self-attention layers are stored in memory. For subsequent frames, the model retrieves these cached key-value (KV) pairs as tokens reference instead of recomputing them, significantly reducing the computational complexity from O(T²) to O(T) per step, where T is the sequence length. We select both specific long-term and short-term KV-tokens to enhance long-term temporal consistency within only 30 tokens.

    • This factorized architecture effectively decouples spatial modeling, temporal dynamics, and conditional control, significantly reducing the complexity compared to full spatio-temporal attention while enhancing generalization across various scenarios.

    Unified Multi-Modal Conditioning. To handle heterogeneous inputs, we adopt a unified conditioning scheme. Each condition type (e.g., action, weather, time, frame-rate) is first processed by a dedicated embedding layer and tokenized into a fixed-dimensional vector. Subsequently, these tokens are concatenated into a unified condition sequence. This sequence is then injected into the model through the Cross-Attention modules at each stage. This design not only standardizes the input interface for various modalities but also allows the model to selectively attend to relevant conditions during different stages of denoising.

    Training and Convergence. By operating within the compact latent space provided by our VAE, the diffusion model achieves stable convergence. The efficient design ensures a high inference throughput, making it suitable for practical applications requiring multi-conditional control.

    4.5 Modeling Long-horizon Uncertainty with Diffusion-forcing Pre-training

    We adopt the Diffusion Forcing (DF) [9] paradigm in the pretraining stage of our streaming-AAA model pretraining, whose core innovation of per-frame independent noise scheduling aligns naturally with the requirements of long-horizon, controllable world simulation. Instead of enforcing a globally shared noise level across all frames, DF samples an independent noise step kᵢ∼p(k) (e.g., uniform or logit-normal distribution over the DDPM [24] timestep range [0,K]) for each frame i, where the per-frame noised latent follows the standard DDPM forward formulation:

    zᵢ^kᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ·zᵢ⁰+√1-ᾱ_kᵢ·εᵢ, εᵢ∼ℕ(0,I),

    		(2)

    with zᵢ⁰ denoting the clean VAE-encoded frame latent, and ᾱ_kᵢ=∏ₛ₌₁^kᵢ(1-βₛ) representing the cumulative product of noise retention coefficients under a predefined DDPM schedule (e.g., cosine schedule), where βₛ∈(0,1) is the pre-defined noise addition ratio at step s. Stacking these per-frame noised latents forms a 2D noise schedule matrix that encodes the inductive bias of growing uncertainty for farther temporal horizons—matching the intrinsic causal dynamics of open-world physical evolution. This design, combined with velocity (v-)prediction, enables stable arbitrary-length rollouts. Crucially, the per-frame noise assignment is natively compatible with the rich, frame-aligned metadata, enabling frame-level acute dynamic variation and transition modeling.

    For diffusion training, we opt for v-prediction instead of conventional ε-prediction. The velocity vᵢ for frame i is defined as the linear combination of the clean latent and noise term in the forward process:

    vᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ·εᵢ-√1-ᾱ_kᵢ·zᵢ⁰,

    		(3)

    Let zᵏ\triangleq{zᵢ^kᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ be the whole noised latent sequence, k={kᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ the per-frame noise steps, and c the control condition sequence (aggregating action, weather, time, and frame-rate signals). We denote f(·)ᵢ as the i-th frame of its output, and optimize the per-frame v-prediction objective:

    L_DF=𝔼_{zᵢ⁰},c,k,{vᵢ} 1/T∑ᵢ₌₁ᵀ∥f (zᵏ,c,k)ᵢ-vᵢ∥₂²,

    		(4)

    where T is the sequence length. This contrasts with the unified-timestep v-prediction loss that enforces a single noise level t for all frames. The per-frame independent (zᵢ^kᵢ,kᵢ,vᵢ) pairs act as an implicit curriculum, stabilizing pretraining on our heterogeneous AAA dataset and enabling continuous post-training distributions for infinite rollouts. Empirically, v-prediction mitigates error accumulation during long-horizon generation compared to ε-prediction, further reinforcing the stability of our streaming inference pipeline.

    Stage 1: Short-range Dynamics Modeling. In the initial phase, we focus on stabilizing the foundational visual and short-term motion patterns. The model is trained on short video clips consisting of 64 frames. This shorter sequence length allows for larger batch sizes and faster convergence, enabling the model to efficiently learn low-level textures, spatial structures, and plausible short-term dynamics without the interference of long-range dependencies. We train the model for 200 epochs in this stage.

    Stage 2: Long-range Contextual Understanding. Subsequently, we extend the temporal context to capture long-term consistency and memory. We increase the input sequence length from 64 to 640 frames (∼21 seconds of video content). This extension forces the Temporal Modules and Cross-Attention mechanisms to reason over extended horizons, mitigating temporal drift and maintaining spatial stability across distant frames. Although computationally intensive, training for 20 epochs on this extended context is sufficient to adapt the model from short-term generation to long-form video synthesis.

    4.6 Post-Training Alignment for Streaming Inference

    As illustrated in Figure 3, during streaming inference the model conditions on clean historical frames and control signals to generate future latents.
