Although diffusion-forcing pre-training already equips the model with an initial ability for streaming generation, there remains a non-negligible mismatch between pre-training and practical inference. During diffusion-forcing training, each latent token is independently assigned a random noise level and the model learns to denoise under a wide range of partially corrupted historical contexts. This large training space improves the model’s generative capacity and enables it to exploit ambiguous historical information. In actual streaming inference, however, we adopt a teacher-forcing-style rollout, where historical frames are clean observations with zero noise. Therefore, inference only corresponds to a restricted subset of the diffusion-forcing training distribution, which can lead to degraded generation quality and weaker temporal consistency.

    To reduce this gap, we further align the model with its inference-time behavior through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [51, 52]. Inspired by the second stage of self-forcing distillation [26], we optimize the generator to directly learn how to generate future latent tokens under fixed denoising timesteps and clean historical contexts. Unlike standard self-forcing and DMD settings, our pre-trained model already supports self-rollout after diffusion-forcing pre-training. We therefore initialize the generator, the real score model, and the fake score model from the same pre-trained checkpoint. This initialization provides a stable starting point for distribution matching and avoids the instability caused by training the rollout generator from scratch.

    Randomized Score-Model Perturbation for DMD. A key departure from conventional DMD in our streaming pipeline is the adoption of randomized score-model perturbation, which better preserves the stochastic training behavior of Diffusion Forcing (DF) by applying independent noise to each latent token, rather than a shared global noise level. Let ẑ⁰={ẑᵢ⁰}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ be the denoised clean latents from the streaming rollout of the student model, and let k={kᵢ}, ε={εᵢ} collect the per-frame noise steps kᵢ∼p(k) and Gaussian draws εᵢ∼ℕ(0,I). We define the DF-consistent perturbation operator frame-wise as

    (𝔼ₖ[ẑ⁰;ε])ᵢ=√ᾱ_kᵢ ẑᵢ⁰+√1-ᾱ_kᵢ εᵢ.

    		(5)

    The perturbed sequence z̃\triangleq𝔼ₖ[ẑ⁰;ε] is fed into the score networks together with the control condition sequence c. We denote μ(·)ᵢ as the i-th frame of the score network output. With the stop-gradient operator sg(·), the DMD objective on latent i is

    L_DMDⁱ=𝔼_ẑ⁰,c,k,ε[\tfrac12∥ẑᵢ⁰-sg(ẑᵢ⁰-(μᵣₑₐₗ(z̃,c,k)ᵢ-μ_fake^φ(z̃,c,k)ᵢ))∥₂²],

    		(6)

    where μᵣₑₐₗ denotes the fixed real score network and μ_fake^φ denotes the fake score network with parameter φ. The fake score network is trained on the streaming rollout of student network with the DF loss (Eq. 4). Empirically, this randomized perturbation yields superior generation quality over vanilla shared-noise DMD. We attribute this improvement to the alignment between the independently noised inputs and DF’s pre-training distribution, which enables the teacher to provide more informative gradients for stable long-horizon streaming generation, while the decoupled noise samples for teacher and student prevent overfitting to fixed noise patterns.

    Extended-Horizon Post-Training. Long-term playability requires the model to maintain stable memory over extended interactive rollouts. In post-training, we therefore further increase the training horizon as much as possible under hardware constraints. After extensive optimization, we train the model with sequences of 512 frames, corresponding to approximately 17 seconds of gameplay, on 96GB H20 GPUs. This extended horizon substantially improves the model’s ability to preserve scene context, action-dependent dynamics, and temporal consistency over long periods, reducing the probability of drift or collapse during continuous play.

    Hybrid KV-Cache Memory for Efficient Infinite Streaming. Extending the model’s temporal memory also requires increasing the effective length of the KV cache during inference. However, directly retaining a dense KV cache over a long horizon significantly increases computation and memory consumption, resulting in higher latency and lower frame rate. This directly conflicts with the goal of playable low-latency generation. To address this issue, we propose a hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory design that preserves long-range context while keeping the number of cached tokens small.

    Specifically, we divide the KV cache into two complementary parts. The long-term memory stores sparsely sampled historical tokens, retaining global scene context and slow-changing gameplay state over an extended period. The short-term memory stores a consecutive window of the most recent tokens, preserving local temporal continuity and fine-grained motion consistency. This hybrid design enables the model to access both distant context and recent dynamics without attending to every historical token.

    In our implementation, the KV cache stores 30 tokens in total. The first 22 tokens are used as long-term memory and are selected at an interval of 5 frames, while the last 8 tokens are used as short-term memory and are stored consecutively. With this design, the model can maintain an effective memory span of up to 16 seconds with a limited number of cached tokens. Importantly, we apply the same hybrid memory policy during both post-training distillation and streaming inference. This keeps the memory layout consistent between training and testing, preventing the generator from overfitting to a dense historical context that is unavailable at inference time. One visualization can be viewed at Figure 4.

    Parallelized Teacher-Forcing Inference. For streaming generation, we adopt teacher-forcing inference rather than shifted-window denoising. Since the model always conditions on finalized clean historical frames, teacher forcing reduces the ambiguity of historical context and improves generation quality. It also avoids repeatedly denoising overlapping windows, which is important for low-latency interactive gameplay. However, a naive implementation still suffers from limited parallelism because cache writing and next-frame denoising are executed sequentially.

    To improve inference efficiency, we fuse the KV-cache writing step with the initial denoising step of the next frame. As shown in Figure 5, instead of performing three separate forward passes with batch size 1, we execute one forward pass with batch size 2 followed by one forward pass with batch size 1. This batching strategy improves hardware utilization and reduces per-frame latency without changing the teacher-forcing rollout formulation. As a result, Streaming-AAA retains the quality benefits of clean-history conditioning while achieving higher inference throughput for real-time play.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Implementation Details

    Training. The VAE is optimized using a composite loss function combining L₂ (MSE) for pixel-wise fidelity and LPIPS for perceptual quality. We use a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁵. Our diffusion model is initialized from Stable Diffusion v1.5 [35]. To reduce computational overhead, we remove the two self-attention modules at the largest spatial resolution. For temporal modeling, we incorporate Motion Modules [18] to perform attention along the temporal axis, where we reduce the number of temporal blocks from 2 to 1 to further improve efficiency. The resulting model has a total of 1.2B parameters. Training proceeds in three stages. In Stage 1, we train the model with the diffusion-forcing strategy on short video clips of 64 frames (∼2 s). In Stage 2, to enhance long-term memory, we significantly extend the training sequence length to 640 frames (∼21 s). In Stage 3, we perform post-training alignment using a self-forcing-style distillation approach [26] combined with our hybrid short-long memory design, with a training length of 512 frames (∼17 s).

    Inference. We evaluate our model on NVIDIA A800 GPUs. To maximize throughput, the diffusion model and the VAE decoder are deployed on separate GPUs for pipelined execution. We set the number of denoising steps to 2, with specific timesteps at 999 and 666. To further reduce per-frame latency, we fuse the KV-cache writing step with the first denoising step (timestep 999) into a single batched forward pass. Additionally, we apply torch.compile to accelerate the diffusion model and convert the VAE decoder to TensorRT for optimized inference.

    5.2 Qualitative Results

    In-domain visualization. The upper eleven rows of Figure 6 show in-domain generation results. Our method synthesizes scenes across different times of day, including daytime (first and second rows) and night (third row). It also faithfully reproduces the wild monsters that populate the game world: as shown in the third row, our model generates the cryo slimes commonly encountered in Genshin Impact. Beyond running on flat ground, the avatar further supports climbing and swimming. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across diverse scenarios.

    Out-of-domain visualization. The bottom two rows of Figure 6 show generation results in out-of-domain scenes, where we use FLUX [31] to replace the background with a pyramid and a busy city street, respectively. As illustrated in the second-to-last row, the pyramid retains its shape without noticeable distortion even as the avatar moves through the scene, and the content gradually transitions back into the in-domain distribution. This indicates that our method generalizes to a certain degree beyond the training distribution.

    Comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. We compare our method against HY-World1.5 [29], Lingbot [43], Matrix Game 3.0 [38], and YUME [33] on Genshin Impact. As shown in Figure 7, our method surpasses all competing approaches in generation quality. In the first dusk scene, HY-World1.5 produces repeated shadow patterns that substantially degrade the visual result. Lingbot develops black blotchy artifacts after roughly 30 s of rollout. Matrix Game 3.0 renders both cases with a slightly overexposed appearance. YUME drifts rapidly from the cartoon style of the source domain toward photorealism, synthesizing realistic human bodies and washing the overall palette out to gray. In contrast, our method sustains high-quality generation throughout, without quality degradation as the rollout extends, which confirms the effectiveness of our design.

    Infinite-length gameplay. Our method is capable of supporting infinite-length gameplay. In our comparison with state-of-the-art approaches, we observe that most existing methods struggle to sustain long-horizon generation—typically, their outputs collapse within the first 30 seconds. In contrast, our method exhibits no signs of visual collapse even after one minute of continuous generation. To further verify the infinite-length gameplay capability of our method, we conduct a stress test by playing continuously for one hour. As shown in Figure 8, throughout the entire hour of gameplay, our method neither encounters catastrophic collapse that halts generation nor suffers from gradual visual degradation as the play duration extends. These results clearly demonstrate the infinite-length gameplay capability of our approach.

    5.3 Quantitative Results

    Following the protocol of Section 5, we evaluate all methods with VBench [27, 28, 57] in custom_input mode on subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, and imaging quality, and report in Table 2 the scores averaged over both evaluation titles.

    As shown in Table 2, our method outperforms all competing approaches—HY-World1.5 [29], Lingbot [43], Matrix Game 3.0 [38], and YUME [33]—on subject consistency, background consistency, and imaging quality, and leads by a clear margin on the average score. Compared with HY-World1.5, we are on par on subject consistency and background consistency, but substantially better on imaging quality (0.677 vs. 0.589). Figure 7 explains the gap: beyond roughly 30 s of rollout HY-World1.5 develops pronounced repetitive patterns, which severely hurt imaging quality. Our motion smoothness is marginally lower than that of the baselines. A plausible explanation is that the baselines move very slowly, so their rollouts consist of comparatively gentle frame-to-frame changes, whereas our rollouts contain fast locomotion and abrupt events such as jumping off a cliff, which naturally depress this metric. Our advantage is even more pronounced in efficiency: we run about 20× faster than HY-World1.5 while cutting latency by more than 98%, and we do so at 1080p rather than 480p–720p. Taken together, these results show that our method dominates existing state-of-the-art approaches in both generation quality and inference efficiency.

    5.4 Ablation Study

    Figure 9 presents our ablation study, comparing the pre-trained model against post-training with a short and an extended training horizon.

    Normal scenes. Case 1 and Case 2 report results from in-domain and out-of-domain starting frames, respectively. The pre-trained model degenerates within the first 5 s of rollout, with the generated content collapsing toward a monotonous appearance, whereas both post-trained models stay stable in either case. Post-training therefore yields a substantial quality gain within our framework.

    Static scenes. When the avatar is not moved, the pre-trained model already breaks down after 20 s, and post-training with a short horizon becomes blurry after 60 s. Only the extended-horizon variant preserves a sharp and stable scene throughout.

    Memory. We rotate the camera away and then turn back to the original viewpoint. With a short post-training horizon, the scene is already slightly altered after 4 s and differs substantially after 8 s; with the extended training horizon and longer training, it remains essentially unchanged even after 8 s. These comparisons show that both extending the post-training horizon and increasing training length are necessary to confer markedly stronger resistance to collapse in static scenes and a genuine degree of memory.

    5.5 Efficiency and Latency Analysis

    Frame rate and action-to-pixel latency are critical to interactive experience. End-to-end latency comprises the diffusion model (93 ms on an A800) and the VAE decoder (58 ms). Since player actions may arrive mid-execution, we budget an expected extra half-step of diffusion, giving 93×1.5+58≈198 ms; this is the theoretical computation latency, excluding network transmission and codec overhead. Deploying the diffusion model and VAE decoder on separate GPUs for pipelined execution further yields 1000/93×4≈43 fps, enabling real-time interactive gameplay. Relative to existing streaming systems, which operate at 480p–720p with single-digit frame rates and multi-second latency, our system delivers 1080p output at 43 fps with 198 ms latency; the detailed comparison is reported in Table 2.

    6 Conclusion

    We have presented Streaming-AAA, a controllable infinite AAA game video generation framework that achieves high-resolution (1080p), high-frame-rate (∼43 fps), and low-latency (∼200 ms) streaming gameplay synthesis. Our framework integrates an efficient high-resolution video VAE with pixel-shuffle decoding, a factorized UNet-based latent diffusion model with unified multi-modal conditioning, and a progressive training pipeline spanning short-range dynamics modeling, long-context pre-training, and post-training alignment via distribution matching distillation. The proposed hybrid short-term and long-term KV-cache memory, combined with parallelized teacher-forcing inference, enables stable infinite-horizon generation while maintaining real-time interactivity. Experiments on Genshin Impact demonstrate that Streaming-AAA produces visually rich and temporally consistent gameplay across diverse environments, weather conditions, and character actions.

    Limitations. Our current approach is primarily designed and optimized for playability within a specific game title. The model is trained on domain-specific data from a single game, and its generalization to unseen game environments, art styles, or game mechanics remains limited. Extending the framework to a universal game generation model that handles diverse titles without per-game fine-tuning is an important open challenge.

    Future Work. Looking ahead, we believe the core techniques developed in Streaming-AAA—efficient high-resolution VAE, controllable streaming diffusion, and long-horizon memory—can serve as building blocks for a broader range of downstream applications beyond playable generation. For instance, the framework could be adapted for game-specific visual enhancement, where the model upscales or refines low-quality rendered frames into high-fidelity outputs in real time. We hope that Streaming-AAA provides a solid foundation toward bridging generative video models and practical interactive entertainment systems.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 代理变了、风格也要变：ContextRenderer 让生成式渲染器在持续游玩中既跟得上条件、又不断片 ｜ ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds
item.description:
一句话：把引擎给的场景表示渲染成细致画面时，条件会变、风格要保——两者现有渲染器都做不好。

要点：

  • 定位清楚：交互式游戏世界模型把**可执行的世界演化**与**视觉生成**分开，用视频模型把引擎提供的场景表示渲染成细致观测
  • 困难在持续性：在持续游玩过程中，现有生成式渲染器既**难以跟随不断变化的条件**，又难以在多样的代理（proxy）与目标风格之间保持**视觉连续性**
  • ContextRenderer 因此以「动态上下文」为核心，处理条件与风格的同时切换

为什么值得看：这是「引擎出代理、模型出画面」这条链路上最实际的一环：代理质量在变、风格要稳。与 11-19 的 Code World Model 2.0（代理粒度跨度）互补——一个管粒度，一个管上下文与风格连续性。

中文摘要：交互式游戏世界模型把「可执行的世界演化」与「视觉生成」分开：由引擎负责世界状态与场景表示，再用视频模型把这些表示渲染成细致的画面。但作者指出，在持续游玩的过程中，现有生成式渲染器有两个短板——既难以跟随不断变化的条件，也难以在不同的代理表示与目标风格之间维持视觉连续性。ContextRenderer 因此以「动态上下文」为核心来组织生成，目标是在条件与风格同时变化时仍保持连续、可信的画面。对已经在做这条链路的团队，它针对的是「代理与风格都在变，画面还不能断片」这个现实问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation
for Interactive Game Worlds

Abstract

Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page:https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/

1 Introduction

Video generation models synthesize realistic footage, while video world models extend this capability to action-responsive environments for gaming [2, 29]. Yet visual realism alone does not ensure correct geometry, interactions, or persistent state [15, 1, 23]. To maintain explicit control over the world, recent game world models separate state management from visual generation [4, 14]. Game engines or executable programs built by coding agents maintain state, enforce rules, and specify scene layouts, motion, and interactions, while video generation models act as generative renderers, turning these specifications into detailed observations [38, 34, 19, 9]. This separation offers a promising direction for interactive game world modeling.

Existing generative renderers learn to convert scene representations into detailed videos through paired training, supporting tasks such as photorealistic rendering and appearance editing [17, 3]. Text prompts or reference images guide appearance. Autoregressive variants generate successive video chunks conditioned on generated history, and some also support online text updates [38, 19, 39]. However, these methods still face two limitations when applied to extended gameplay in interactive world models. First, limited support for sustained interaction: existing streaming interfaces primarily accommodate changing proxy videos or text prompts [38, 19, 39]. Introducing new subject references and appearance requirements during generation, while preserving visual continuity over long sessions, is less well supported. Second, limited generalization across representations: many renderers are trained and evaluated on specific proxy formats [38, 19, 39]. Transfer across proxy representations and target visual styles remains underexplored.

We therefore aim to build a generative renderer for sustained exploration and interaction across diverse game worlds. This requires addressing two challenges. First, dynamic conditioning for long-horizon interaction: updated conditions may describe a state different from that recorded in generated history. The model must follow these updates while preserving the appearance of unaffected content and temporal continuity. It must also retain useful visual history with bounded memory and computation. Second, diverse conditioning across proxy representations: proxies with different appearances and levels of detail may describe the same world content. The model must recover shared layout, motion, and event semantics, then combine them with target conditions to generate detailed appearance, fine-grained character motion, and interaction effects without changing the specified event timing or outcomes.

To address these challenges, we introduce ContextRenderer (Fig. 1), an autoregressive video diffusion framework. Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) trains next-chunk prediction from refreshed world context and preceding history context using chunk-level interaction supervision. The world context is a view-dependent projection of the evolving world, combining proxy video, text, and subject references to specify scene content and desired appearance. Recurrent History Compression (RHC) retains a first-frame anchor and compresses older observations more strongly than recent ones within a fixed token budget [40, 37, 41]. This pairing teaches the model to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity.

Within this framework, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) uses a shared high-fidelity reconstruction as a common target for different proxies of the same trajectory and as a condition for appearance and interaction variation. Joint flow-matching objectives train these two mappings alongside direct proxy-to-target generation, enabling inference without the intermediate reconstruction.

To support these training objectives, we construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric, multi-proxy dataset from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos. For each trajectory, m proxy representations and n target variants form m×n pairs, with a shared high-fidelity reconstruction supporting CRFA. Each temporally synchronized chunk is paired with subject references and a prompt describing scene appearance, interactions, and state changes. These annotations supervise condition updates in DCL, while corresponding renderings support CRFA across proxy representations and target appearances.

Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality over the evaluated autoregressive baselines. We further demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references, with diverse appearances and interaction effects across proxy representations (Fig. 1).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework combining DCL and RHC to follow changing world conditions while preserving visual continuity with bounded history.

  • •

    We introduce Cross-Representation Flow Alignment, which connects diverse proxies with target appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction, supporting direct proxy-to-target inference.

  • •

    We construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric, multi-proxy dataset providing trajectory renderings, chunk-level interaction annotations, and subject references.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive world models. Interactive world models generate visual observations in response to user actions. Genie [2] and GameNGen [29] learn action-conditioned visual dynamics, while LingBot-World [28] supports longer interactive rollouts. ActWorld [36] extends object interaction through chunk-level supervision and action-aware memory. Another line separates world evolution from visual generation: Code World Model [4] and Programmable World Model [14] maintain world states and rules through executable programs, while video models render the resulting observations. Matrix-Game 4.0 [39] combines an executable game engine with an autoregressive renderer conditioned on low-poly proxies, dynamic captions, and memory references. Within this division, ContextRenderer focuses on learning continuous rendering under changing world conditions across diverse proxy representations while maintaining visual continuity.

    Generative rendering. Generative renderers condition on coarse renderings [10, 38] or engine geometry and buffers [5, 19]. StreamRender-H3 [24] streams engine output with fixed session conditioning, while EdenLive [13] supports dynamic prompt updates. SolarRenderer [9] accepts diverse structural inputs and aligns structure tokens with the frames they describe, a design we adopt. These advances motivate a distinction beyond updating text or accepting multiple input formats. ContextRenderer organizes geometry, event descriptions, and subject references into a world context whose components can be replaced at chunk boundaries. It also imposes cross-rendering consistency on the generator’s predictions: different coarse depictions of one trajectory should yield the same canonical rendering. This auxiliary constraint targets invariance to input style while allowing the main rendering task to produce different target appearances.

    Long-horizon video generation. Long-horizon video generation follows two complementary directions: autoregressive rollout and context representation. The former studies how to sustain generation, with Self Forcing [12] training on self-generated rollouts to reduce the training–inference gap. The latter studies how past information is retained and accessed. Retrieval methods such as WorldMem [35] select relevant past observations. Compression methods reduce history tokens: FramePack [40] and Helios [37] use multiscale representations, while TinyHistory [41] learns an encoder through frame-query pretraining and video-continuation adaptation. Recurrent approaches instead accumulate context in hidden states; TTT-Video [6] uses neural networks as these states. ContextRenderer uses compressed visual history for continuity alongside engine-supplied geometry, event descriptions, and subject references updated at each chunk.

    3 Method

    Our goal is to support sustained exploration and interaction in game worlds through continuous video generation. As interaction changes the world, the video model must depict updated content while preserving the visual continuity of unaffected elements. ContextRenderer organizes this process as successive chunk predictions conditioned on the evolving world and visual history (Fig. 3).

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    We consider interactive game world models in which players explore the world, interact with entities, and observe the consequences of their actions (Fig. 2). At time n, a world engine E updates the world state sₙ in response to player action aₙ, following executable rules [4, 14]. A generative renderer G then produces the next visual observation oₙ₊₁, using the updated state and preceding observations o_≤n:

    sₙ₊₁=E(sₙ,aₙ), oₙ₊₁∼G( ·|sₙ₊₁,o_≤n).

    		(1)

    To render the evolving world with updated state, G needs a description of what is visible from the current viewpoint and how it should appear. We generate observations in video chunks. For each target chunk Xₖ, the engine provides a proxy video chunk Pₖ covering the same time interval. This coarse representation conveys the visible scene layout, object motion, and interaction states to the video model, while leaving detailed appearance and interaction effects partially specified. A prompt yₖ and subject reference images Iₖ supply semantic and appearance requirements. Together, they form the world context Wₖ=(Pₖ,yₖ,Iₖ), a view-dependent description refreshed as interaction unfolds.

    The preceding video chunks form the visual history X_

    3.2 ContextRenderer

    We implement G as an autoregressive video diffusion model built on pretrained models [30, 25]. It learns the conditional distribution of the next video chunk given the current world context and visual history, denoted by p_θ(Xₖ|Wₖ,X_

    Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL). During interaction, rendering conditions can change while visual history still depicts the preceding state. DCL trains the model to respond to these updates through chunk-level supervision. Each target chunk is paired with its corresponding proxy segment and a text prompt derived from its interaction annotations to describe the interactions within that interval. Subject references are updated when subjects or appearance requirements change and retained otherwise. Together with the history context from the same sequence, these pairs supervise the model to depict interaction-driven changes while preserving the appearance of unaffected content.

    We fine-tune the pretrained Transformer as the conditional velocity network v_θ through in-context learning. Clean visual context tokens are processed jointly with noisy target tokens, while the current prompt enters through the backbone’s text-conditioning pathway. For target latent z₀⁽ᵏ⁾=Enc(Xₖ), we construct zₜ⁽ᵏ⁾=(1-t)z₀⁽ᵏ⁾+tε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t∈[0,1]. Conditioned on Wₖ and Hₖ, v_θ is trained through conditional flow matching, with the loss evaluated only on the target chunk [21, 22]:

    L_FM=𝔼 [∥v_θ (zₜ⁽ᵏ⁾,t|Wₖ,Hₖ)-(ε-z₀⁽ᵏ⁾)∥₂²].

    		(2)

    We maintain a consistent organization of token roles and local positions as content changes across chunks. Each visual token receives a learned role embedding:

    ũᵢ=uᵢ+eᵣ₍ᵢ₎,

    		(3)

    where uᵢ is the token feature and r(i) denotes its video, proxy, or reference-image role. History and target tokens share the video embedding, while all proxy representations share the proxy embedding. Flow-time embeddings distinguish clean visual conditions at t=0 from the noisy target at the sampled time t. Since proxy and target describe the same interval from the same viewpoint, corresponding tokens receive matching spatiotemporal RoPE coordinates:

    ρₖ^P(j,h,w)=ρₖ^X(j,h,w)=(τ_⋆+j,h,w).

    		(4)

    Here, (j,h,w) indexes the local token grid, and τ_⋆ fixes the target’s starting temporal position independently of the global chunk index k. History occupies earlier positions, while reference images use separate slots.

    Recurrent History Compression (RHC). As interaction continues, visual history grows beyond the budget of a single prediction. Recent observations supply detailed appearance and motion cues for continuation, while older observations provide broader visual context. Following multiscale history compression [37], RHC uses finer patches for recent frames and larger spatiotemporal patches for older ones. We encode each video chunk independently with the VAE and concatenate the resulting latent grids along time. A rolling window retains up to N recent latent frames, partitioned into recent, intermediate, and distant groups Zₖ⁽¹⁾,Zₖ⁽²⁾,Zₖ⁽³⁾. Each group is converted into a token sequence by φᵢ, a scale-specific 3D patch embedding followed by flattening, yielding the compressed history:

    Hₖ=(φ₁(z_anchor) ;φ₃(Zₖ⁽³⁾) ;φ₂(Zₖ⁽²⁾) ;φ₁(Zₖ⁽¹⁾)),

    		(5)

    where z_anchor denotes the first-frame latent from the initial chunk X₀, retained separately from the rolling window and embedded at the finest scale using φ₁. Fixed group capacities and patch sizes bound the total history token budget, including the anchor.

    At inference, X₀ is generated from W₀ without video history and initializes the rolling window. Subsequent chunks append latent frames, replacing the oldest entries when capacity is exceeded. Retained frames are regrouped and patchified for the next prediction under refreshed world conditions. Recent history occupies positions immediately before the fixed target position; unused earlier slots are zero-padded. Training covers empty, partially filled, and full windows with the same context organization, using paired-sequence history rather than generated outputs.

    3.3 Cross-Representation Flow Alignment

    Rendering from diverse coarse proxies requires both enriching their visual content and expressing it through varied appearances and interaction details. Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects these learning tasks through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction Xʳ. It enriches character modeling, scene appearance, and material detail while preserving the motion and event progression expressed by the proxies.

    Omitting chunk indices, let P and X denote proxy and target chunks, and let c=(y,I,H) and cʳ denote target- and reconstruction-side conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 3(c), the model learns p_θ(Xʳ|P,cʳ) by reconstructing a shared high-fidelity video from different proxies of the same trajectory. Under the flow-matching objective, the conditional velocity fields are trained toward a common reconstruction, encouraging the model to recover shared layout, motion, and event semantics across proxy representations. The reconstruction then serves as a condition for learning p_θ(X|Xʳ,c), enabling variations in appearance, environmental style, and interaction details while preserving the specified event timing and outcomes. We jointly learn these distributions alongside direct rendering p_θ(X|P,c), using the same renderer and the conditional flow-matching objective in Sec. 3.2:

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=L_P→X+λ₁L_P→Xʳ+λ₂L_Xʳ→X.

    		(6)

    The three terms supervise direct rendering, shared reconstruction, and reconstruction-conditioned target variation, respectively; we set λ₁=0.8 and λ₂=0.2. At inference, the renderer generates directly from the proxy and target-side conditions without producing Xʳ.

    3.4 WorldPrism Dataset

    Learning across proxy representations and target variations requires corresponding videos that preserve the same underlying trajectory while varying its visual realization. We construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric dataset providing these correspondences and chunk-level interaction annotations. Figure 4 shows the construction pipeline.

    Paired video construction. We collect source videos from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, driving simulations, and open-source scene datasets such as DL3DV [20]. Structural signals and interaction events are extracted directly from engines when available; otherwise, geometry, instance semantics, and event boundaries are estimated using MoGe [32], SAM 2 [27], and a vision-language model (VLM). Scene semantics and subject references guide the generation of a spatially aligned first frame, establishing the layout and subject appearance for subsequent video generation. Conditioned on this frame, structural videos, and action/style prompts, MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [25] generates coarse proxies and detailed target variants offline. The variants differ in character and scene appearance, motion details, and interaction effects. VLM filtering checks these requested changes against camera motion, spatial layout, and event timing to retain variants consistent with the source trajectory. For each trajectory, m proxy representations—including depth maps, semantic maps, low-poly renderings, and primitive renderings—are paired with n target variants to form m×n pairs. A shared high-fidelity reconstruction Xʳ, drawn from a suitable source recording or generated as a canonical rendering, connects proxy reconstruction with target variation for CRFA.

    Interaction annotations and coverage. We divide corresponding videos into temporally synchronized chunks and annotate each chunk with a prompt describing its scene appearance, active interactions, and state changes. Subject references are selected for the depicted subjects and updated when their appearance requirements change. Scene-only clips are annotated with environment descriptions and viewpoint motion. Together, these annotations provide chunk-level world conditions for DCL. WorldPrism contains 20K retained clips: 11K coarse proxy clips across 11 formats and 9K target variants across 150 visual styles, covering over 20 interaction and locomotion categories.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate reconstruction, visual variation, and sustained interaction across diverse proxies and appearance conditions. Comparisons include EdenLive, SolarRenderer-AR, StreamRender-H3, and Streaming-CWM, followed by component comparisons of DCL, RHC, and CRFA.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks and tasks. We construct GWM-Bench with 200 reconstruction pairs with real targets and 120 visual-variation pairs with generated references for alternative appearances and interaction details under proxy-specified content. Solar-Bench uses Heldout53 for reconstruction and Hard208 for variation [9]. Clips contain 124 (GWM) or 158 (Solar) frames at 24 fps; results are aggregated separately by benchmark and task.

    Implementation and baselines. ContextRenderer uses pretrained Wan (5B/14B) and MiniMax-H3 (33B) [30, 31, 25]. Wan generates 33-frame chunks (9 latent frames) at 640×384 with 50 denoising steps; H3 generates 34-frame chunks (10 latent frames) at 1344×768 with 30 steps. The final H3 chunk may be shorter. Our reference configuration uses 2,000 updates on 8 GPUs at learning rate 2×10⁻⁵. GWM baselines are EdenLive (5B/14B), SolarRenderer-AR, StreamRender-H3, and Streaming-CWM (33B) [13, 9, 24, 18]; the latter two use proxy video, target first frame, and a global prompt. Solar-Bench compares the 33B autoregressive models.

    Evaluation metrics. PSNR and LPIPS measure reconstruction fidelity; DOVER and VideoScore2’s visual-quality score assess visual variation [42, 33, 11]. Motion Error uses CoTracker3 trajectories, and Edge F1 measures structural adherence [16, 9]. Adjacent-Frame Similarity uses consecutive-frame DINOv2 similarity to assess temporal consistency [26, 9].

    4.2 Reconstruction and Visual Variation

    Reconstruction. ContextRenderer improves perceptual reconstruction across scales (Table 1). The 33B model outperforms StreamRender-H3 and Streaming-CWM on all reported reconstruction metrics and matches SolarRenderer-AR in adjacent-frame similarity. Solar-Bench shows higher fidelity but weaker motion and structural preservation.

    Visual variation. ContextRenderer improves visual quality and adjacent-frame similarity over size-matched EdenLive and SolarRenderer-AR (Table 2). GWM quality, temporal consistency, and motion preservation improve with model size. Our 33B model exceeds StreamRender-H3 on all reported metrics and Streaming-CWM on motion, structure, and adjacent-frame similarity. SolarRenderer-AR better preserves motion and structure on Solar-Bench.

    4.3 Qualitative Results

    Sustained interaction and long-horizon rendering. Sustained interaction requires incorporating new rendering conditions without disrupting previously established content. Fig. 5 illustrates a minute-long session across driving, exploration, and combat under successive prompt and subject-reference updates, where later views combine current engine-specified states with recognizable earlier appearances to maintain both responsiveness and continuity.

    Diverse proxies and visual realizations. Fig. 6 shows how ContextRenderer combines diverse proxy representations—capsule, primitive, and semantic—with prompts and dynamic subject references to generate varied character appearances, environments, and interaction effects. Presenting shooting as lightning illustrates variation in how an interaction is depicted while retaining event progression, alongside new subject references introduced mid-generation.

    Visual quality comparison. Fig. 7 compares vehicle-exit rendering from a voxel proxy under an ukiyo-e appearance condition. ContextRenderer better preserves the wooden palanquin’s structure and more coherently depicts the character’s door-opening and exit actions than size-matched baselines, which exhibit car-like geometry or structural deformation. Across our 5B, 14B, and 33B models, larger variants further improve structural stability and the coherence of character–object interactions.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Table 3 examines how each component contributes when new subjects and interactions appear mid-clip. (1) DCL. Because the proxy still supplies layout and motion, freezing prompts and references barely affects edge structure, but leaves newly arriving characters and state changes unspecified, hurting target appearance match and visual quality. (2) RHC. Keeping only the first frame still yields reasonable per-chunk quality, yet removing recent frames breaks continuity between consecutive chunks, causing the largest jump in temporal flicker and weaker structure. (3) CRFA. Unlike the two inference-time ablations, omitting shared-reconstruction training degrades visual quality, alignment, and structure all at once, confirming that bridging diverse proxies through a common reconstruction is essential for geometry and appearance.

    5 Conclusion and Limitations

    We presented ContextRenderer for continuous generative rendering of interactive game worlds. Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) learns responses to updated world conditions, while Recurrent History Compression (RHC) maintains multiscale visual history within a bounded token budget. Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects diverse proxies with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism supplies corresponding renderings and chunk-level interaction annotations for training. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench demonstrate improved perceptual reconstruction and visual quality, alongside minute-long rendering with changing prompts and subject references.

    Limitations. Real-time interaction requires further inference acceleration through techniques such as quantization, distillation, and runtime optimization. Our bounded visual history lacks explicit retrieval of distant observations, motivating stronger memory mechanisms for long sessions and revisits. Broader training data is also needed to cover more diverse worlds, interactions, and visual styles.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把引擎给的场景表示渲染成细致画面时，条件会变、风格要保——两者现有渲染器都做不好。

要点：

  • 定位清楚：交互式游戏世界模型把**可执行的世界演化**与**视觉生成**分开，用视频模型把引擎提供的场景表示渲染成细致观测
  • 困难在持续性：在持续游玩过程中，现有生成式渲染器既**难以跟随不断变化的条件**，又难以在多样的代理（proxy）与目标风格之间保持**视觉连续性**
  • ContextRenderer 因此以「动态上下文」为核心，处理条件与风格的同时切换

为什么值得看：这是「引擎出代理、模型出画面」这条链路上最实际的一环：代理质量在变、风格要稳。与 11-19 的 Code World Model 2.0（代理粒度跨度）互补——一个管粒度，一个管上下文与风格连续性。

中文摘要：交互式游戏世界模型把「可执行的世界演化」与「视觉生成」分开：由引擎负责世界状态与场景表示，再用视频模型把这些表示渲染成细致的画面。但作者指出，在持续游玩的过程中，现有生成式渲染器有两个短板——既难以跟随不断变化的条件，也难以在不同的代理表示与目标风格之间维持视觉连续性。ContextRenderer 因此以「动态上下文」为核心来组织生成，目标是在条件与风格同时变化时仍保持连续、可信的画面。对已经在做这条链路的团队，它针对的是「代理与风格都在变，画面还不能断片」这个现实问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation
for Interactive Game Worlds

Abstract

Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page:https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/

1 Introduction

Video generation models synthesize realistic footage, while video world models extend this capability to action-responsive environments for gaming [2, 29]. Yet visual realism alone does not ensure correct geometry, interactions, or persistent state [15, 1, 23]. To maintain explicit control over the world, recent game world models separate state management from visual generation [4, 14]. Game engines or executable programs built by coding agents maintain state, enforce rules, and specify scene layouts, motion, and interactions, while video generation models act as generative renderers, turning these specifications into detailed observations [38, 34, 19, 9]. This separation offers a promising direction for interactive game world modeling.

Existing generative renderers learn to convert scene representations into detailed videos through paired training, supporting tasks such as photorealistic rendering and appearance editing [17, 3]. Text prompts or reference images guide appearance. Autoregressive variants generate successive video chunks conditioned on generated history, and some also support online text updates [38, 19, 39]. However, these methods still face two limitations when applied to extended gameplay in interactive world models. First, limited support for sustained interaction: existing streaming interfaces primarily accommodate changing proxy videos or text prompts [38, 19, 39]. Introducing new subject references and appearance requirements during generation, while preserving visual continuity over long sessions, is less well supported. Second, limited generalization across representations: many renderers are trained and evaluated on specific proxy formats [38, 19, 39]. Transfer across proxy representations and target visual styles remains underexplored.

We therefore aim to build a generative renderer for sustained exploration and interaction across diverse game worlds. This requires addressing two challenges. First, dynamic conditioning for long-horizon interaction: updated conditions may describe a state different from that recorded in generated history. The model must follow these updates while preserving the appearance of unaffected content and temporal continuity. It must also retain useful visual history with bounded memory and computation. Second, diverse conditioning across proxy representations: proxies with different appearances and levels of detail may describe the same world content. The model must recover shared layout, motion, and event semantics, then combine them with target conditions to generate detailed appearance, fine-grained character motion, and interaction effects without changing the specified event timing or outcomes.

To address these challenges, we introduce ContextRenderer (Fig. 1), an autoregressive video diffusion framework. Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) trains next-chunk prediction from refreshed world context and preceding history context using chunk-level interaction supervision. The world context is a view-dependent projection of the evolving world, combining proxy video, text, and subject references to specify scene content and desired appearance. Recurrent History Compression (RHC) retains a first-frame anchor and compresses older observations more strongly than recent ones within a fixed token budget [40, 37, 41]. This pairing teaches the model to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity.

Within this framework, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) uses a shared high-fidelity reconstruction as a common target for different proxies of the same trajectory and as a condition for appearance and interaction variation. Joint flow-matching objectives train these two mappings alongside direct proxy-to-target generation, enabling inference without the intermediate reconstruction.

To support these training objectives, we construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric, multi-proxy dataset from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos. For each trajectory, m proxy representations and n target variants form m×n pairs, with a shared high-fidelity reconstruction supporting CRFA. Each temporally synchronized chunk is paired with subject references and a prompt describing scene appearance, interactions, and state changes. These annotations supervise condition updates in DCL, while corresponding renderings support CRFA across proxy representations and target appearances.

Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality over the evaluated autoregressive baselines. We further demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references, with diverse appearances and interaction effects across proxy representations (Fig. 1).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework combining DCL and RHC to follow changing world conditions while preserving visual continuity with bounded history.

  • •

    We introduce Cross-Representation Flow Alignment, which connects diverse proxies with target appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction, supporting direct proxy-to-target inference.

  • •

    We construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric, multi-proxy dataset providing trajectory renderings, chunk-level interaction annotations, and subject references.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive world models. Interactive world models generate visual observations in response to user actions. Genie [2] and GameNGen [29] learn action-conditioned visual dynamics, while LingBot-World [28] supports longer interactive rollouts. ActWorld [36] extends object interaction through chunk-level supervision and action-aware memory. Another line separates world evolution from visual generation: Code World Model [4] and Programmable World Model [14] maintain world states and rules through executable programs, while video models render the resulting observations. Matrix-Game 4.0 [39] combines an executable game engine with an autoregressive renderer conditioned on low-poly proxies, dynamic captions, and memory references. Within this division, ContextRenderer focuses on learning continuous rendering under changing world conditions across diverse proxy representations while maintaining visual continuity.

    Generative rendering. Generative renderers condition on coarse renderings [10, 38] or engine geometry and buffers [5, 19]. StreamRender-H3 [24] streams engine output with fixed session conditioning, while EdenLive [13] supports dynamic prompt updates. SolarRenderer [9] accepts diverse structural inputs and aligns structure tokens with the frames they describe, a design we adopt. These advances motivate a distinction beyond updating text or accepting multiple input formats. ContextRenderer organizes geometry, event descriptions, and subject references into a world context whose components can be replaced at chunk boundaries. It also imposes cross-rendering consistency on the generator’s predictions: different coarse depictions of one trajectory should yield the same canonical rendering. This auxiliary constraint targets invariance to input style while allowing the main rendering task to produce different target appearances.

    Long-horizon video generation. Long-horizon video generation follows two complementary directions: autoregressive rollout and context representation. The former studies how to sustain generation, with Self Forcing [12] training on self-generated rollouts to reduce the training–inference gap. The latter studies how past information is retained and accessed. Retrieval methods such as WorldMem [35] select relevant past observations. Compression methods reduce history tokens: FramePack [40] and Helios [37] use multiscale representations, while TinyHistory [41] learns an encoder through frame-query pretraining and video-continuation adaptation. Recurrent approaches instead accumulate context in hidden states; TTT-Video [6] uses neural networks as these states. ContextRenderer uses compressed visual history for continuity alongside engine-supplied geometry, event descriptions, and subject references updated at each chunk.

    3 Method

    Our goal is to support sustained exploration and interaction in game worlds through continuous video generation. As interaction changes the world, the video model must depict updated content while preserving the visual continuity of unaffected elements. ContextRenderer organizes this process as successive chunk predictions conditioned on the evolving world and visual history (Fig. 3).

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    We consider interactive game world models in which players explore the world, interact with entities, and observe the consequences of their actions (Fig. 2). At time n, a world engine E updates the world state sₙ in response to player action aₙ, following executable rules [4, 14]. A generative renderer G then produces the next visual observation oₙ₊₁, using the updated state and preceding observations o_≤n:

    sₙ₊₁=E(sₙ,aₙ), oₙ₊₁∼G( ·|sₙ₊₁,o_≤n).

    		(1)

    To render the evolving world with updated state, G needs a description of what is visible from the current viewpoint and how it should appear. We generate observations in video chunks. For each target chunk Xₖ, the engine provides a proxy video chunk Pₖ covering the same time interval. This coarse representation conveys the visible scene layout, object motion, and interaction states to the video model, while leaving detailed appearance and interaction effects partially specified. A prompt yₖ and subject reference images Iₖ supply semantic and appearance requirements. Together, they form the world context Wₖ=(Pₖ,yₖ,Iₖ), a view-dependent description refreshed as interaction unfolds.

    The preceding video chunks form the visual history X_

    3.2 ContextRenderer

    We implement G as an autoregressive video diffusion model built on pretrained models [30, 25]. It learns the conditional distribution of the next video chunk given the current world context and visual history, denoted by p_θ(Xₖ|Wₖ,X_

    Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL). During interaction, rendering conditions can change while visual history still depicts the preceding state. DCL trains the model to respond to these updates through chunk-level supervision. Each target chunk is paired with its corresponding proxy segment and a text prompt derived from its interaction annotations to describe the interactions within that interval. Subject references are updated when subjects or appearance requirements change and retained otherwise. Together with the history context from the same sequence, these pairs supervise the model to depict interaction-driven changes while preserving the appearance of unaffected content.

    We fine-tune the pretrained Transformer as the conditional velocity network v_θ through in-context learning. Clean visual context tokens are processed jointly with noisy target tokens, while the current prompt enters through the backbone’s text-conditioning pathway. For target latent z₀⁽ᵏ⁾=Enc(Xₖ), we construct zₜ⁽ᵏ⁾=(1-t)z₀⁽ᵏ⁾+tε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t∈[0,1]. Conditioned on Wₖ and Hₖ, v_θ is trained through conditional flow matching, with the loss evaluated only on the target chunk [21, 22]:

    L_FM=𝔼 [∥v_θ (zₜ⁽ᵏ⁾,t|Wₖ,Hₖ)-(ε-z₀⁽ᵏ⁾)∥₂²].

    		(2)

    We maintain a consistent organization of token roles and local positions as content changes across chunks. Each visual token receives a learned role embedding:

    ũᵢ=uᵢ+eᵣ₍ᵢ₎,

    		(3)

    where uᵢ is the token feature and r(i) denotes its video, proxy, or reference-image role. History and target tokens share the video embedding, while all proxy representations share the proxy embedding. Flow-time embeddings distinguish clean visual conditions at t=0 from the noisy target at the sampled time t. Since proxy and target describe the same interval from the same viewpoint, corresponding tokens receive matching spatiotemporal RoPE coordinates:

    ρₖ^P(j,h,w)=ρₖ^X(j,h,w)=(τ_⋆+j,h,w).

    		(4)

    Here, (j,h,w) indexes the local token grid, and τ_⋆ fixes the target’s starting temporal position independently of the global chunk index k. History occupies earlier positions, while reference images use separate slots.

    Recurrent History Compression (RHC). As interaction continues, visual history grows beyond the budget of a single prediction. Recent observations supply detailed appearance and motion cues for continuation, while older observations provide broader visual context. Following multiscale history compression [37], RHC uses finer patches for recent frames and larger spatiotemporal patches for older ones. We encode each video chunk independently with the VAE and concatenate the resulting latent grids along time. A rolling window retains up to N recent latent frames, partitioned into recent, intermediate, and distant groups Zₖ⁽¹⁾,Zₖ⁽²⁾,Zₖ⁽³⁾. Each group is converted into a token sequence by φᵢ, a scale-specific 3D patch embedding followed by flattening, yielding the compressed history:

    Hₖ=(φ₁(z_anchor) ;φ₃(Zₖ⁽³⁾) ;φ₂(Zₖ⁽²⁾) ;φ₁(Zₖ⁽¹⁾)),

    		(5)

    where z_anchor denotes the first-frame latent from the initial chunk X₀, retained separately from the rolling window and embedded at the finest scale using φ₁. Fixed group capacities and patch sizes bound the total history token budget, including the anchor.

    At inference, X₀ is generated from W₀ without video history and initializes the rolling window. Subsequent chunks append latent frames, replacing the oldest entries when capacity is exceeded. Retained frames are regrouped and patchified for the next prediction under refreshed world conditions. Recent history occupies positions immediately before the fixed target position; unused earlier slots are zero-padded. Training covers empty, partially filled, and full windows with the same context organization, using paired-sequence history rather than generated outputs.

    3.3 Cross-Representation Flow Alignment

    Rendering from diverse coarse proxies requires both enriching their visual content and expressing it through varied appearances and interaction details. Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects these learning tasks through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction Xʳ. It enriches character modeling, scene appearance, and material detail while preserving the motion and event progression expressed by the proxies.

    Omitting chunk indices, let P and X denote proxy and target chunks, and let c=(y,I,H) and cʳ denote target- and reconstruction-side conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 3(c), the model learns p_θ(Xʳ|P,cʳ) by reconstructing a shared high-fidelity video from different proxies of the same trajectory. Under the flow-matching objective, the conditional velocity fields are trained toward a common reconstruction, encouraging the model to recover shared layout, motion, and event semantics across proxy representations. The reconstruction then serves as a condition for learning p_θ(X|Xʳ,c), enabling variations in appearance, environmental style, and interaction details while preserving the specified event timing and outcomes. We jointly learn these distributions alongside direct rendering p_θ(X|P,c), using the same renderer and the conditional flow-matching objective in Sec. 3.2:

    Lₜₒₜₐₗ=L_P→X+λ₁L_P→Xʳ+λ₂L_Xʳ→X.

    		(6)

    The three terms supervise direct rendering, shared reconstruction, and reconstruction-conditioned target variation, respectively; we set λ₁=0.8 and λ₂=0.2. At inference, the renderer generates directly from the proxy and target-side conditions without producing Xʳ.

    3.4 WorldPrism Dataset

    Learning across proxy representations and target variations requires corresponding videos that preserve the same underlying trajectory while varying its visual realization. We construct WorldPrism, an interaction-centric dataset providing these correspondences and chunk-level interaction annotations. Figure 4 shows the construction pipeline.

    Paired video construction. We collect source videos from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, driving simulations, and open-source scene datasets such as DL3DV [20]. Structural signals and interaction events are extracted directly from engines when available; otherwise, geometry, instance semantics, and event boundaries are estimated using MoGe [32], SAM 2 [27], and a vision-language model (VLM). Scene semantics and subject references guide the generation of a spatially aligned first frame, establishing the layout and subject appearance for subsequent video generation. Conditioned on this frame, structural videos, and action/style prompts, MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [25] generates coarse proxies and detailed target variants offline. The variants differ in character and scene appearance, motion details, and interaction effects. VLM filtering checks these requested changes against camera motion, spatial layout, and event timing to retain variants consistent with the source trajectory. For each trajectory, m proxy representations—including depth maps, semantic maps, low-poly renderings, and primitive renderings—are paired with n target variants to form m×n pairs. A shared high-fidelity reconstruction Xʳ, drawn from a suitable source recording or generated as a canonical rendering, connects proxy reconstruction with target variation for CRFA.

    Interaction annotations and coverage. We divide corresponding videos into temporally synchronized chunks and annotate each chunk with a prompt describing its scene appearance, active interactions, and state changes. Subject references are selected for the depicted subjects and updated when their appearance requirements change. Scene-only clips are annotated with environment descriptions and viewpoint motion. Together, these annotations provide chunk-level world conditions for DCL. WorldPrism contains 20K retained clips: 11K coarse proxy clips across 11 formats and 9K target variants across 150 visual styles, covering over 20 interaction and locomotion categories.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate reconstruction, visual variation, and sustained interaction across diverse proxies and appearance conditions. Comparisons include EdenLive, SolarRenderer-AR, StreamRender-H3, and Streaming-CWM, followed by component comparisons of DCL, RHC, and CRFA.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks and tasks. We construct GWM-Bench with 200 reconstruction pairs with real targets and 120 visual-variation pairs with generated references for alternative appearances and interaction details under proxy-specified content. Solar-Bench uses Heldout53 for reconstruction and Hard208 for variation [9]. Clips contain 124 (GWM) or 158 (Solar) frames at 24 fps; results are aggregated separately by benchmark and task.

    Implementation and baselines. ContextRenderer uses pretrained Wan (5B/14B) and MiniMax-H3 (33B) [30, 31, 25]. Wan generates 33-frame chunks (9 latent frames) at 640×384 with 50 denoising steps; H3 generates 34-frame chunks (10 latent frames) at 1344×768 with 30 steps. The final H3 chunk may be shorter. Our reference configuration uses 2,000 updates on 8 GPUs at learning rate 2×10⁻⁵. GWM baselines are EdenLive (5B/14B), SolarRenderer-AR, StreamRender-H3, and Streaming-CWM (33B) [13, 9, 24, 18]; the latter two use proxy video, target first frame, and a global prompt. Solar-Bench compares the 33B autoregressive models.

    Evaluation metrics. PSNR and LPIPS measure reconstruction fidelity; DOVER and VideoScore2’s visual-quality score assess visual variation [42, 33, 11]. Motion Error uses CoTracker3 trajectories, and Edge F1 measures structural adherence [16, 9]. Adjacent-Frame Similarity uses consecutive-frame DINOv2 similarity to assess temporal consistency [26, 9].

    4.2 Reconstruction and Visual Variation

    Reconstruction. ContextRenderer improves perceptual reconstruction across scales (Table 1). The 33B model outperforms StreamRender-H3 and Streaming-CWM on all reported reconstruction metrics and matches SolarRenderer-AR in adjacent-frame similarity. Solar-Bench shows higher fidelity but weaker motion and structural preservation.

    Visual variation. ContextRenderer improves visual quality and adjacent-frame similarity over size-matched EdenLive and SolarRenderer-AR (Table 2). GWM quality, temporal consistency, and motion preservation improve with model size. Our 33B model exceeds StreamRender-H3 on all reported metrics and Streaming-CWM on motion, structure, and adjacent-frame similarity. SolarRenderer-AR better preserves motion and structure on Solar-Bench.

    4.3 Qualitative Results

    Sustained interaction and long-horizon rendering. Sustained interaction requires incorporating new rendering conditions without disrupting previously established content. Fig. 5 illustrates a minute-long session across driving, exploration, and combat under successive prompt and subject-reference updates, where later views combine current engine-specified states with recognizable earlier appearances to maintain both responsiveness and continuity.

    Diverse proxies and visual realizations. Fig. 6 shows how ContextRenderer combines diverse proxy representations—capsule, primitive, and semantic—with prompts and dynamic subject references to generate varied character appearances, environments, and interaction effects. Presenting shooting as lightning illustrates variation in how an interaction is depicted while retaining event progression, alongside new subject references introduced mid-generation.

    Visual quality comparison. Fig. 7 compares vehicle-exit rendering from a voxel proxy under an ukiyo-e appearance condition. ContextRenderer better preserves the wooden palanquin’s structure and more coherently depicts the character’s door-opening and exit actions than size-matched baselines, which exhibit car-like geometry or structural deformation. Across our 5B, 14B, and 33B models, larger variants further improve structural stability and the coherence of character–object interactions.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Table 3 examines how each component contributes when new subjects and interactions appear mid-clip. (1) DCL. Because the proxy still supplies layout and motion, freezing prompts and references barely affects edge structure, but leaves newly arriving characters and state changes unspecified, hurting target appearance match and visual quality. (2) RHC. Keeping only the first frame still yields reasonable per-chunk quality, yet removing recent frames breaks continuity between consecutive chunks, causing the largest jump in temporal flicker and weaker structure. (3) CRFA. Unlike the two inference-time ablations, omitting shared-reconstruction training degrades visual quality, alignment, and structure all at once, confirming that bridging diverse proxies through a common reconstruction is essential for geometry and appearance.

    5 Conclusion and Limitations

    We presented ContextRenderer for continuous generative rendering of interactive game worlds. Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) learns responses to updated world conditions, while Recurrent History Compression (RHC) maintains multiscale visual history within a bounded token budget. Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects diverse proxies with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism supplies corresponding renderings and chunk-level interaction annotations for training. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench demonstrate improved perceptual reconstruction and visual quality, alongside minute-long rendering with changing prompts and subject references.

    Limitations. Real-time interaction requires further inference acceleration through techniques such as quantization, distillation, and runtime optimization. Our bounded visual history lacks explicit retrieval of distant observations, motivating stronger memory mechanisms for long sessions and revisits. Broader training data is also needed to cover more diverse worlds, interactions, and visual styles.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 只追求画面好看的世界模型没法用来规划：Plan4D 要连未来视频一起输出稠密 4D 几何 ｜ Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
item.description:
一句话：缺少显式 4D 建模，导致时间上几何一致性很弱。

要点：

  • 批评很直接：多数用于未来预测的世界模型**优先追求生成视频的美学质量**，但由于缺乏显式 4D 建模，**随时间变化的几何一致性**很有限
  • Plan4D 的目标是「可规划的 4D 世界模型」：在预测未来 RGB 视频的同时，输出**稠密 4D 几何**（深度、相机、点云等）
  • 「可规划（plannable）」意味着这些几何要能被下游用来做决策，而不只是给人看

为什么值得看：「世界模型能不能用来规划」取决于它输出的几何能不能被消费。把稠密 4D 几何与视频一起生成，等于把世界模型从「视频生成器」升级成「可查询的场景演化器」——这正是引擎需要的接口形态。

中文摘要：多数面向未来预测的世界模型把重点放在生成视频的美学质量上，但由于缺少显式的 4D 建模，它们在时间维度上的几何一致性相当有限。Plan4D 因此提出「可规划的 4D 世界模型」这一目标：在预测未来 RGB 视频的同时，输出稠密的 4D 几何，包括深度、相机参数与点云等，使结果可以被下游规划模块消费，而不只是给人观看。作者把它定位为通向「生成式可规划 4D 世界」的下一个里程碑——关键在于让世界模型输出的不只是画面，还有能被查询与利用的空间结构。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds

Abstract

Most world models for future prediction prioritize the aesthetic quality of generated videos, but offer only limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce Plan4D, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow, from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, Plan4D leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that Plan4D achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project.

††footnotetext: †Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Given an observed scene context and a set of text-specified actions, we consider the task of generative plannable 4D worlds, a new paradigm for predicting reliable futures for the physical world that jointly produces visually plausible RGB frames and physically grounded 4D geometry –including depth, camera dynamics, and scene flow –within a single feed-forward model. Prior observation-prediction models formulate future prediction largely as RGB synthesis [25, 86], often on a per-frame basis, notably UniSim [106], Genie 1–3 [13, 76, 8], NWM [10], and V-JEPA 2 [4]. By contrast, with our actionable 4D future world model, humans and AI agents can plan and execute complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in the explicit 3D environment, such as picking up a cup, opening a bottle, or navigating through a cluttered room. These dynamic 3D quantities are essential for accurate measurement, reliable simulation, and effective execution of downstream tasks [54, 24, 59, 41, 33].

A major bottleneck of this task is the lack of suitable datasets, namely action-conditioned video sequences paired with rich text and comprehensive 3D annotations, including camera trajectories, accurate dense depth and motion. For example, large-scale video-caption datasets [7, 98, 18] may still lack detailed captions for physical fine-grained actions; the latest Action-100M [15] dataset provides detailed action annotations but without 3D annotations, while most dynamic 3D datasets [31, 30, 51] are relatively small in scale or lack natural actions.

Correspondingly, powerful baselines have emerged in parallel on these separate data sources, including video generators [35, 12, 11, 81, 34, 53, 108, 90, 66, 87], action-conditioned world models [106, 13, 76, 8, 10, 4, 48, 58], and 3D reconstructors [97, 57, 96, 92, 52, 99, 64, 114]. Despite being trained to build the same physical world, these models still operate as isolated systems for particular tasks. Standard pixel-level generators excel at synthesizing visually realistic RGB frames [102], but typically lack physical consistency [101, 61]; and 3D models recover explicit geometry well [95] but are largely reconstruction-centric and static. Even advanced 4D frameworks [116, 47, 82, 121, 50, 73, 72, 55] only infer motion from observed frames and cannot generate action-conditioned future worlds. As a result, none of these families alone provides a generative plannable 4D world, in which appearance, geometry, camera and action-conditioned future dynamics evolve consistently over time.

What if, given these different dataset sources, we stitch them together to model the same underlying 4D world? To achieve such a generative plannable 4D world, we propose Plan4D, a unified framework for planning and generating dense 4D worlds from observed context and action descriptions. Our core insight is to decouple the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnect them through a stitched latent world model that jointly plans RGB appearance and dense 4D geometry, unlike recent methods [85, 117, 22, 71, 27] that attempt to learn a 4D world model’s geometry from scratch. Such a paradigm reduces the task’s learning difficulty and data requirements, while allowing us to leverage the powerful priors of pretrained video generators and 3D reconstructors to achieve complex, long-horizon and fine-grained dynamics.

In practice, this paradigm requires solving several coupled challenges. i) the model must extend a frozen 3D foundation model from static scenes to dynamic 4D prediction while preserving its geometric consistency. ii) it must align geometry tokens with the latent space of a video generator without destroying the pretrained generative prior. iii) it must learn from real, unlabeled action videos without dense 4D supervision [112]. iv) it must also ensure consistency across the generated RGB, depth, camera, point clouds, and scene flow. Recent methods, including VIST3A [29], Geometry Forcing [100], and Gen3R [37], couple 3D reconstructors with video generators for static text-to-3D or scene-level 3D generation. We extend this direction to full actionable 4D world generation, jointly predicting full 4D geometry and appearance in future video sequences depicting fine-grained actions.

Unlike prior approaches that use geometry mainly as an auxiliary constraint [100, 6, 110, 26, 3], or decode geometry only after RGB generation [24], our Plan4D turns a video generator into an actionable 4D world model, which explicitly aligns future appearance and 4D structure inside the shared evolving video latent state. To preserve strong geometric priors while extending them beyond reconstruction, we augment Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3) with a lightweight token-only scene-flow head that predicts dense forward 3D motion from intermediate geometry tokens, while keeping its pretrained depth and camera-ray predictions intact. To connect this geometric readout with future generation, we learn a latent-to-geometry stitching module that maps video VAE latents into a selected DA3 block and trains it with token distillation and geometric supervision. The resulting stitched decoder provides a stable, differentiable interface from video latents to full 4D geometry. We then train the video generator against this frozen geometric interface, so unlabeled action videos can supervise not only visual prediction but also physically grounded 4D consistency. At inference time, a single generated latent future yields RGB frames and dense 4D geometry in one feed-forward pass.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We take a step towards the new paradigm of generative plannable 4D worlds, which jointly generates future RGB appearance and corresponding full 4D geometry, including depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions.

  • •

    We propose Plan4D, a unified framework with a scene-flow head and a geometry-video stitching mechanism that connect a frozen 3D foundation model with a pretrained video generator, preserving geometric priors while enabling action-conditioned dynamic 4D future prediction from unlabeled videos.

  • •

    We illustrate how Plan4D can achieve state-of-the-art performance in dense 4D world generation, improving both visual realism and geometric accuracy across scene flow, 3D reconstruction, and action-conditioned video prediction through extensive experiments.

    • 2 Related Works

    4D world models. Recent work has begun to model 4D worlds from two complementary directions. Explicit dynamics methods such as ParticleFormer [40] and PointWorld [41] predict particle trajectories or point-level motion, but mainly operate in structured 3D state spaces rather than generating rich future 4D. 4D-native generative models instead learn spatiotemporal world evolution, ranging from dynamic reconstruction, visual planning, and image-to-4D generation in Aether [85] and 4DNeX [21], to RGB-D or geometry-aware scene generation in TesserAct [117] and Robo4DGen [69]. GWM [70], iMoWM [113], and Kinema4D [105] further explore Gaussian, tokenized, and kinematics-driven representations, while FantasyWorld [22], WorldReel [27], TeleWorld [20], HY-World 2.0 [43], and Lyra 2.0 [80] couple video generation with geometric prediction for more unified world modeling. Despite this progress, existing systems typically emphasize either explicit geometric forecasting or large-scale generative simulation, and they rarely integrate the complementary priors of pretrained geometry foundation models into the latent dynamics of video generation.

    Aligning 3D Reconstruction and Video Generation.
