Early uses of generative priors for 3D synthesis mostly follow a cascade, where geometric constraints are applied to generated outputs rather than to internal generative states [77, 28, 94]. Later methods tighten this link through reconstruction-guided diffusion or distillation, as in GenFusion [103], VideoScene [91], and Lyra [5]. Recent work moves the alignment into feature or latent spaces. Geometry Forcing [100] aligns intermediate diffusion features with pretrained geometric representations [111], Gen3R [37] aligns geometry and appearance latents for joint generation, and GLD [46] repurposes geometric features as multi-view diffusion latents. From the model-stitching view [56, 9], VIST3A [29] connects a pretrained video VAE with a 3D network at linearly matchable layers. Our method builds on this direction, but stitches a video diffusion model to a 3D foundation model so that RGB synthesis and dense 4D geometry can be optimized and decoded from a shared latent rollout.

    3 Plan4D

    Given an observed context O={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^M and the planned action space A, our goal is to learn a generative plannable 4D world model f_θ that is conditioned on O and A and predicts a set of future 4D representations: f_θ:{O,A}↦{Iₜ,Dₜ,rₜ,Vₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, where A is a sequence of textual action descriptions p. The model f_θ learns a video latent trajectory that is conditioned on the observed context and the action description, and reads out the future RGB video frames Iₜ∈ℝ^H×W×3; and its corresponding depth maps Dₜ∈ℝ^H×W, camera ray maps rₜ∈ℝ^H×W×6, and full 4D scene flow Vₜ∈ℝ^H×W×3. The ray maps rₜ encode the camera origin and the ray directions for each pixel, which can be used to reconstruct the 3D point cloud of the scene. The scene flow Vₜ encodes the 3D motion of each pixel from time t to t+1111 Since we only define the forward flow, we then simplify V_t→t+1 as Vₜ..

    We parametrize f_θ with a model-stitching architecture that couples a video generator, LongCat-Video [87] (which uses the Wan 2.1 VAE [90]), with a foundational 3D reconstructor, Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3). The key insight is that, by building on the pretrained video generator and 3D reconstructor, our model can leverage the complementary priors of these two foundational models to achieve both high visual fidelity and strong geometric consistency in the generated future videos, unlike training it from scratch [85, 117, 22, 27], which is extremely challenging and data-hungry. To improve the motion modeling capability of DA3, we first augment it with an auxiliary DPT-style scene flow head in section3.1. In section3.2, we then stitch the video generator and the augmented DA3 together through a learnable latent-to-geometry stitching module, followed by a distillation and geometric supervision process to calibrate the stitched model in section3.3. Finally, we train the joint model in section3.4.

    3.1 Augmenting DA3 for Dynamic Scene Flow Prediction

    The physical world is not a collection of independent per-frame geometries. To model the dynamics and correspondence of the 4D world, we augment DA3 [64] with a dense scene flow head that predicts the 3D motion of each pixel. Following the original DPT-style decoder in DA3, the new head ingests the four intermediate token maps of the frozen encoder, and outputs a dense three-channel motion field via a lightweight prediction layer. Note that, the original encoder, as well as the depth and camera pose branches, remains unchanged; we simply add a dedicated motion branch. Our analysis in AppendixA shows that frozen DA3 tokens already encode cross-frame motion cues, which supports using this branch as a lightweight readout rather than a full motion model. In particular, for each frame t, the new head predicts a scene flow on the pixel lattice of that frame. Each valid pixel stores the forward 3D displacement from time t to t+1. The raw prediction is produced in the local camera basis of frame t and is mapped to a common reference frame with a lightweight adapter,

    V⁽⁰⁾ₜ(u,v)=R_t→0 V⁽ᶜᵃᵐ⁾ₜ(u,v),

    		(1)

    where R_t→0 denotes the rotation from the camera basis of frame t to the first-frame camera basis. We apply only rotation because scene flow is a vector quantity rather than a 3D point. This representation keeps spatial indexing local to each frame while expressing all motion vectors in a temporally stable basis. As a result, the predicted dynamics remain consistent under camera motion and align naturally with the depth, ray, and point-based geometry produced by DA3. Despite being a seemingly minor change, the new head has a substantial effect in practice: it consistently improves reconstruction, camera, and depth estimation quality on various dynamic scenes compared with stitched variants without motion modeling, as shown in our experiments.

    3.2 Latent-to-Geometry Model Stitching

    Following recent works in model stitching [75, 29, 37], we design a simple learnable module to stitch the video generator and the augmented DA3 together, allowing the video latent to be directly decoded into full 4D geometry, including depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow. Let I^1:T be a video clip and let z₀^1:T=𝔼ᵥₐₑ(I^1:T) be its Wan 2.1 VAE latent [90]. We first upsample the latent to the spatial and temporal resolution required by DA3: z̃₀^1:T=Up_(sₜ,sₕ,s_w)(z₀^1:T)∈ℝ^(sₜt)×(sₕh)×(s_ww)×C. A learnable 3D stitching module S_θ then maps the upsampled latent tensor into the channel dimension of a DA3 encoder block, h⁽ᵏ⁾=S_θ(z̃₀^1:T). In our implementation S_θ is a compact spatiotemporal projection, instantiated as a 3D convolution. Its temporal kernel aggregates neighboring latent frames, and its spatial stride matches the VAE grid to the DA3 patch grid.

    The injection layer is not chosen heuristically. For a set of paired clips, we extract Wan 2.1 VAE latents and frozen DA3 candidate features from several early encoder blocks. For each candidate block k, we solve a regularized linear fitting problem,

    (k^⋆,θ₀)=\arg\min_k,θ∑ᵢ∥S_θ(z̃₀^1:T)-g⁽ᵏ⁾ᵢ∥₂²+λ∥θ∥₂²,

    		(2)

    where g⁽ᵏ⁾ᵢ is the frozen DA3 feature grid at block k for clip i. This procedure selects the block whose representation is most linearly reachable from the video VAE latent [29, 3]. It also provides a stable initialization θ₀ for the stitching module. The selected block acts as the interface between the generative video prior and the geometric reconstruction prior.

    After stitching, the original RGB patch embedding and the encoder blocks before k^⋆ in DA3 are bypassed. The projected latent tokens are combined with DA3 special tokens and positional encodings, then processed by the remaining DA3 encoder blocks and the native dense heads, Ĝ=H^DA3_k^⋆:L(h^(k^⋆)). The output Ĝ contains depth, camera rays, confidence maps, and scene flow. This design is important because the stitched decoder reads the denoised video latent directly. It does not need to first decode the latent into RGB and then run a separate geometry model. Visual RGB generation and 3D reconstruction are instead two synchronized readouts of the same latent video state.

    3.3 Stitched Decoder Finetuning

    Here, we describe how to finetune the stitched decoder to adapt to the new latent input distribution and obtain accurate geometry predictions. Unlike VIST3A [29] which only distills RGB features, we employ a hybrid training strategy that combines teacher-student distillation with ground-truth (GT) supervision. The teacher-student distillation follows the same principle as VIST3A, where the teacher is the original frozen DA3 model augmented with the new scene flow head. This teacher model takes the ground-truth RGB video clip as input and produces all types of 4D geometric outputs as supervision signals. The student is the stitched decoder, which takes the Wan VAE latent of the same clip as input and produces the same set of geometric outputs. For the GT supervision, we utilize the 3D annotations provided in the dataset as explicit regression targets.

    Following the formulation in [Lin et al. [64]], our training objective integrates dense geometric matching with spatial and temporal regularization constraints,

    L_geo=λ_DL_depth+λ_RL_ray+λ_CL_camera+λ_MLₘₒₜᵢₒₙ+λ_TLₜₑₘₚₒᵣₐₗ.

    		(3)

    We also apply distillation to the depth and ray confidence maps using small weighting factors. The training details are discussed in AppendixB in detail. We keep the video diffusion transformer strictly frozen throughout this stage. This entire training phase exclusively focuses on transforming the DA3 decoder into a robust geometric readout mechanism for the Wan latent space.

    3.4 Joint Video and 4D Geometry Training

    Once the stitched decoder is finetuned, we use it as a differentiable geometry critic for the video diffusion model. The video model is trained with the standard latent flow-matching objective [115]. For each clip, we sample a scalar diffusion time τ∈[0,1] and use the corresponding scheduler noise scale σ_τ∈ℝ. Both values are shared by all latent frames in the clip and broadcast over space and channels. Omitting the batch dimension, let z_τ^1:T∈ℝ^T_ℓ×h×w×C_z denote the noisy Wan latent trajectory at time τ, where T_ℓ is the latent-frame length, (h,w) is the VAE spatial grid, and C_z=16 for Wan. The conditioning tuple c=(eₚ,z_ctx,m_ctx) contains the text-action embeddings eₚ∈ℝ^Lₚ×d_c and context-frame latents z_ctx∈ℝ^T_c×h×w×C_z with a binary prefix mask m_ctx∈{0,1}^T_ℓ×h×w×1. Given z_τ^1:T, τ, and c, the diffusion transformer predicts a velocity field v_φ(z_τ^1:T,τ,c)∈ℝ^T_ℓ×h×w×C_z. We convert the velocity prediction into a clean-latent estimate

    ẑ₀^1:T=z_τ^1:T-σ_τ v_φ(z_τ^1:T,τ,c),

    		(4)

    where ẑ₀^1:T has the same tensor shape as z_τ^1:T and is passed directly into the frozen stitched decoder. The joint objective is

    Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ=L_FM+λ_geo L_geo(D_stitch(ẑ₀)),

    		(5)

    where L_FM denotes the latent flow-matching loss and D_stitch represents the frozen stitched decoder. The geometric penalty L_geo is strictly identical to the objective formulated in Equation3. During this joint optimization phase, we exclusively utilize the teacher-student distillation mechanism for action-conditioned videos. As introduced previously, an independently loaded raw DA3 model serves as the teacher network. It processes the ground-truth RGB clip to provide the reference targets for depth, ray maps, and scene flow. For image-to-video generation, the first frame is encoded as the conditioning prefix [87]. The diffusion loss can mask the conditioned prefix, while the geometry loss can be applied to the generated suffix. As a result, Plan4D learns a single latent trajectory that must satisfy both appearance realism and dense 4D consistency. At inference time, the final latent sequence is decoded by the Wan VAE into RGB video and by the stitched DA3 decoder into depth, camera rays, and scene flow.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Settings.

    Implementation.Plan4D is trained in three stages on diverse datasets due to the lack of large-scale data with paired action and dense 4D annotations. (1) We train the designed scene-flow head on top of frozen DA3 using PointOdyssey [118], Dynamic Replica [49], Virtual KITTI 2 [14], BlinkVision [62], and OmniWorld-Game [119] for 20 epochs on 16 H100 GPUs. (2) We fit the latent-to-geometry stitching module on a small subset of the above datasets to initialize the interface from Wan latents to DA3 tokens. Then we finetune the stitched decoder with the scene-flow-head data mixture augmented by ScanNet++ [109] and MVS-Synth [39]. This stage uses 64 H20 GPUs and runs one hybrid epoch over the full data mixture, where the same mixed sampling schedule is traversed once with ground-truth geometric supervision and once with teacher-student distillation. When a ground-truth-supervised sample does not provide scene-flow annotations, we set its scene-flow loss to zero. (3) We finally train the DiT on a subset of Action100M [15] for one epoch using 64 H20 GPUs. All stages use a per-GPU batch size of 1. Additional dataset details, optimization details, losses, and supervision definitions are provided in AppendixB.

    Evaluation.

    We evaluate Plan4D along three axes that correspond to its intended use as a generative 4D world model. (1) we evaluate dynamic 4D geometry through scene flow on MOVi-F [31], Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips, and report endpoint error together with APD_0.05 against reconstruction and motion baselines. (2) we test whether the stitched decoder preserves DA3 geometry after replacing the RGB encoder with a Wan-latent input pathway. This evaluation covers reconstruction, camera, and depth benchmarks, including ETH3D [79], ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K [19], MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal [83], with comparisons to RGB-based 3D foundation models and latent-to-geometry baselines. Scene-flow metrics are computed after rescaling predictions to the target point-map scale. Depth uses per-clip scale-shift alignment, while camera and reconstruction follow the official DA3 bench protocol, with first-camera pose alignment for relative-pose metrics and Umeyama scale alignment for reconstruction. (3) finally, we evaluate full action-conditioned 4D world generation on RLBench [45] (210 samples), HOIGen-1M [67] (200 samples), Dynamic Replica (480 samples), and PointOdyssey (375 samples). To further assess in-the-wild generalization, we additionally sample 100 five-second clips from Epic-Kitchens-100 [23], which contains everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments, and evaluate all compared methods under the same joint-generation protocol. These benchmarks test whether a single generated rollout can jointly preserve visual quality [65, 120], action-text alignment [16], and temporally coherent 4D structure. We report video quality and instruction following with VBench-style video metrics and video-caption similarity [42]. For depth, reconstruction, and camera estimation, we follow the same protocol as the stitched-decoder evaluation. We compare with recent 4D world-generation and geometry-generation baselines, including VIST3A [29], TesserAct [117], and Gen3R [37], on the modalities each method supports.

    4.2 Main Results

    Scene Flow Estimation.

    We first test whether a frozen DA3 geometry prior can support dynamic 4D motion prediction beyond static reconstruction. This is a stringent setting because scene flow requires temporally coherent geometry rather than accurate per-frame depth alone. Table1 shows that both scene-flow variants remain competitive on all three benchmarks while using the smallest training set among the compared methods. The RGB-based DA3 variant is particularly strong on the harder real dynamic benchmarks, suggesting that frozen DA3 tokens already support reliable dense 4D motion readout. The stitched variant performs best on the controlled synthetic benchmark and remains near the top on Dynamic Replica, which matters because it is the decoder interface used during joint video training. The qualitative results in Figure3 show cleaner boundaries, more stable articulated motion, and better global 3D structure than the baselines. Overall, these results validate the first step of Plan4D: DA3 can be extended from geometry reconstruction to strong dynamic 4D readout, and this capability largely survives the latent-to-geometry stitching step.

    Stitched Geometry Decoder Preserves DA3 Behavior.

    We evaluate whether replacing DA3’s RGB input with Wan video latents preserves its depth, camera, and reconstruction behavior on held-out benchmarks. We compare against the latest state-of-the-art RGB-based DA3 and VGGT, and the aligned VIST3A-Stitched and Gen3R-VAE decoders. Table2 shows that our decoder remains closer to the RGB-based models than prior aligned decoders across all three geometry families. It slightly exceeds DA3 on Dynamic-RE10K camera estimation and remains competitive with VGGT on Dynamic Replica. Depth changes little on MOVi-F and declines moderately on RobbySimVal. Reconstruction shifts are larger, but our decoder remains closer to DA3 and VGGT in most settings and achieves the best completeness on Dynamic Replica. Figure4 shows that our decoder preserves DA3-like surface layout and global scene organization, while competing aligned models produce less faithful structure. This preserved geometry allows the frozen decoder to provide stable supervision for the video generator directly from latent rollouts.

    Joint 4D World Generation

    Table3 reports a compact subset of the full joint 4D generation benchmark in Table8. The subset covers HoiGen, Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey across video quality, depth and reconstruction, and camera estimation. On the 100 five-second Epic-Kitchens-100 clips, Plan4D leads on 10 of the 13 metrics in the full comparison. On video quality, Plan4D achieves the best subject consistency on all four datasets and the best caption similarity on Epic-Kitchens-100 and PointOdyssey. VIST3A has the highest caption similarity on HoiGen and Dynamic Replica. On Epic-Kitchens-100, Plan4D also achieves the best background consistency and image quality, while TesserAct has the best motion smoothness and VIST3A the highest aesthetic quality. These results show that the shared latent rollout supports strong visual consistency and action-text alignment across diverse scenes.

    For depth and reconstruction, Plan4D gives the lowest AbsRel on all four datasets in the subset. It also obtains the best Chamfer-L1 on Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey, while Gen3R has the lowest Chamfer-L1 on HoiGen. On Epic-Kitchens-100, Plan4D leads on all three depth metrics. The HoiGen exception separates local reconstruction quality from the full world-generation objective. Gen3R can produce a strong point-cloud distance on one hand-object benchmark, but its video quality and camera stability are much weaker in the same setting.

    Camera metrics show the largest gap in global 4D consistency. Plan4D obtains the best RRA@5 on all four datasets in the subset and the best RPE-R on HoiGen, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey. On Epic-Kitchens-100, it leads on both relative-rotation accuracy thresholds. TesserAct has the lowest RPE-R on Epic-Kitchens-100, while Plan4D maintains strong performance across datasets and metric families. The Epic-Kitchens-100 results complement HoiGen with quantitative evidence across two real-world human-object interaction benchmarks, supporting the applicability of Plan4D to everyday interactions beyond the original evaluation setting. The qualitative comparisons in Figure5 and Figure6 show the same pattern visually: the generated RGB frames, RGB-D structure, and global dynamic point clouds remain better aligned under complex action-conditioned rollouts. These results support the core design choice of supervising a pretrained video generator with a frozen geometric readout rather than learning dense 4D structure from scratch.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    We conduct an ablation study to understand the contribution of each component in our joint-training objective. The results are summarized in Table4, with results on HoiGen and Dynamic Replica using the same action-conditioned generation protocol. The RGB-only variant retains strong subject and background consistency, but its depth and camera estimates are less accurate than those of the full model on both datasets. The geometry-only variant improves depth on HoiGen, but sacrifices visual consistency and performs worse across all reported metrics on Dynamic Replica. The full objective gives the best subject and background consistency and camera estimation on both datasets, and also leads on depth on Dynamic Replica. These results support combining flow matching with geometric supervision to preserve action-conditioned video quality while improving the depth and camera structure decoded from the same future latent state. Additional settings and analysis appear in SectionC.1.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduce the problem of generative plannable 4D worlds, where a model must generate future scenes with rich 4D attributes, including RGB appearance, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions. To this end, we propose Plan4D, a unified framework that decouples the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnects them through a stitched latent world model. By augmenting frozen DA3 with a token-only scene-flow head and learning a latent-to-geometry stitching interface from video VAE latents to geometry tokens, Plan4D turns a pretrained video generator into an actionable 4D world model whose RGB, depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow are read out from the same evolving latent state in a single feed-forward pass. Experiments show that this design preserves strong geometric behavior while improving dense 4D world generation across scene flow, reconstruction, and action-conditioned future prediction, without requiring manual 4D annotations for action videos. We hope this perspective helps move future world modeling beyond video-only prediction toward unified, measurable, and plannable 4D world models.

    Appendix A Frozen DA3 Tokens Already Encode Cross-Frame Motion Cues

    The lightweight DPT scene flow head above is only useful if the frozen DA3 encoder tokens already preserve motion-relevant structure. The central question of this section is therefore simple: before any scene-flow supervision reaches the decoder, do frozen DA3 tokens already know which location in frame t+1 corresponds to a location in frame t? If the answer is yes, then a shallow head can decode dense motion by reading out a representation that already contains cross-frame geometry and correspondence cues. If the answer is no, then good scene-flow predictions would have to come from the capacity of the head alone.

    To make this question concrete, let zₜ(p) denote the frozen DA3 token at spatial cell p in frame t. Point Odyssey [118] provides ground-truth tracks, which let us identify the corresponding target cell p⁺ in frame t+1 for each valid source cell p. We then probe the token space without using the scene flow head. Our analysis uses the Point Odyssey test split with 128 clips from 5 scenes. All values in Table 5 are weighted over clips by the number of valid token pairs or valid flow tokens. Figure 7 aggregates all 6,132,636 positive pairs, 6,132,636 negative pairs, and 2,160,723 token-difference vectors.

    We use four complementary probes, each answering a different question about the frozen representation. The first probe is correspondence similarity[84]. It asks whether a token is more similar to its true match than to an unrelated token from the next frame:

    sₚₒₛ=\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(p⁺)), s_neg=\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(q⁻)),

    		(6)

    where q⁻ is a random negative sampled from frame t+1. This is the cleanest test of whether correspondence information is present [44]. If frozen DA3 tokens contain motion-relevant structure, the sₚₒₛ distribution should shift to the right of the s_neg distribution. The margin Δs=sₚₒₛ-s_neg and the probability \Pr(sₚₒₛ>s_neg) summarize how reliably the two distributions separate.

    The second probe is token retrieval[74]. Instead of comparing one positive and one negative, we search over all target tokens in frame t+1:

    p̂=\arg\max_q∈ℙₜ₊₁\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(q)).

    		(7)

    This is a stronger operational test. It asks whether nearest-neighbor search in frozen token space can recover the correct destination cell. We report Top-1 exact, which measures whether the retrieved cell is exactly the ground-truth cell, and PCK@1 and PCK@3, which measure whether retrieval falls within 1 or 3 token cells of the ground-truth location [107]. High retrieval accuracy means that the token space is not only separable on average, but also organized enough to support direct correspondence lookup.

    The third probe is a token-flow readout. After retrieval returns p̂, we interpret it as a token-level motion estimate d̂=p̂-p and compare it with the ground-truth token displacement. This probe is more demanding than similarity or retrieval because it asks a single nearest-neighbor lookup to act as a motion predictor. The resulting endpoint error and direction cosine should be interpreted as evidence for how directly motion can be read out from the frozen tokens without a learned decoder [104].

    The fourth probe is PCA on token differences. For each matched pair, we form

    Δzₜ(p)=zₜ₊₁(p⁺)-zₜ(p).

    		(8)

    We then perform PCA on these token differences [78]. This analysis does not test whether motion is present at all. The earlier probes already answer that question more directly. Instead, PCA asks a more specific question: is the motion signal concentrated in a small linear subspace, or is it distributed across many token dimensions? If the first few principal components explain most of the variance, then motion could be close to linearly disentangled [2]. If the variance remains spread out, then motion is still present, but encoded in a more distributed form. This distinction matters for interpreting the role of the DPT head. A low-dimensional linear code would be easy to read out with almost any linear probe, while a distributed code benefits from structured multiscale decoding.

    Before discussing the numbers, it is useful to clarify how they should be interpreted. Similarity and retrieval are the strongest probes in this section because they make the fewest modeling assumptions. They only ask whether true cross-frame matches are already nearby in frozen token space. Token flow is a harder probe because it asks nearest-neighbor retrieval to behave like a motion estimator. PCA is the most indirect probe because a failure to find a low-dimensional linear motion axis does not mean that motion information is absent. It only means that the information is not cleanly isolated in the top principal components.

    Figure 7 and Table 5 provide direct evidence that frozen DA3 tokens preserve cross-frame correspondence structure. The similarity distributions are cleanly separated, with ground-truth matches consistently closer in token space than random negatives. Nearest-neighbor retrieval leads to the same conclusion under a stronger all-candidates test. These two probes show that, even without any learned motion decoder, the frozen representation already places true future matches near the source token and usually retrieves a target very close to the correct location.

    The token-flow probe refines this picture. A simple nearest-neighbor displacement readout already recovers meaningful motion, which indicates that the frozen tokens encode where points are likely to move. At the same time, this probe is weaker than similarity and retrieval, which suggests that the motion signal is not exposed as a trivial one-step velocity code. This is precisely where a structured decoder becomes useful. Our DPT head can pool multiscale context and impose spatial coherence to transform this latent correspondence signal into dense scene flow.

    The PCA results should be read as auxiliary evidence. The dominant components explain only a limited portion of the token-difference variance, and their alignment with flow magnitude remains weak. This does not argue against motion information in the frozen tokens. Instead, PCA indicates that motion is encoded in a distributed high-dimensional form rather than concentrated in a single linear direction.

    These results support a precise interpretation of our method. Frozen DA3 encoder tokens already contain scene-flow-relevant information, especially in the form of cross-frame correspondence structure. The strongest evidence comes from the probes that require almost no decoder assumptions, namely similarity separation and nearest-neighbor retrieval. The weaker token-flow and PCA probes refine this picture. They suggest that the motion signal is real, but distributed and not trivially linearized. Our DPT head succeeds because it decodes and regularizes this latent signal into dense metric predictions. In other words, the scene flow branch acts as an informed readout of the pretrained geometry representation, rather than a separate module that has to create motion information from scratch.

    Appendix B Training Details

    B.1 Dataset and Optimization Summary

    All dataset statistics in this paper correspond to the 81-frame manifests. Every manifest row therefore satisfies the temporal constraint T=4k+1 with T=81. Table6 summarizes the stage-wise training data. Stage 1 trains only the DA3 scene-flow readout. Stage 2 finetunes the stitched decoder with hybrid ground-truth and teacher-student supervision. Stage 3 optimizes the action-conditioned video model, where Action100M contributes text-conditioned video clips without paired 4D labels.

    Stage 1 mixes 11,956 training clips from five dynamic datasets. The sampler uses dataset-wise mixture weights of 1.0 together with a size-aware mixing exponent α=0.5, which interpolates between uniform-over-datasets and proportional-to-size sampling. The stage-1 manifest directory also contains held-out or diagnostic subsets such as PointOdyssey test, PointOdyssey sample, and Dynamic Replica valid clips for validation and smoke tests.

    Stage 2 contains 122,225 GT-capable training clips. Among them, 13,521 clips expose scene-flow labels, while the remaining 108,704 clips provide only depth, ray, camera, and point-cloud supervision. In hybrid decoder training, we build separate GT and distill dataloaders from the same manifest list and randomly shuffle the union of GT and distill steps once per epoch. This realizes one GT pass and one distillation pass over the full mixture in a single hybrid epoch.

    The stage-3 Action100M subset is constructed in two steps. We first start from the filtered 81-frame TI2V manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.filtered.jsonl, whose rows already satisfy task_type=ti2v, cond_frames=1, and num_frames=81. We then score the corresponding clip-level entries from action100m_clip_index_81f.filtered.jsonl and keep only clips that pass a high-precision action-quality filter. The clip-level decision uses fields such as prompt_action, level, and node_duration_sec. We drop clips with node duration shorter than 1.6 seconds, hierarchy depth above 10, missing action text, action text identical to the generic description, action text shorter than four words, prompt patterns dominated by on-screen text or audio-style narration, uncertain descriptions, or generic action stubs. The retained manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.action_hq.keep.jsonl contains 249,422 clips, which is 28.6% of the 871,785 filtered TI2V rows. Because Action100M does not provide paired 4D geometry, these clips are used only in the distillation branch during stage 3.

    Per-dataset roles.

    PointOdyssey provides articulated outdoor motion with sparse track supervision that we rasterize into dense forward scene flow, which makes it particularly useful for supervising correspondence-aware motion. Dynamic Replica contributes denser dynamic stereo geometry with strong camera and scene-flow signals. BlinkVision, Virtual KITTI 2, and OmniWorld broaden the synthetic motion distribution across indoor scenes, driving scenes, and open-world gameplay trajectories. ScanNet++ and MVS-Synth do not provide scene flow in our 81-frame setup, but they substantially enrich multiview depth, camera, and point-cloud supervision during stitched-decoder finetuning. Action100M serves a different purpose from the geometry datasets. It injects large-scale action-conditioned video semantics into the joint model while relying on the frozen DA3 teacher for geometric targets.

    Evaluation datasets.

    We report three groups of held-out evaluations. For dynamic 4D motion, we evaluate on MOVi-F, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips. MOVi-F tests controlled synthetic object motion, Dynamic Replica tests realistic dynamic stereo scenes, and PointOdyssey emphasizes articulated motion with long temporal support. For stitched-decoder geometry preservation, we evaluate on ETH3D, ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K, MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal. These datasets cover static reconstruction, indoor multiview geometry, dynamic camera estimation, and robot-centric depth prediction. For action-conditioned world generation, we evaluate on RLBench with 210 samples, HOIGen-1M with 200 samples, Dynamic Replica with 480 samples, and PointOdyssey with 375 samples, which together span manipulation, hand-object interaction, and general dynamic-scene futures. We additionally evaluate 100 five-second Epic-Kitchens-100 clips to assess in-the-wild generalization to everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments. This evaluation complements HoiGen with a second real-world human-object interaction benchmark.

    Stage-3 comparison scope.

    We exclude several recent world-generation systems from the stage-3 comparison because they assume additional control inputs beyond the setting targeted in this paper. PointWorld requires depth input [41]. FantasyWorld, HY-World 2.0, Lyra 2.0, Geometry Forcing, and TeleWorld rely on trajectory-level control signals [22, 43, 80, 100, 20]. Kinema4D further requires robot-action kinematic representations [105]. These methods therefore do not match the task of predicting future RGB video together with dense 4D geometry from only an observed scene context and a text-specified action, so we do not include them in the stage-3 comparison.

    Evaluation protocol and metric definitions.

    We follow the same three-way evaluation split as in the main paper and expand the scoring protocol here. Scene flow. We score only valid moving pixels indicated by the deformation mask. Predictions are first rescaled to the target point-map scale of each clip. When a model predicts relative flow, we restore the target scale with the clip-level scene-flow scale before metric computation. If a benchmark provides native-resolution labels, we resize predictions to that evaluation resolution before scoring. We report

    EPE=(1)/(|V_sf|)∑_(t,p)∈V_sf∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₂, APD_0.05=(1)/(|V_sf|)∑_(t,p)∈V_sf1 [∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₂<0.05],

    		(9)

    where V_sf is the set of valid motion pixels, m̂_t,p is the predicted 3D displacement from frame t to frame t+1, and m_t,p is the ground-truth displacement. Lower EPE is better, while higher APD_0.05 is better.

    Depth. Depth metrics use per-clip scale-shift alignment. For each clip, we solve one scale a and one shift b jointly over all valid depth pixels and evaluate ad̂+b against ground-truth depth:

    (a^⋆,b^⋆)=\arg\min_a,b∑_(t,p)∈V_d(ad̂_t,p+b-d_t,p)².

    		(10)

    We report

    AbsRel=(1)/(|V_d|)∑_(t,p)∈V_d(|a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆-d_t,p|)/(d_t,p)

    		(11)

    δ₁=(1)/(|V_d|)∑_(t,p)∈V_d1 [\max ((a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆)/(d_t,p),(d_t,p)/(a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆))<1.25].

    		(12)

    Lower AbsRel is better, while higher δ₁ is better.

    Camera. Camera metrics follow the official DA3 bench. Predicted and ground-truth camera trajectories are first converted to the first-camera gauge. We then evaluate all frame pairs (i,j) through their relative transforms. Let eʳᵢⱼ denote the relative rotation error in degrees and let eᵗᵢⱼ denote the angle between the predicted and ground-truth relative translation directions. On Dynamic Replica we report

    RRA@5^∘=(1)/(|ℙ|)∑_(i,j)∈ℙ1 [eʳᵢⱼ<5^∘],

    		(13)

    which measures relative rotation accuracy over all frame pairs. On Dynamic-RE10K we report AUC₁₅ and AUC₃₀. These metrics are computed from the per-pair error

    mᵢⱼ=\max (eʳᵢⱼ,eᵗᵢⱼ),

    		(14)

    and summarize the cumulative accuracy curve of mᵢⱼ up to the corresponding angular threshold. Higher camera metrics are better.

    3D reconstruction. Reconstruction also follows the official DA3 bench. We estimate a global Umeyama alignment between predicted and ground-truth camera trajectories and use the recovered scale to place predicted depth in metric units before TSDF fusion. When predicted poses are used for reconstruction, the same fit also aligns the fused camera trajectory. The fused prediction is then compared with the benchmark ground-truth geometry using the dataset-specific threshold and downsampling settings from the DA3 bench. ETH3D and ScanNet++ evaluate against points sampled from the ground-truth mesh, and ScanNet++ additionally crops the predicted point cloud to the ground-truth bounding box with a small margin before scoring. For predicted points P and ground-truth points G, we report

    Acc.=(1)/(|P|)∑_x∈P\min_y∈G∥x-y∥₂, Comp.=(1)/(|G|)∑_y∈G\min_x∈P∥x-y∥₂.

    		(15)

    Precision and recall are the fractions of predicted and ground-truth points whose nearest-neighbor distance is below the dataset threshold ε, and the F-score is their harmonic mean:

    Prec.=(1)/(|P|)∑_x∈P1 [\min_y∈G∥x-y∥₂<ε],

    		(16)

    Rec.=(1)/(|G|)∑_y∈G1 [\min_x∈P∥x-y∥₂<ε],

    		(17)

    F-score=(2 Prec. Rec.)/(Prec.+Rec.).

    		(18)

    Lower Acc. and Comp. are better, while higher F-score is better.

    Joint world generation. For RGB video quality, higher video-caption similarity indicates stronger alignment between the generated video and the conditioning action text. RLBench and HOIGen-1M use their native action annotations, while Dynamic Replica and PointOdyssey do not provide action-level text in our stage-3 evaluation split, so we generate per-clip action captions with Qwen-VL-30B-Thinking and use them as the conditioning text for all compared methods. When a baseline exposes a compatible geometry output, we score its generated 4D structure with the same geometry protocol described above.

    Epic-Kitchens-100 evaluation setting.

    We sample 100 clips, each five seconds long, and follow the same action-conditioned joint 4D generation protocol as the original comparison. Each method receives the initial RGB frame and an action description. We compare Plan4D, TesserAct, Gen3R, and VIST3A using the same metric definitions and alignment procedures. The full evaluation reports six video metrics, namely subject consistency (SC), background consistency (BC), aesthetic quality (AQ), image quality (IQ), motion smoothness (MS), and video-caption similarity (Cap.Sim). Geometry is evaluated with depth AbsRel, δ₁, δ₂, and Chamfer-L1, together with camera RPE-R, RRA@10, and RRA@5. Higher scores are better except for AbsRel, Chamfer-L1, and RPE-R. The complete results appear in Table8, and Table3 retains six representative metrics for comparison with the other benchmarks.

    Stage-wise optimization details.

    For stage 1, the 81-frame manifest configuration uses AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁵, weight decay 10⁻², β=(0.9,0.999), 100 warmup steps, gradient accumulation 2, and bf16 mixed precision. Inputs are resized to 504×504 with upper-bound resizing, the clip overlap is 1 frame, and the scene-flow loss adds a zero-last-frame penalty with weight 0.1. The main paper reports a 20-epoch run on 16 H100 GPUs with per-GPU batch size 1.

    For stage 2, the stitched-decoder hybrid launchers use AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻⁴, bf16 mixed precision, 504×504 inputs, and per-GPU batch size 1. The representative 81-frame launchers use a 50-step warmup and train the stitching layer together with LoRA adapters on the stitched DA3 blocks by default, while still supporting full finetuning of the stitched parts. The main paper reports one hybrid epoch on 64 H20 GPUs.

    For stage 3, the stitched joint LoRA launcher uses AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁴, cosine decay, 1000 warmup steps, LoRA rank 32 on the DiT, gradient checkpointing, 81 frames at 532×532 resolution, condition dropout 0.1, and geometry-loss warmup from 0.001 to 1.0 over the first 500 steps. We apply mask_condition_loss on conditioned prefixes and geo_supervise_generated_only on the generated suffix. The main paper reports one epoch on 64 H20 GPUs with per-GPU batch size 1.

    B.2 Scene Flow Head Training

    We train the scene-flow branch as a readout on top of a fixed DA3 representation. The DA3 backbone, depth head, ray head, and camera modules are loaded from the pretrained checkpoint and kept frozen. We inject the DPT-style scene-flow head and its coordinate adapter from the scene-flow preset, load the original DA3 weights with non-strict matching, and optimize only the parameters of the new head. During training, each clip is passed through the frozen DA3 encoder to extract the four multiscale token maps. The head decodes these tokens into a dense three-channel motion field, and the adapter rotates the local camera-frame prediction into the first-frame camera basis.

    The training target is a forward displacement field from frame t to frame t+1. All datasets expose the same fields: RGB frames, camera intrinsics, world-to-camera extrinsics, a scene-flow tensor, a per-clip scale, and a binary deformation mask. We use relative scene flow by default. Metric displacements are expressed in the first-frame camera basis and normalized by a robust clip-level scale, which makes the head less sensitive to the absolute size of a scene.

    Let m̂_t,p be the predicted motion at pixel p in frame t, let m_t,p be the target, and let a_t,p∈{0,1} be the deformation mask. The scene-flow loss [60, 88] is

    L_sf=(∑_t,pa_t,p∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₁)/(\max(1,∑_t,pa_t,p))+λₗₐₛₜ1/HW∑ₚ∥m̂_T,p∥₂.

    		(19)

    The first term is evaluated only at valid motion pixels. It never falls back to full-image supervision, which is important for datasets where motion labels come from sparse tracks. The second term softly enforces the last frame to be zero because there is no target frame T+1. We use masked L1 loss in the main configuration.

    B.3 Latent-to-Geometry Model Stitching Training

    The stitching stage determines where the video latent space should enter DA3 and initializes the projection into that token space. For each training clip, we encode the RGB video with the frozen Wan VAE and extract candidate DA3 token maps from encoder blocks. The Wan latent has 16 channels and is temporally compressed. Before fitting the stitch, we upsample it back to the video frame rate with T=4(Tᵥₐₑ-1)+1 and resize it to the spatial resolution required by the DA3 patch grid.

    For each candidate block k, we fit a 3D convolutional stitch S_θ⁽ᵏ⁾ from the upsampled Wan latent to the frozen DA3 token grid. The fit is a streaming ridge regression problem shown in Equation2.

    The streaming solver accumulates normal-equation statistics over cached tensor batches, which avoids storing a large design matrix. We rank candidate blocks by the reconstruction mean squared error and choose the block with the lowest error. In our DA3 setting, the stitch maps the 16-channel Wan latent to the 1536-channel DA3 token width through a compact spatiotemporal convolution. This procedure gives both the injection layer and the initial weights for the later trainable stitched decoder.

    B.4 Stitched Decoder Finetuning

    The linear stitch is only an initialization. We next train a stitched decoder that accepts Wan latents but preserves the geometry behavior of DA3. The Wan VAE is frozen. The pretrained DA3 teacher is frozen. The trainable student contains the stitching module and stitched DA3 parts. The video diffusion transformer is not trained in this stage.

    We use two complementary sources of supervision. In the distillation branch, the teacher consumes the ground-truth RGB clip, while the student consumes the Wan latent of the same clip. The teacher and student outputs are aligned in time and space before computing losses. The distillation objective is

    L_distill=λ_D∥D̂-Dᵀ∥₁+λ_∇DL_∇D(D̂,Dᵀ)+λ_R∥R̂-Rᵀ∥₁(20)
    +λ_cD∥Ĉ^D-C^D,T∥₁+λ_cR∥Ĉ^R-C^R,T∥₁+λ_CL_C
    +λ_M∥M̂-Mᵀ∥₁+λ_TL_T.

    Here D denotes depth, R denotes the six-channel ray map, C^D and C^R denote confidence maps, and M denotes scene flow. The camera term L_C compares decoded intrinsics and relative camera motion. The temporal term L_T matches depth differences between adjacent frames, which discourages frame-wise geometry flicker.

    In the ground-truth branch, the student is supervised against dataset depth, ray, camera, valid-mask, and optional scene-flow annotations. The objective is

    L_GT=λ_DL_D+λ_∇DL_∇D+λ_RL_R+λ_PL_P(21)
    +λ_CL_C+λ_ML_M+λ_TL_T.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：缺少显式 4D 建模，导致时间上几何一致性很弱。

要点：

  • 批评很直接：多数用于未来预测的世界模型**优先追求生成视频的美学质量**，但由于缺乏显式 4D 建模，**随时间变化的几何一致性**很有限
  • Plan4D 的目标是「可规划的 4D 世界模型」：在预测未来 RGB 视频的同时，输出**稠密 4D 几何**（深度、相机、点云等）
  • 「可规划（plannable）」意味着这些几何要能被下游用来做决策，而不只是给人看

为什么值得看：「世界模型能不能用来规划」取决于它输出的几何能不能被消费。把稠密 4D 几何与视频一起生成，等于把世界模型从「视频生成器」升级成「可查询的场景演化器」——这正是引擎需要的接口形态。

中文摘要：多数面向未来预测的世界模型把重点放在生成视频的美学质量上，但由于缺少显式的 4D 建模，它们在时间维度上的几何一致性相当有限。Plan4D 因此提出「可规划的 4D 世界模型」这一目标：在预测未来 RGB 视频的同时，输出稠密的 4D 几何，包括深度、相机参数与点云等，使结果可以被下游规划模块消费，而不只是给人观看。作者把它定位为通向「生成式可规划 4D 世界」的下一个里程碑——关键在于让世界模型输出的不只是画面，还有能被查询与利用的空间结构。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds

Abstract

Most world models for future prediction prioritize the aesthetic quality of generated videos, but offer only limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce Plan4D, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow, from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, Plan4D leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that Plan4D achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project.

††footnotetext: †Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Given an observed scene context and a set of text-specified actions, we consider the task of generative plannable 4D worlds, a new paradigm for predicting reliable futures for the physical world that jointly produces visually plausible RGB frames and physically grounded 4D geometry –including depth, camera dynamics, and scene flow –within a single feed-forward model. Prior observation-prediction models formulate future prediction largely as RGB synthesis [25, 86], often on a per-frame basis, notably UniSim [106], Genie 1–3 [13, 76, 8], NWM [10], and V-JEPA 2 [4]. By contrast, with our actionable 4D future world model, humans and AI agents can plan and execute complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in the explicit 3D environment, such as picking up a cup, opening a bottle, or navigating through a cluttered room. These dynamic 3D quantities are essential for accurate measurement, reliable simulation, and effective execution of downstream tasks [54, 24, 59, 41, 33].

A major bottleneck of this task is the lack of suitable datasets, namely action-conditioned video sequences paired with rich text and comprehensive 3D annotations, including camera trajectories, accurate dense depth and motion. For example, large-scale video-caption datasets [7, 98, 18] may still lack detailed captions for physical fine-grained actions; the latest Action-100M [15] dataset provides detailed action annotations but without 3D annotations, while most dynamic 3D datasets [31, 30, 51] are relatively small in scale or lack natural actions.

Correspondingly, powerful baselines have emerged in parallel on these separate data sources, including video generators [35, 12, 11, 81, 34, 53, 108, 90, 66, 87], action-conditioned world models [106, 13, 76, 8, 10, 4, 48, 58], and 3D reconstructors [97, 57, 96, 92, 52, 99, 64, 114]. Despite being trained to build the same physical world, these models still operate as isolated systems for particular tasks. Standard pixel-level generators excel at synthesizing visually realistic RGB frames [102], but typically lack physical consistency [101, 61]; and 3D models recover explicit geometry well [95] but are largely reconstruction-centric and static. Even advanced 4D frameworks [116, 47, 82, 121, 50, 73, 72, 55] only infer motion from observed frames and cannot generate action-conditioned future worlds. As a result, none of these families alone provides a generative plannable 4D world, in which appearance, geometry, camera and action-conditioned future dynamics evolve consistently over time.

What if, given these different dataset sources, we stitch them together to model the same underlying 4D world? To achieve such a generative plannable 4D world, we propose Plan4D, a unified framework for planning and generating dense 4D worlds from observed context and action descriptions. Our core insight is to decouple the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnect them through a stitched latent world model that jointly plans RGB appearance and dense 4D geometry, unlike recent methods [85, 117, 22, 71, 27] that attempt to learn a 4D world model’s geometry from scratch. Such a paradigm reduces the task’s learning difficulty and data requirements, while allowing us to leverage the powerful priors of pretrained video generators and 3D reconstructors to achieve complex, long-horizon and fine-grained dynamics.

In practice, this paradigm requires solving several coupled challenges. i) the model must extend a frozen 3D foundation model from static scenes to dynamic 4D prediction while preserving its geometric consistency. ii) it must align geometry tokens with the latent space of a video generator without destroying the pretrained generative prior. iii) it must learn from real, unlabeled action videos without dense 4D supervision [112]. iv) it must also ensure consistency across the generated RGB, depth, camera, point clouds, and scene flow. Recent methods, including VIST3A [29], Geometry Forcing [100], and Gen3R [37], couple 3D reconstructors with video generators for static text-to-3D or scene-level 3D generation. We extend this direction to full actionable 4D world generation, jointly predicting full 4D geometry and appearance in future video sequences depicting fine-grained actions.

Unlike prior approaches that use geometry mainly as an auxiliary constraint [100, 6, 110, 26, 3], or decode geometry only after RGB generation [24], our Plan4D turns a video generator into an actionable 4D world model, which explicitly aligns future appearance and 4D structure inside the shared evolving video latent state. To preserve strong geometric priors while extending them beyond reconstruction, we augment Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3) with a lightweight token-only scene-flow head that predicts dense forward 3D motion from intermediate geometry tokens, while keeping its pretrained depth and camera-ray predictions intact. To connect this geometric readout with future generation, we learn a latent-to-geometry stitching module that maps video VAE latents into a selected DA3 block and trains it with token distillation and geometric supervision. The resulting stitched decoder provides a stable, differentiable interface from video latents to full 4D geometry. We then train the video generator against this frozen geometric interface, so unlabeled action videos can supervise not only visual prediction but also physically grounded 4D consistency. At inference time, a single generated latent future yields RGB frames and dense 4D geometry in one feed-forward pass.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We take a step towards the new paradigm of generative plannable 4D worlds, which jointly generates future RGB appearance and corresponding full 4D geometry, including depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions.

  • •

    We propose Plan4D, a unified framework with a scene-flow head and a geometry-video stitching mechanism that connect a frozen 3D foundation model with a pretrained video generator, preserving geometric priors while enabling action-conditioned dynamic 4D future prediction from unlabeled videos.

  • •

    We illustrate how Plan4D can achieve state-of-the-art performance in dense 4D world generation, improving both visual realism and geometric accuracy across scene flow, 3D reconstruction, and action-conditioned video prediction through extensive experiments.

    • 2 Related Works

    4D world models. Recent work has begun to model 4D worlds from two complementary directions. Explicit dynamics methods such as ParticleFormer [40] and PointWorld [41] predict particle trajectories or point-level motion, but mainly operate in structured 3D state spaces rather than generating rich future 4D. 4D-native generative models instead learn spatiotemporal world evolution, ranging from dynamic reconstruction, visual planning, and image-to-4D generation in Aether [85] and 4DNeX [21], to RGB-D or geometry-aware scene generation in TesserAct [117] and Robo4DGen [69]. GWM [70], iMoWM [113], and Kinema4D [105] further explore Gaussian, tokenized, and kinematics-driven representations, while FantasyWorld [22], WorldReel [27], TeleWorld [20], HY-World 2.0 [43], and Lyra 2.0 [80] couple video generation with geometric prediction for more unified world modeling. Despite this progress, existing systems typically emphasize either explicit geometric forecasting or large-scale generative simulation, and they rarely integrate the complementary priors of pretrained geometry foundation models into the latent dynamics of video generation.

    Aligning 3D Reconstruction and Video Generation. Early uses of generative priors for 3D synthesis mostly follow a cascade, where geometric constraints are applied to generated outputs rather than to internal generative states [77, 28, 94]. Later methods tighten this link through reconstruction-guided diffusion or distillation, as in GenFusion [103], VideoScene [91], and Lyra [5]. Recent work moves the alignment into feature or latent spaces. Geometry Forcing [100] aligns intermediate diffusion features with pretrained geometric representations [111], Gen3R [37] aligns geometry and appearance latents for joint generation, and GLD [46] repurposes geometric features as multi-view diffusion latents. From the model-stitching view [56, 9], VIST3A [29] connects a pretrained video VAE with a 3D network at linearly matchable layers. Our method builds on this direction, but stitches a video diffusion model to a 3D foundation model so that RGB synthesis and dense 4D geometry can be optimized and decoded from a shared latent rollout.

    3 Plan4D

    Given an observed context O={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^M and the planned action space A, our goal is to learn a generative plannable 4D world model f_θ that is conditioned on O and A and predicts a set of future 4D representations: f_θ:{O,A}↦{Iₜ,Dₜ,rₜ,Vₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, where A is a sequence of textual action descriptions p. The model f_θ learns a video latent trajectory that is conditioned on the observed context and the action description, and reads out the future RGB video frames Iₜ∈ℝ^H×W×3; and its corresponding depth maps Dₜ∈ℝ^H×W, camera ray maps rₜ∈ℝ^H×W×6, and full 4D scene flow Vₜ∈ℝ^H×W×3. The ray maps rₜ encode the camera origin and the ray directions for each pixel, which can be used to reconstruct the 3D point cloud of the scene. The scene flow Vₜ encodes the 3D motion of each pixel from time t to t+1111 Since we only define the forward flow, we then simplify V_t→t+1 as Vₜ..

    We parametrize f_θ with a model-stitching architecture that couples a video generator, LongCat-Video [87] (which uses the Wan 2.1 VAE [90]), with a foundational 3D reconstructor, Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3). The key insight is that, by building on the pretrained video generator and 3D reconstructor, our model can leverage the complementary priors of these two foundational models to achieve both high visual fidelity and strong geometric consistency in the generated future videos, unlike training it from scratch [85, 117, 22, 27], which is extremely challenging and data-hungry. To improve the motion modeling capability of DA3, we first augment it with an auxiliary DPT-style scene flow head in section3.1. In section3.2, we then stitch the video generator and the augmented DA3 together through a learnable latent-to-geometry stitching module, followed by a distillation and geometric supervision process to calibrate the stitched model in section3.3. Finally, we train the joint model in section3.4.

    3.1 Augmenting DA3 for Dynamic Scene Flow Prediction

    The physical world is not a collection of independent per-frame geometries. To model the dynamics and correspondence of the 4D world, we augment DA3 [64] with a dense scene flow head that predicts the 3D motion of each pixel. Following the original DPT-style decoder in DA3, the new head ingests the four intermediate token maps of the frozen encoder, and outputs a dense three-channel motion field via a lightweight prediction layer. Note that, the original encoder, as well as the depth and camera pose branches, remains unchanged; we simply add a dedicated motion branch. Our analysis in AppendixA shows that frozen DA3 tokens already encode cross-frame motion cues, which supports using this branch as a lightweight readout rather than a full motion model. In particular, for each frame t, the new head predicts a scene flow on the pixel lattice of that frame. Each valid pixel stores the forward 3D displacement from time t to t+1. The raw prediction is produced in the local camera basis of frame t and is mapped to a common reference frame with a lightweight adapter,

    V⁽⁰⁾ₜ(u,v)=R_t→0 V⁽ᶜᵃᵐ⁾ₜ(u,v),

    		(1)

    where R_t→0 denotes the rotation from the camera basis of frame t to the first-frame camera basis. We apply only rotation because scene flow is a vector quantity rather than a 3D point. This representation keeps spatial indexing local to each frame while expressing all motion vectors in a temporally stable basis. As a result, the predicted dynamics remain consistent under camera motion and align naturally with the depth, ray, and point-based geometry produced by DA3. Despite being a seemingly minor change, the new head has a substantial effect in practice: it consistently improves reconstruction, camera, and depth estimation quality on various dynamic scenes compared with stitched variants without motion modeling, as shown in our experiments.

    3.2 Latent-to-Geometry Model Stitching

    Following recent works in model stitching [75, 29, 37], we design a simple learnable module to stitch the video generator and the augmented DA3 together, allowing the video latent to be directly decoded into full 4D geometry, including depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow. Let I^1:T be a video clip and let z₀^1:T=𝔼ᵥₐₑ(I^1:T) be its Wan 2.1 VAE latent [90]. We first upsample the latent to the spatial and temporal resolution required by DA3: z̃₀^1:T=Up_(sₜ,sₕ,s_w)(z₀^1:T)∈ℝ^(sₜt)×(sₕh)×(s_ww)×C. A learnable 3D stitching module S_θ then maps the upsampled latent tensor into the channel dimension of a DA3 encoder block, h⁽ᵏ⁾=S_θ(z̃₀^1:T). In our implementation S_θ is a compact spatiotemporal projection, instantiated as a 3D convolution. Its temporal kernel aggregates neighboring latent frames, and its spatial stride matches the VAE grid to the DA3 patch grid.

    The injection layer is not chosen heuristically. For a set of paired clips, we extract Wan 2.1 VAE latents and frozen DA3 candidate features from several early encoder blocks. For each candidate block k, we solve a regularized linear fitting problem,

    (k^⋆,θ₀)=\arg\min_k,θ∑ᵢ∥S_θ(z̃₀^1:T)-g⁽ᵏ⁾ᵢ∥₂²+λ∥θ∥₂²,

    		(2)

    where g⁽ᵏ⁾ᵢ is the frozen DA3 feature grid at block k for clip i. This procedure selects the block whose representation is most linearly reachable from the video VAE latent [29, 3]. It also provides a stable initialization θ₀ for the stitching module. The selected block acts as the interface between the generative video prior and the geometric reconstruction prior.

    After stitching, the original RGB patch embedding and the encoder blocks before k^⋆ in DA3 are bypassed. The projected latent tokens are combined with DA3 special tokens and positional encodings, then processed by the remaining DA3 encoder blocks and the native dense heads, Ĝ=H^DA3_k^⋆:L(h^(k^⋆)). The output Ĝ contains depth, camera rays, confidence maps, and scene flow. This design is important because the stitched decoder reads the denoised video latent directly. It does not need to first decode the latent into RGB and then run a separate geometry model. Visual RGB generation and 3D reconstruction are instead two synchronized readouts of the same latent video state.

    3.3 Stitched Decoder Finetuning

    Here, we describe how to finetune the stitched decoder to adapt to the new latent input distribution and obtain accurate geometry predictions. Unlike VIST3A [29] which only distills RGB features, we employ a hybrid training strategy that combines teacher-student distillation with ground-truth (GT) supervision. The teacher-student distillation follows the same principle as VIST3A, where the teacher is the original frozen DA3 model augmented with the new scene flow head. This teacher model takes the ground-truth RGB video clip as input and produces all types of 4D geometric outputs as supervision signals. The student is the stitched decoder, which takes the Wan VAE latent of the same clip as input and produces the same set of geometric outputs. For the GT supervision, we utilize the 3D annotations provided in the dataset as explicit regression targets.

    Following the formulation in [Lin et al. [64]], our training objective integrates dense geometric matching with spatial and temporal regularization constraints,

    L_geo=λ_DL_depth+λ_RL_ray+λ_CL_camera+λ_MLₘₒₜᵢₒₙ+λ_TLₜₑₘₚₒᵣₐₗ.

    		(3)

    We also apply distillation to the depth and ray confidence maps using small weighting factors. The training details are discussed in AppendixB in detail. We keep the video diffusion transformer strictly frozen throughout this stage. This entire training phase exclusively focuses on transforming the DA3 decoder into a robust geometric readout mechanism for the Wan latent space.

    3.4 Joint Video and 4D Geometry Training

    Once the stitched decoder is finetuned, we use it as a differentiable geometry critic for the video diffusion model. The video model is trained with the standard latent flow-matching objective [115]. For each clip, we sample a scalar diffusion time τ∈[0,1] and use the corresponding scheduler noise scale σ_τ∈ℝ. Both values are shared by all latent frames in the clip and broadcast over space and channels. Omitting the batch dimension, let z_τ^1:T∈ℝ^T_ℓ×h×w×C_z denote the noisy Wan latent trajectory at time τ, where T_ℓ is the latent-frame length, (h,w) is the VAE spatial grid, and C_z=16 for Wan. The conditioning tuple c=(eₚ,z_ctx,m_ctx) contains the text-action embeddings eₚ∈ℝ^Lₚ×d_c and context-frame latents z_ctx∈ℝ^T_c×h×w×C_z with a binary prefix mask m_ctx∈{0,1}^T_ℓ×h×w×1. Given z_τ^1:T, τ, and c, the diffusion transformer predicts a velocity field v_φ(z_τ^1:T,τ,c)∈ℝ^T_ℓ×h×w×C_z. We convert the velocity prediction into a clean-latent estimate

    ẑ₀^1:T=z_τ^1:T-σ_τ v_φ(z_τ^1:T,τ,c),

    		(4)

    where ẑ₀^1:T has the same tensor shape as z_τ^1:T and is passed directly into the frozen stitched decoder. The joint objective is

    Lⱼₒᵢₙₜ=L_FM+λ_geo L_geo(D_stitch(ẑ₀)),

    		(5)

    where L_FM denotes the latent flow-matching loss and D_stitch represents the frozen stitched decoder. The geometric penalty L_geo is strictly identical to the objective formulated in Equation3. During this joint optimization phase, we exclusively utilize the teacher-student distillation mechanism for action-conditioned videos. As introduced previously, an independently loaded raw DA3 model serves as the teacher network. It processes the ground-truth RGB clip to provide the reference targets for depth, ray maps, and scene flow. For image-to-video generation, the first frame is encoded as the conditioning prefix [87]. The diffusion loss can mask the conditioned prefix, while the geometry loss can be applied to the generated suffix. As a result, Plan4D learns a single latent trajectory that must satisfy both appearance realism and dense 4D consistency. At inference time, the final latent sequence is decoded by the Wan VAE into RGB video and by the stitched DA3 decoder into depth, camera rays, and scene flow.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Settings.

    Implementation.Plan4D is trained in three stages on diverse datasets due to the lack of large-scale data with paired action and dense 4D annotations. (1) We train the designed scene-flow head on top of frozen DA3 using PointOdyssey [118], Dynamic Replica [49], Virtual KITTI 2 [14], BlinkVision [62], and OmniWorld-Game [119] for 20 epochs on 16 H100 GPUs. (2) We fit the latent-to-geometry stitching module on a small subset of the above datasets to initialize the interface from Wan latents to DA3 tokens. Then we finetune the stitched decoder with the scene-flow-head data mixture augmented by ScanNet++ [109] and MVS-Synth [39]. This stage uses 64 H20 GPUs and runs one hybrid epoch over the full data mixture, where the same mixed sampling schedule is traversed once with ground-truth geometric supervision and once with teacher-student distillation. When a ground-truth-supervised sample does not provide scene-flow annotations, we set its scene-flow loss to zero. (3) We finally train the DiT on a subset of Action100M [15] for one epoch using 64 H20 GPUs. All stages use a per-GPU batch size of 1. Additional dataset details, optimization details, losses, and supervision definitions are provided in AppendixB.

    Evaluation.

    We evaluate Plan4D along three axes that correspond to its intended use as a generative 4D world model. (1) we evaluate dynamic 4D geometry through scene flow on MOVi-F [31], Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips, and report endpoint error together with APD_0.05 against reconstruction and motion baselines. (2) we test whether the stitched decoder preserves DA3 geometry after replacing the RGB encoder with a Wan-latent input pathway. This evaluation covers reconstruction, camera, and depth benchmarks, including ETH3D [79], ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K [19], MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal [83], with comparisons to RGB-based 3D foundation models and latent-to-geometry baselines. Scene-flow metrics are computed after rescaling predictions to the target point-map scale. Depth uses per-clip scale-shift alignment, while camera and reconstruction follow the official DA3 bench protocol, with first-camera pose alignment for relative-pose metrics and Umeyama scale alignment for reconstruction. (3) finally, we evaluate full action-conditioned 4D world generation on RLBench [45] (210 samples), HOIGen-1M [67] (200 samples), Dynamic Replica (480 samples), and PointOdyssey (375 samples). To further assess in-the-wild generalization, we additionally sample 100 five-second clips from Epic-Kitchens-100 [23], which contains everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments, and evaluate all compared methods under the same joint-generation protocol. These benchmarks test whether a single generated rollout can jointly preserve visual quality [65, 120], action-text alignment [16], and temporally coherent 4D structure. We report video quality and instruction following with VBench-style video metrics and video-caption similarity [42]. For depth, reconstruction, and camera estimation, we follow the same protocol as the stitched-decoder evaluation. We compare with recent 4D world-generation and geometry-generation baselines, including VIST3A [29], TesserAct [117], and Gen3R [37], on the modalities each method supports.

    4.2 Main Results

    Scene Flow Estimation.

    We first test whether a frozen DA3 geometry prior can support dynamic 4D motion prediction beyond static reconstruction. This is a stringent setting because scene flow requires temporally coherent geometry rather than accurate per-frame depth alone. Table1 shows that both scene-flow variants remain competitive on all three benchmarks while using the smallest training set among the compared methods. The RGB-based DA3 variant is particularly strong on the harder real dynamic benchmarks, suggesting that frozen DA3 tokens already support reliable dense 4D motion readout. The stitched variant performs best on the controlled synthetic benchmark and remains near the top on Dynamic Replica, which matters because it is the decoder interface used during joint video training. The qualitative results in Figure3 show cleaner boundaries, more stable articulated motion, and better global 3D structure than the baselines. Overall, these results validate the first step of Plan4D: DA3 can be extended from geometry reconstruction to strong dynamic 4D readout, and this capability largely survives the latent-to-geometry stitching step.

    Stitched Geometry Decoder Preserves DA3 Behavior.

    We evaluate whether replacing DA3’s RGB input with Wan video latents preserves its depth, camera, and reconstruction behavior on held-out benchmarks. We compare against the latest state-of-the-art RGB-based DA3 and VGGT, and the aligned VIST3A-Stitched and Gen3R-VAE decoders. Table2 shows that our decoder remains closer to the RGB-based models than prior aligned decoders across all three geometry families. It slightly exceeds DA3 on Dynamic-RE10K camera estimation and remains competitive with VGGT on Dynamic Replica. Depth changes little on MOVi-F and declines moderately on RobbySimVal. Reconstruction shifts are larger, but our decoder remains closer to DA3 and VGGT in most settings and achieves the best completeness on Dynamic Replica. Figure4 shows that our decoder preserves DA3-like surface layout and global scene organization, while competing aligned models produce less faithful structure. This preserved geometry allows the frozen decoder to provide stable supervision for the video generator directly from latent rollouts.

    Joint 4D World Generation

    Table3 reports a compact subset of the full joint 4D generation benchmark in Table8. The subset covers HoiGen, Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey across video quality, depth and reconstruction, and camera estimation. On the 100 five-second Epic-Kitchens-100 clips, Plan4D leads on 10 of the 13 metrics in the full comparison. On video quality, Plan4D achieves the best subject consistency on all four datasets and the best caption similarity on Epic-Kitchens-100 and PointOdyssey. VIST3A has the highest caption similarity on HoiGen and Dynamic Replica. On Epic-Kitchens-100, Plan4D also achieves the best background consistency and image quality, while TesserAct has the best motion smoothness and VIST3A the highest aesthetic quality. These results show that the shared latent rollout supports strong visual consistency and action-text alignment across diverse scenes.

    For depth and reconstruction, Plan4D gives the lowest AbsRel on all four datasets in the subset. It also obtains the best Chamfer-L1 on Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey, while Gen3R has the lowest Chamfer-L1 on HoiGen. On Epic-Kitchens-100, Plan4D leads on all three depth metrics. The HoiGen exception separates local reconstruction quality from the full world-generation objective. Gen3R can produce a strong point-cloud distance on one hand-object benchmark, but its video quality and camera stability are much weaker in the same setting.

    Camera metrics show the largest gap in global 4D consistency. Plan4D obtains the best RRA@5 on all four datasets in the subset and the best RPE-R on HoiGen, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey. On Epic-Kitchens-100, it leads on both relative-rotation accuracy thresholds. TesserAct has the lowest RPE-R on Epic-Kitchens-100, while Plan4D maintains strong performance across datasets and metric families. The Epic-Kitchens-100 results complement HoiGen with quantitative evidence across two real-world human-object interaction benchmarks, supporting the applicability of Plan4D to everyday interactions beyond the original evaluation setting. The qualitative comparisons in Figure5 and Figure6 show the same pattern visually: the generated RGB frames, RGB-D structure, and global dynamic point clouds remain better aligned under complex action-conditioned rollouts. These results support the core design choice of supervising a pretrained video generator with a frozen geometric readout rather than learning dense 4D structure from scratch.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    We conduct an ablation study to understand the contribution of each component in our joint-training objective. The results are summarized in Table4, with results on HoiGen and Dynamic Replica using the same action-conditioned generation protocol. The RGB-only variant retains strong subject and background consistency, but its depth and camera estimates are less accurate than those of the full model on both datasets. The geometry-only variant improves depth on HoiGen, but sacrifices visual consistency and performs worse across all reported metrics on Dynamic Replica. The full objective gives the best subject and background consistency and camera estimation on both datasets, and also leads on depth on Dynamic Replica. These results support combining flow matching with geometric supervision to preserve action-conditioned video quality while improving the depth and camera structure decoded from the same future latent state. Additional settings and analysis appear in SectionC.1.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduce the problem of generative plannable 4D worlds, where a model must generate future scenes with rich 4D attributes, including RGB appearance, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions. To this end, we propose Plan4D, a unified framework that decouples the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnects them through a stitched latent world model. By augmenting frozen DA3 with a token-only scene-flow head and learning a latent-to-geometry stitching interface from video VAE latents to geometry tokens, Plan4D turns a pretrained video generator into an actionable 4D world model whose RGB, depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow are read out from the same evolving latent state in a single feed-forward pass. Experiments show that this design preserves strong geometric behavior while improving dense 4D world generation across scene flow, reconstruction, and action-conditioned future prediction, without requiring manual 4D annotations for action videos. We hope this perspective helps move future world modeling beyond video-only prediction toward unified, measurable, and plannable 4D world models.

    Appendix A Frozen DA3 Tokens Already Encode Cross-Frame Motion Cues

    The lightweight DPT scene flow head above is only useful if the frozen DA3 encoder tokens already preserve motion-relevant structure. The central question of this section is therefore simple: before any scene-flow supervision reaches the decoder, do frozen DA3 tokens already know which location in frame t+1 corresponds to a location in frame t? If the answer is yes, then a shallow head can decode dense motion by reading out a representation that already contains cross-frame geometry and correspondence cues. If the answer is no, then good scene-flow predictions would have to come from the capacity of the head alone.

    To make this question concrete, let zₜ(p) denote the frozen DA3 token at spatial cell p in frame t. Point Odyssey [118] provides ground-truth tracks, which let us identify the corresponding target cell p⁺ in frame t+1 for each valid source cell p. We then probe the token space without using the scene flow head. Our analysis uses the Point Odyssey test split with 128 clips from 5 scenes. All values in Table 5 are weighted over clips by the number of valid token pairs or valid flow tokens. Figure 7 aggregates all 6,132,636 positive pairs, 6,132,636 negative pairs, and 2,160,723 token-difference vectors.

    We use four complementary probes, each answering a different question about the frozen representation. The first probe is correspondence similarity[84]. It asks whether a token is more similar to its true match than to an unrelated token from the next frame:

    sₚₒₛ=\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(p⁺)), s_neg=\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(q⁻)),

    		(6)

    where q⁻ is a random negative sampled from frame t+1. This is the cleanest test of whether correspondence information is present [44]. If frozen DA3 tokens contain motion-relevant structure, the sₚₒₛ distribution should shift to the right of the s_neg distribution. The margin Δs=sₚₒₛ-s_neg and the probability \Pr(sₚₒₛ>s_neg) summarize how reliably the two distributions separate.

    The second probe is token retrieval[74]. Instead of comparing one positive and one negative, we search over all target tokens in frame t+1:

    p̂=\arg\max_q∈ℙₜ₊₁\cos (zₜ(p),zₜ₊₁(q)).

    		(7)

    This is a stronger operational test. It asks whether nearest-neighbor search in frozen token space can recover the correct destination cell. We report Top-1 exact, which measures whether the retrieved cell is exactly the ground-truth cell, and PCK@1 and PCK@3, which measure whether retrieval falls within 1 or 3 token cells of the ground-truth location [107]. High retrieval accuracy means that the token space is not only separable on average, but also organized enough to support direct correspondence lookup.

    The third probe is a token-flow readout. After retrieval returns p̂, we interpret it as a token-level motion estimate d̂=p̂-p and compare it with the ground-truth token displacement. This probe is more demanding than similarity or retrieval because it asks a single nearest-neighbor lookup to act as a motion predictor. The resulting endpoint error and direction cosine should be interpreted as evidence for how directly motion can be read out from the frozen tokens without a learned decoder [104].

    The fourth probe is PCA on token differences. For each matched pair, we form

    Δzₜ(p)=zₜ₊₁(p⁺)-zₜ(p).

    		(8)

    We then perform PCA on these token differences [78]. This analysis does not test whether motion is present at all. The earlier probes already answer that question more directly. Instead, PCA asks a more specific question: is the motion signal concentrated in a small linear subspace, or is it distributed across many token dimensions? If the first few principal components explain most of the variance, then motion could be close to linearly disentangled [2]. If the variance remains spread out, then motion is still present, but encoded in a more distributed form. This distinction matters for interpreting the role of the DPT head.
