A low-dimensional linear code would be easy to read out with almost any linear probe, while a distributed code benefits from structured multiscale decoding.

    Before discussing the numbers, it is useful to clarify how they should be interpreted. Similarity and retrieval are the strongest probes in this section because they make the fewest modeling assumptions. They only ask whether true cross-frame matches are already nearby in frozen token space. Token flow is a harder probe because it asks nearest-neighbor retrieval to behave like a motion estimator. PCA is the most indirect probe because a failure to find a low-dimensional linear motion axis does not mean that motion information is absent. It only means that the information is not cleanly isolated in the top principal components.

    Figure 7 and Table 5 provide direct evidence that frozen DA3 tokens preserve cross-frame correspondence structure. The similarity distributions are cleanly separated, with ground-truth matches consistently closer in token space than random negatives. Nearest-neighbor retrieval leads to the same conclusion under a stronger all-candidates test. These two probes show that, even without any learned motion decoder, the frozen representation already places true future matches near the source token and usually retrieves a target very close to the correct location.

    The token-flow probe refines this picture. A simple nearest-neighbor displacement readout already recovers meaningful motion, which indicates that the frozen tokens encode where points are likely to move. At the same time, this probe is weaker than similarity and retrieval, which suggests that the motion signal is not exposed as a trivial one-step velocity code. This is precisely where a structured decoder becomes useful. Our DPT head can pool multiscale context and impose spatial coherence to transform this latent correspondence signal into dense scene flow.

    The PCA results should be read as auxiliary evidence. The dominant components explain only a limited portion of the token-difference variance, and their alignment with flow magnitude remains weak. This does not argue against motion information in the frozen tokens. Instead, PCA indicates that motion is encoded in a distributed high-dimensional form rather than concentrated in a single linear direction.

    These results support a precise interpretation of our method. Frozen DA3 encoder tokens already contain scene-flow-relevant information, especially in the form of cross-frame correspondence structure. The strongest evidence comes from the probes that require almost no decoder assumptions, namely similarity separation and nearest-neighbor retrieval. The weaker token-flow and PCA probes refine this picture. They suggest that the motion signal is real, but distributed and not trivially linearized. Our DPT head succeeds because it decodes and regularizes this latent signal into dense metric predictions. In other words, the scene flow branch acts as an informed readout of the pretrained geometry representation, rather than a separate module that has to create motion information from scratch.

    Appendix B Training Details

    B.1 Dataset and Optimization Summary

    All dataset statistics in this paper correspond to the 81-frame manifests. Every manifest row therefore satisfies the temporal constraint T=4k+1 with T=81. Table6 summarizes the stage-wise training data. Stage 1 trains only the DA3 scene-flow readout. Stage 2 finetunes the stitched decoder with hybrid ground-truth and teacher-student supervision. Stage 3 optimizes the action-conditioned video model, where Action100M contributes text-conditioned video clips without paired 4D labels.

    Stage 1 mixes 11,956 training clips from five dynamic datasets. The sampler uses dataset-wise mixture weights of 1.0 together with a size-aware mixing exponent α=0.5, which interpolates between uniform-over-datasets and proportional-to-size sampling. The stage-1 manifest directory also contains held-out or diagnostic subsets such as PointOdyssey test, PointOdyssey sample, and Dynamic Replica valid clips for validation and smoke tests.

    Stage 2 contains 122,225 GT-capable training clips. Among them, 13,521 clips expose scene-flow labels, while the remaining 108,704 clips provide only depth, ray, camera, and point-cloud supervision. In hybrid decoder training, we build separate GT and distill dataloaders from the same manifest list and randomly shuffle the union of GT and distill steps once per epoch. This realizes one GT pass and one distillation pass over the full mixture in a single hybrid epoch.

    The stage-3 Action100M subset is constructed in two steps. We first start from the filtered 81-frame TI2V manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.filtered.jsonl, whose rows already satisfy task_type=ti2v, cond_frames=1, and num_frames=81. We then score the corresponding clip-level entries from action100m_clip_index_81f.filtered.jsonl and keep only clips that pass a high-precision action-quality filter. The clip-level decision uses fields such as prompt_action, level, and node_duration_sec. We drop clips with node duration shorter than 1.6 seconds, hierarchy depth above 10, missing action text, action text identical to the generic description, action text shorter than four words, prompt patterns dominated by on-screen text or audio-style narration, uncertain descriptions, or generic action stubs. The retained manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.action_hq.keep.jsonl contains 249,422 clips, which is 28.6% of the 871,785 filtered TI2V rows. Because Action100M does not provide paired 4D geometry, these clips are used only in the distillation branch during stage 3.

    Per-dataset roles.

    PointOdyssey provides articulated outdoor motion with sparse track supervision that we rasterize into dense forward scene flow, which makes it particularly useful for supervising correspondence-aware motion. Dynamic Replica contributes denser dynamic stereo geometry with strong camera and scene-flow signals. BlinkVision, Virtual KITTI 2, and OmniWorld broaden the synthetic motion distribution across indoor scenes, driving scenes, and open-world gameplay trajectories. ScanNet++ and MVS-Synth do not provide scene flow in our 81-frame setup, but they substantially enrich multiview depth, camera, and point-cloud supervision during stitched-decoder finetuning. Action100M serves a different purpose from the geometry datasets. It injects large-scale action-conditioned video semantics into the joint model while relying on the frozen DA3 teacher for geometric targets.

    Evaluation datasets.

    We report three groups of held-out evaluations. For dynamic 4D motion, we evaluate on MOVi-F, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips. MOVi-F tests controlled synthetic object motion, Dynamic Replica tests realistic dynamic stereo scenes, and PointOdyssey emphasizes articulated motion with long temporal support. For stitched-decoder geometry preservation, we evaluate on ETH3D, ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K, MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal. These datasets cover static reconstruction, indoor multiview geometry, dynamic camera estimation, and robot-centric depth prediction. For action-conditioned world generation, we evaluate on RLBench with 210 samples, HOIGen-1M with 200 samples, Dynamic Replica with 480 samples, and PointOdyssey with 375 samples, which together span manipulation, hand-object interaction, and general dynamic-scene futures. We additionally evaluate 100 five-second Epic-Kitchens-100 clips to assess in-the-wild generalization to everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments. This evaluation complements HoiGen with a second real-world human-object interaction benchmark.

    Stage-3 comparison scope.

    We exclude several recent world-generation systems from the stage-3 comparison because they assume additional control inputs beyond the setting targeted in this paper. PointWorld requires depth input [41]. FantasyWorld, HY-World 2.0, Lyra 2.0, Geometry Forcing, and TeleWorld rely on trajectory-level control signals [22, 43, 80, 100, 20]. Kinema4D further requires robot-action kinematic representations [105]. These methods therefore do not match the task of predicting future RGB video together with dense 4D geometry from only an observed scene context and a text-specified action, so we do not include them in the stage-3 comparison.

    Evaluation protocol and metric definitions.

    We follow the same three-way evaluation split as in the main paper and expand the scoring protocol here. Scene flow. We score only valid moving pixels indicated by the deformation mask. Predictions are first rescaled to the target point-map scale of each clip. When a model predicts relative flow, we restore the target scale with the clip-level scene-flow scale before metric computation. If a benchmark provides native-resolution labels, we resize predictions to that evaluation resolution before scoring. We report

    EPE=(1)/(|V_sf|)∑_(t,p)∈V_sf∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₂, APD_0.05=(1)/(|V_sf|)∑_(t,p)∈V_sf1 [∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₂<0.05],

    		(9)

    where V_sf is the set of valid motion pixels, m̂_t,p is the predicted 3D displacement from frame t to frame t+1, and m_t,p is the ground-truth displacement. Lower EPE is better, while higher APD_0.05 is better.

    Depth. Depth metrics use per-clip scale-shift alignment. For each clip, we solve one scale a and one shift b jointly over all valid depth pixels and evaluate ad̂+b against ground-truth depth:

    (a^⋆,b^⋆)=\arg\min_a,b∑_(t,p)∈V_d(ad̂_t,p+b-d_t,p)².

    		(10)

    We report

    AbsRel=(1)/(|V_d|)∑_(t,p)∈V_d(|a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆-d_t,p|)/(d_t,p)

    		(11)

    δ₁=(1)/(|V_d|)∑_(t,p)∈V_d1 [\max ((a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆)/(d_t,p),(d_t,p)/(a^⋆d̂_t,p+b^⋆))<1.25].

    		(12)

    Lower AbsRel is better, while higher δ₁ is better.

    Camera. Camera metrics follow the official DA3 bench. Predicted and ground-truth camera trajectories are first converted to the first-camera gauge. We then evaluate all frame pairs (i,j) through their relative transforms. Let eʳᵢⱼ denote the relative rotation error in degrees and let eᵗᵢⱼ denote the angle between the predicted and ground-truth relative translation directions. On Dynamic Replica we report

    RRA@5^∘=(1)/(|ℙ|)∑_(i,j)∈ℙ1 [eʳᵢⱼ<5^∘],

    		(13)

    which measures relative rotation accuracy over all frame pairs. On Dynamic-RE10K we report AUC₁₅ and AUC₃₀. These metrics are computed from the per-pair error

    mᵢⱼ=\max (eʳᵢⱼ,eᵗᵢⱼ),

    		(14)

    and summarize the cumulative accuracy curve of mᵢⱼ up to the corresponding angular threshold. Higher camera metrics are better.

    3D reconstruction. Reconstruction also follows the official DA3 bench. We estimate a global Umeyama alignment between predicted and ground-truth camera trajectories and use the recovered scale to place predicted depth in metric units before TSDF fusion. When predicted poses are used for reconstruction, the same fit also aligns the fused camera trajectory. The fused prediction is then compared with the benchmark ground-truth geometry using the dataset-specific threshold and downsampling settings from the DA3 bench. ETH3D and ScanNet++ evaluate against points sampled from the ground-truth mesh, and ScanNet++ additionally crops the predicted point cloud to the ground-truth bounding box with a small margin before scoring. For predicted points P and ground-truth points G, we report

    Acc.=(1)/(|P|)∑_x∈P\min_y∈G∥x-y∥₂, Comp.=(1)/(|G|)∑_y∈G\min_x∈P∥x-y∥₂.

    		(15)

    Precision and recall are the fractions of predicted and ground-truth points whose nearest-neighbor distance is below the dataset threshold ε, and the F-score is their harmonic mean:

    Prec.=(1)/(|P|)∑_x∈P1 [\min_y∈G∥x-y∥₂<ε],

    		(16)

    Rec.=(1)/(|G|)∑_y∈G1 [\min_x∈P∥x-y∥₂<ε],

    		(17)

    F-score=(2 Prec. Rec.)/(Prec.+Rec.).

    		(18)

    Lower Acc. and Comp. are better, while higher F-score is better.

    Joint world generation. For RGB video quality, higher video-caption similarity indicates stronger alignment between the generated video and the conditioning action text. RLBench and HOIGen-1M use their native action annotations, while Dynamic Replica and PointOdyssey do not provide action-level text in our stage-3 evaluation split, so we generate per-clip action captions with Qwen-VL-30B-Thinking and use them as the conditioning text for all compared methods. When a baseline exposes a compatible geometry output, we score its generated 4D structure with the same geometry protocol described above.

    Epic-Kitchens-100 evaluation setting.

    We sample 100 clips, each five seconds long, and follow the same action-conditioned joint 4D generation protocol as the original comparison. Each method receives the initial RGB frame and an action description. We compare Plan4D, TesserAct, Gen3R, and VIST3A using the same metric definitions and alignment procedures. The full evaluation reports six video metrics, namely subject consistency (SC), background consistency (BC), aesthetic quality (AQ), image quality (IQ), motion smoothness (MS), and video-caption similarity (Cap.Sim). Geometry is evaluated with depth AbsRel, δ₁, δ₂, and Chamfer-L1, together with camera RPE-R, RRA@10, and RRA@5. Higher scores are better except for AbsRel, Chamfer-L1, and RPE-R. The complete results appear in Table8, and Table3 retains six representative metrics for comparison with the other benchmarks.

    Stage-wise optimization details.

    For stage 1, the 81-frame manifest configuration uses AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁵, weight decay 10⁻², β=(0.9,0.999), 100 warmup steps, gradient accumulation 2, and bf16 mixed precision. Inputs are resized to 504×504 with upper-bound resizing, the clip overlap is 1 frame, and the scene-flow loss adds a zero-last-frame penalty with weight 0.1. The main paper reports a 20-epoch run on 16 H100 GPUs with per-GPU batch size 1.

    For stage 2, the stitched-decoder hybrid launchers use AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻⁴, bf16 mixed precision, 504×504 inputs, and per-GPU batch size 1. The representative 81-frame launchers use a 50-step warmup and train the stitching layer together with LoRA adapters on the stitched DA3 blocks by default, while still supporting full finetuning of the stitched parts. The main paper reports one hybrid epoch on 64 H20 GPUs.

    For stage 3, the stitched joint LoRA launcher uses AdamW with learning rate 10⁻⁴, cosine decay, 1000 warmup steps, LoRA rank 32 on the DiT, gradient checkpointing, 81 frames at 532×532 resolution, condition dropout 0.1, and geometry-loss warmup from 0.001 to 1.0 over the first 500 steps. We apply mask_condition_loss on conditioned prefixes and geo_supervise_generated_only on the generated suffix. The main paper reports one epoch on 64 H20 GPUs with per-GPU batch size 1.

    B.2 Scene Flow Head Training

    We train the scene-flow branch as a readout on top of a fixed DA3 representation. The DA3 backbone, depth head, ray head, and camera modules are loaded from the pretrained checkpoint and kept frozen. We inject the DPT-style scene-flow head and its coordinate adapter from the scene-flow preset, load the original DA3 weights with non-strict matching, and optimize only the parameters of the new head. During training, each clip is passed through the frozen DA3 encoder to extract the four multiscale token maps. The head decodes these tokens into a dense three-channel motion field, and the adapter rotates the local camera-frame prediction into the first-frame camera basis.

    The training target is a forward displacement field from frame t to frame t+1. All datasets expose the same fields: RGB frames, camera intrinsics, world-to-camera extrinsics, a scene-flow tensor, a per-clip scale, and a binary deformation mask. We use relative scene flow by default. Metric displacements are expressed in the first-frame camera basis and normalized by a robust clip-level scale, which makes the head less sensitive to the absolute size of a scene.

    Let m̂_t,p be the predicted motion at pixel p in frame t, let m_t,p be the target, and let a_t,p∈{0,1} be the deformation mask. The scene-flow loss [60, 88] is

    L_sf=(∑_t,pa_t,p∥m̂_t,p-m_t,p∥₁)/(\max(1,∑_t,pa_t,p))+λₗₐₛₜ1/HW∑ₚ∥m̂_T,p∥₂.

    		(19)

    The first term is evaluated only at valid motion pixels. It never falls back to full-image supervision, which is important for datasets where motion labels come from sparse tracks. The second term softly enforces the last frame to be zero because there is no target frame T+1. We use masked L1 loss in the main configuration.

    B.3 Latent-to-Geometry Model Stitching Training

    The stitching stage determines where the video latent space should enter DA3 and initializes the projection into that token space. For each training clip, we encode the RGB video with the frozen Wan VAE and extract candidate DA3 token maps from encoder blocks. The Wan latent has 16 channels and is temporally compressed. Before fitting the stitch, we upsample it back to the video frame rate with T=4(Tᵥₐₑ-1)+1 and resize it to the spatial resolution required by the DA3 patch grid.

    For each candidate block k, we fit a 3D convolutional stitch S_θ⁽ᵏ⁾ from the upsampled Wan latent to the frozen DA3 token grid. The fit is a streaming ridge regression problem shown in Equation2.

    The streaming solver accumulates normal-equation statistics over cached tensor batches, which avoids storing a large design matrix. We rank candidate blocks by the reconstruction mean squared error and choose the block with the lowest error. In our DA3 setting, the stitch maps the 16-channel Wan latent to the 1536-channel DA3 token width through a compact spatiotemporal convolution. This procedure gives both the injection layer and the initial weights for the later trainable stitched decoder.

    B.4 Stitched Decoder Finetuning

    The linear stitch is only an initialization. We next train a stitched decoder that accepts Wan latents but preserves the geometry behavior of DA3. The Wan VAE is frozen. The pretrained DA3 teacher is frozen. The trainable student contains the stitching module and stitched DA3 parts. The video diffusion transformer is not trained in this stage.

    We use two complementary sources of supervision. In the distillation branch, the teacher consumes the ground-truth RGB clip, while the student consumes the Wan latent of the same clip. The teacher and student outputs are aligned in time and space before computing losses. The distillation objective is

    L_distill=λ_D∥D̂-Dᵀ∥₁+λ_∇DL_∇D(D̂,Dᵀ)+λ_R∥R̂-Rᵀ∥₁(20)
    +λ_cD∥Ĉ^D-C^D,T∥₁+λ_cR∥Ĉ^R-C^R,T∥₁+λ_CL_C
    +λ_M∥M̂-Mᵀ∥₁+λ_TL_T.

    Here D denotes depth, R denotes the six-channel ray map, C^D and C^R denote confidence maps, and M denotes scene flow. The camera term L_C compares decoded intrinsics and relative camera motion. The temporal term L_T matches depth differences between adjacent frames, which discourages frame-wise geometry flicker.

    In the ground-truth branch, the student is supervised against dataset depth, ray, camera, valid-mask, and optional scene-flow annotations. The objective is

    L_GT=λ_DL_D+λ_∇DL_∇D+λ_RL_R+λ_PL_P(21)
    +λ_CL_C+λ_ML_M+λ_TL_T.

item.title: 让 agent 写建场景的程序，直接写往往布局、尺度、光照全错：SceneAnything 把它做成「写完能验证」的自动系统 ｜ SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
item.description:
一句话：从视频重建可编辑 3D 场景，既要对上可见结构，又要把看不见的表面合理地补出来。

要点：

  • 任务要求双向：从视频重建可编辑三维场景，既要**匹配可见结构**，又要**合理地补全不可见表面**
  • 已知问题：agent 能写「场景构建程序」，但直接照做常常在**布局、尺度与光照**上出错
  • SceneAnything 因此是一个自动化系统：从真实视频与生成视频重建网格场景，并支持**文本到场景**的构建流程

为什么值得看：「agent 写代码建场景」这条路最大的坑不是不会写，而是写错了没人发现。把它做成带验证的自动系统，才可能在资产管线里跑起来——这条与 11-18 的 RemeshingAgent（验证契约）是同一个方法论。

中文摘要：从一段视频重建可编辑的三维场景，需要同时做好两件事：匹配可见的结构，并合理地补全看不见的表面。已有方法让 agent 直接编写「场景构建程序」，但一次到位的重建尝试常常在布局、尺度与光照上出错。SceneAnything 因此把这一过程做成自动化系统，用于从真实视频与生成视频重建网格场景，并支持从文本到场景的构建流程。它的意义在于把「agent 会写代码」推进到「写出来的场景能被验证与使用」，这正是把 agentic 重建接入资产管线的必要条件。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video

Abstract

Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

1 Introduction

An editable 3D scene allows an environment to be explored, relit, and modified beyond a recorded or generated camera path. Recovering such a scene from video requires fitting visible structures and spatial relationships, separating materials from illumination, and completing unseen surfaces. Recent reconstruction and scene-generation models provide useful geometric estimates and priors [18, 37, 16, 22]. We build on these capabilities to reconstruct separate mesh objects, materials, and light sources from real and generated videos. Paired with text-to-video generation, the system also enables text-to-scene construction. Unseen surfaces are completed and marked as inferred.

Language and vision-language model agents can interpret structures, write Blender programs, and revise them from rendered feedback [11, 39, 54, 13]. Directly assigning the entire reconstruction task to an agent leaves it to establish cameras and scale, choose constructions, and assess its own result. In our zero-shot comparisons, two frontier agents produce recognizable content but simplified geometry and materials, with errors in layout, dimensions, and lighting (Fig. , columns 3 and 4). Some attempts project footage onto proxy surfaces, reproducing input views while exposing artifacts from new viewpoints. These failures motivate a process that grounds agent construction in geometric estimates and evaluates revisions in the assembled scene.

We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for coordinated component construction from video (Fig. 2). Pretrained vision models supply shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates. A scene-owner agent plans components and briefs author agents, which return parameterized Blender generators. Agents choose scene-specific constructions; the method specifies their shared inputs, authoring interfaces, level-of-detail policy, and revision procedure. The level-of-detail policy uses visibility and fit to select procedural recipes, fitted instances, or part-by-part construction. Components are assembled with fitted lighting and supported motion, then revisions undergo programmatic checks and render comparisons by separate judge agents. A software harness coordinates agents, models, and graphics tools and applies the acceptance rule. Accepted generators and curated lessons are reused in later runs. Section 3 details this structure and the decisions delegated to agents.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    An observation-grounded reconstruction framework that coordinates component authoring to produce editable scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation (Secs. 3.1–3.4).

  • •

    A level-of-detail policy and scene-level revision procedure that allocate individual modeling according to visibility and fit, and evaluate changes through programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6).

  • •

    An evaluation across 100 scenes, including direct-agent comparisons, a level-of-detail ablation, and open-weight author substitutions (Sec. 4), accompanied by a planned release of code, instructions, libraries, scenes, and evaluation records.

    • 2 Related Work

    Reconstruction from video. Structure from motion and multi-view stereo recover cameras and surfaces [35, 36, 30]; feed-forward models predict point maps, depth, and poses [45, 42, 46, 22, 14]. Neural radiance fields [28, 3] and Gaussian splatting [18, 17] represent appearance for view synthesis, with surface-oriented variants supporting mesh extraction [12, 5]. Dynamic methods recover time-varying scenes [25, 47, 44], while generative models synthesize explorable environments [37, 16, 24]. SceneAnything uses a video-to-3D model as a measurement prior, then constructs separate, named mesh components with explicit materials, lighting, and supported animation.

    Object-level reconstruction. Methods retrieve and align CAD models to scans [2], or generate objects using learned priors from an image [15, 26, 1, 6] or multiple views [29, 50, 48, 51, 34]. Video2Game reconstructs interactive mesh environments from video [49]. Our components are constructed by parameterized programs fitted to video observations, allowing their construction procedures and parameters to be revised and reused.

    Agentic scene construction. Language-model systems arrange assets [53, 10], write scene programs [39, 11], and coordinate generators with critics or verifiers [52, 9, 23]. Image-conditioned approaches predict structured scene descriptions [21], refine programs through rendering [54], orchestrate specialist agents [20, 40], or edit existing scenes [13]. SceneAnything grounds component authoring in shared video-derived measurements and evaluates revisions in a common assembled scene. Separate judges compare matched renders in both display orders, with identical-image controls and a prescribed acceptance rule. This procedure addresses the order sensitivity documented for language-model judges [56, 43].

    Procedural generation, reuse, and level of detail. Infinigen generates natural and indoor environments procedurally [31, 32]. Voyager stores reusable agent programs [41], and SceneCraft builds a scene-function library [11]. Our library retains generators fitted to video observations for adaptation to later scenes (Sec. 3.6). Rendering level-of-detail methods select representations according to viewing conditions [8, 19]. Our policy instead allocates construction detail according to visibility and achieved fit; unresolved detail and unseen surfaces are completed procedurally and recorded as inferred (Sec. 3.5).

    3 Method

    Given a captured or generated video, SceneAnything reconstructs an editable Blender scene containing separate mesh objects, materials, light sources, and animation data for supported moving objects.

    3.1 Overview and Terminology

    A reconstruction run (or simply run) is one complete attempt to reconstruct a scene; all agent sessions, vision model inferences and compute jobs for that attempt belong to the same run.

    Scene representation and agent roles. The current scene is the reconstruction state at a given stage of the run: its cameras and world coordinates, geometry, materials, lighting, and motion. A component is an authored portion of the scene, such as a building or terrain surface. A generator is a parameterized Blender program that constructs geometry and materials. A family groups objects or parts that share construction logic. A family may span several objects, such as windows on different buildings. An instance is one occurrence of an object or part in a family; different instances can have different generator parameters and poses.

    We use three types of agents. A scene owner agent coordinates the run, maintains the current scene, plans components, and assigns construction tasks to author agents. Authors write and revise generators for particular families or spatial regions. Separate judge agents compare candidate reconstructions with the current accepted scene and the observations. All three roles are language or vision-language model agents; our default owner uses Claude Opus 5.5, with alternative author models evaluated in Sec. 4.4.

    Figure 2 shows the stages of a run and Algorithm 1 summarizes it; the comment on each of its lines names who acts. Supp. S8 lists the responsibilities by stage.

    3.2 Video Processing and Geometric Initialization

    Frames and initial reconstruction. The harness extracts timestamped frames and detects shot boundaries; each run reconstructs one continuous shot. Lyra 2’s reconstruction branch [37] estimates cameras, depth, and a Gaussian representation, providing initial geometry for spatial measurements. These estimates serve as correctable priors rather than final scene geometry.

    Camera validation and world coordinates.Geometric diagnostic tools built with OpenCV and numerical routines, rather than large learned models, report reprojection error, trajectory discontinuities, vertical alignment, and near-object parallax (Supp. S1). The owner uses these diagnostics to accept, re-estimate, or correct the cameras before construction. It establishes a gravity-aligned coordinate system and estimates scale from two independent recognizable size references, checking their agreement. All components use these shared cameras and coordinates.

    3.3 Segmentation and 3D Association

    Segmentation and tracking. The owner names target classes and supplies text or box prompts. Mask2Former[7] provides semantic regions, SAM 3.1[4] segments prompted instances, and SAM 2.1[33] propagates instance masks through time. Each covers a case that the others handle poorly: Mask2Former labels continuous far regions that prompted instances miss, and SAM 2.1 keeps instance identities in dense scenes (Supp. S1). A track associates masks of the same instance across frames. Authors obtain masks for constituent parts using the same prompting procedure.

    Association with 3D geometry.Geometric tools project reconstructed points into the views, filter occluded points, and accumulate labels from overlapping masks. Plane fitting estimates supporting surfaces and facades; clustering provides approximate instance locations and extents (Supp. S1). This coarse 3D layout lets the owner plan the scene and assign authors, and lets assembly place each component at its estimated location instead of searching for its pose. These estimates inherit camera, depth, and segmentation errors and describe only observed geometry. For example, labeled building points constrain placement and visible dimensions; an author constructs coherent walls, a roof, and unseen sides.

    3.4 Scene Decomposition, Component Authoring

    Scene planning and briefs. The owner plans components, their relationships, and plausible completions of unseen parts, keeping continuous surfaces such as terrain within one component. Unseen sides and surroundings are built by the same generators as the observed parts and recorded as inferred (Supp. S13). It builds a coarse environment, then delegates families or large structures to parallel authors. Delegation separates the work into bounded tasks: a family’s author shares one generator and its lessons across all instances, and a smaller model can take such a task (Sec. 4.4; Supp. S9). Each author receives a brief specifying relevant observations, dimensions, coordinates, neighboring components, support constraints (what the component rests on or attaches to), and proposed level of detail (Sec. 3.5), together with current lighting, tools, and relevant generators and lessons.

    Parameterized construction and fitting.Authors write Blender generators with parameters for dimensions, placement, orientation, and counts. They choose construction procedures and revise code and parameters by comparing renders with the footage, optionally invoking inverse-rendering tools. Components must remain separate and movable, include unseen sides, and use materials without copied footage pixels (Supp. S5). Material parameters describe reflectance under the fitted illumination (Sec. 3.6).

    Author delivery. Authors deliver generator code, named closed mesh objects, an object-label manifest, declared supports, and records of measurements and inferred parts. The harness checks deliveries and compares rendered silhouettes with observation masks. Failed deliveries return for revision; passing permits assembly. Acceptance of changes to the assembled scene follows Sec. 3.6.

    3.5 Level of Detail

    The video supports different amounts of detail for different scene elements. Our level-of-detail policy chooses how each element is constructed from its own observations, and which detail is generated from regional statistics or structural assumptions. Components have a hierarchy of elements, such as a bed, its plants, and their leaves, or a district, its buildings, and their windows. A construction level describes how an element is built; it is distinct from its depth in this hierarchy. Part-by-part construction can be applied recursively at successive tiers.

    Construction levels. We use the following three levels, abbreviated L0, L1, and L2 in the author briefs:

  • •

    L0: Procedural recipe. Generate the element on its support using density, size, and color estimated for its region.

  • •

    L1: Fitted instance. Fit a generator instance’s position, scale, height, and orientation to the element’s own masks.

  • •

    L2: Part by part. Construct observed parts using their individual masks and spatial measurements, applying the policy recursively to those parts.

    • For example, a plant can be generated from regional statistics, fitted to its own outline, or built from individually observed leaves. The level is proposed during scene planning and reconsidered at each revision. Two visibility tests propose the construction level before building; a subsequent fit test checks a constructed part-by-part candidate.

    Visibility-based proposal. Let T(e) be the frames in which element e has an instance mask, and Mₜ(e) its mask in frame t. Its frame share is aₜ(e)=|Mₜ(e)|/(WH) for a W×H image, and ã(e) is the median share over T(e). Let m(e) count the masks of its parts over all frames of T(e), and let w(e) be the median diameter of the largest circle inscribed in each of these masks. Parts are not tracked at this stage, so a part visible in k frames contributes k masks.

    Tools compute these quantities. Before construction, the owner sets and records the visibility thresholds for each family, with a reason; defaults are in Supp. S3. The instance-visibility test S₁ requires enough views and sufficient median frame share. The part-visibility test S₂ additionally considers sustained image size, part width, and the number of part masks:

    S₁(e):|T(e)|≥n₁, ã(e)≥α₁,(1)
    S₂(e):ã(e)≥α₂, |{t∈T(e):aₜ(e)≥α₀}|≥n₂,
    w(e)≥w₀, m(e)≥m₀.(2)

    An element that passes both tests is proposed as a part-by-part candidate, one that passes only S₁ as a fitted instance, and any other as a procedural recipe. These tests use image measurements, not agent visual verdicts; their outputs depend on the supplied masks and recorded thresholds.

    Construction, fitting, and fallback. For a proposed L2 construction, the author obtains part masks with SAM 3.1 and constructs and refines a candidate Gₑ. Authors deliver a generator shared by the family and a parameter record for each element; fitting tools adjust parameters against the corresponding masks. At L1 this fits the whole instance, optionally using consistent depth for bounded deformation; at L2 the individual parts have their own masks and measurements.

    Let Rₜ(G) be the silhouette of a construction G in a render of the assembled scene at frame t, in which occluders hide the same pixels as in the observed mask Mₜ(e), and define IoUₜ(e,G)=|Rₜ(G)∩Mₜ(e)|/|Rₜ(G)∪Mₜ(e)|. The fit test requires median silhouette intersection-over-union of at least τ=0.6 over the element’s track:

    F(e): *med_t∈T(e)IoUₜ(e,Gₑ)≥τ.

    		(3)

    This is a silhouette-consistency check; agreement with the whole element’s outline alone does not establish the accuracy of its internal parts.

    Tools combine visibility and achieved fit into the level that the policy proposes for an element:

    ℓ(e)=\begincasespart by part&S₁(e)∧S₂(e)∧F(e), fitted instance&otherwise, ifS₁(e), procedural recipe&otherwise.\endcases

    		(4)

    A part-by-part candidate that fails F is thus proposed as a fitted instance. The same policy is applied recursively to retained parts, so instances of one family can have different construction levels. The author decides what is built: the instructions allow it to build individual parts wherever those parts have their own masks, also inside a fitted instance. The record for each element therefore holds the measurements, the proposed level, and the built level.

    The instructions emphasize separability as well as image size: a small, cleanly outlined dormer can be fitted individually, whereas unresolved house fronts are represented by their block’s estimated height, roof line, and window spacing. The visibility tests do not measure separability: the author judges it on the masks while building, and builds an element whose outline merges with its neighbors at a lower level than proposed. Detected elements remain represented even if their masks or tracks cannot support individual fitting.

    Completion and novel-view detail. Below the built level, procedural rules generate unresolved detail using estimated density, size, and color. Structural assumptions and the scene plan provide plausible completions of unseen parts. Generated detail and unseen completions are recorded as inferred. If an element’s placement is uncertain, it remains generated within its parent’s constraints rather than being dropped.

    After assembly, a tool compares each element’s maximum projected size over the delivered views with its size in the input frames. Where a novel view comes closer than any input view, the author generates one additional tier of finer elements. This tier is also inferred: a closer rendered view does not supply new observations of the scene.

    Figure 3 illustrates the policy at plant and city scales. In the city, whose original frame contains about 1,800 buildings, near landmarks are built individually and part by part, further houses are fitted to roof outlines, and unresolved blocks are generated inside their observed regions. On the embankment, theatre columns are built individually, the distant palace row uses fitted instances, and the city behind the frontage uses inferred recipes.

    3.6 Scene Assembly, Fitting, and Revision

    The owner assembles components in the shared coordinate system and fits lighting, materials, and supported motion. The initial assembly must pass the scene checks below. Thereafter, the parent is the current accepted scene and a candidate is a proposed revision, evaluated in the assembled environment to account for changes to shadows, occlusions, and neighboring components.

    Lighting and materials. The owner selects light sources and calibration regions for fitting their strengths. Outdoor scenes use sun and sky; indoor scenes use visible luminaires, with windows and doorways as sky portals. Fitting tools sweep sun directions against observed lit-and-shaded regions, initialized from date, time, and location when available. Authors choose material models; diffuse albedo is estimated under the fitted illumination and checked for consistency between lit and shaded pixels. Inconsistency triggers lighting refitting. Reflective and transmissive surfaces use corresponding material models.

    A fitted camera model maps scene-linear renders to displayed frames through exposure, white balance, and a bounded tone curve (Supp. S1). Its parameters are held fixed while lighting or material revisions are compared, preventing candidate-specific exposure adjustments from compensating for reconstruction errors.

    Motion fitting. The owner selects a rigid-body, mechanism, or water-surface representation; fitting tools estimate its parameters. Rigid poses are fitted to tracked silhouettes through the shared cameras, with trajectories constrained by supports. Mechanisms use axes, periods, and speeds estimated from the sequence; water uses a wave surface fitted to its extent, speed, and pattern. Animation uses the original timestamps, and shape changes trigger pose refitting.

    Candidate revisions and checks. The owner compares the current scene with the original frames, lists defects, and proposes or delegates a revision targeting the most severe defect. Each comparison evaluates one declared revision together with its necessary refits. Missing or inconsistent observations can trigger additional segmentation, measurement, or correction of derived estimates; the original frames remain the reference for image agreement.

    Before comparison, the level-of-detail policy is reconsidered for affected elements and lighting and supported motion are refitted as needed. The harness runs support and physical audits covering attachment relationships, interpenetration, emission from non-light materials, painted reflections, and implausible albedo; all but painted reflections, which the owner inspects, are tested by programs. Each audit counts findings on the assembled scene, and a candidate may not have more findings of a kind than its parent (Supp. S8). For every moving object, median tracked-mask IoU may decrease by at most 0.005. A candidate that fails these scene or motion checks is rejected before visual judging.

    Visual comparison and acceptance. Before judging, the owner declares the render pairs and the primary view group, a set of pairs for one kind of view, such as original or novel views. Candidate and parent use a common camera table, timestamps, observations, and rendering settings. Separate judges, without construction history or candidate identities, see a reference frame and two renders and choose the closer reconstruction or a tie. Judges are separate because agents accept their own work too readily, and the comparison controls two measured judge biases: judges pick a side even between identical images, and prefer the richer background (Supp. S2). Novel views use available reference frames to assess consistency and plausibility, not the correctness of unseen geometry.

    Each pair is evaluated in both display orders and counts as a win only when the same reconstruction wins both; a pair with a tie or with disagreeing orders is left out of the test. Identical-image controls test preferences unrelated to scene differences. The harness accepts a candidate when it wins the primary group under a two-sided sign test over pairs at significance level 0.05, controls tie, and no other evaluated group is lost, that is, won by the parent under the same test. Supp. S2 describes the judging and early-stopping procedure.

    Corrections that the owner declares, before judging, as required for physical validity undergo the same audits and motion checks but are retained unless the parent wins a view group under the same test. Accepted candidates replace the parent; rejected candidates leave it unchanged. A run returns its latest accepted scene when the owner has no further listed defects or the time budget expires; if no initial assembly passes the checks, it returns no scene (Algorithm 1).

    Reuse across runs. The generator library L_g stores accepted construction programs by family. A curation agent distills construction lessons into the experience library Lₑ, recording applicability conditions and supporting observations. Later owners and authors retrieve relevant generators and lessons and adapt them to the new video’s observations. Reused generators undergo the same fitting, checks, and acceptance process as new ones; reuse does not update model weights. Generators are written for a family rather than for one view, which also lets a scene be extended beyond the filmed region.

    4 Results

    4.1 Setup

    Scenes and evaluation subsets. We reconstruct 100 scenes: 39 static and 20 moving-element Wikimedia Commons videos, 17 generated videos, and 24 photo sets and our own captures, including Mip-NeRF 360 [3], LLFF [27]. The videos span indoor and outdoor scenes captured by handheld camera and by drone. Different experiments use subsets of this collection. Video-to-3D methods were run on 21 scenes (8 real, 13 generated). SceneAnything returns a scene on all 21; the reconstruction of a compared method can be registered to the original cameras on 19 scenes for Pi3-X, 15 for PGSR, and 12 for COLMAP (Supp. S12). Table 1 reports the 10 jointly aligned scenes (4 real, 6 generated). Direct-agent comparisons cover 30 scenes.

    Metrics. For video-to-3D comparisons, we report LPIPS [55] and DINOv3 feature similarity [38] against the input video at up to 8 original cameras per scene; these frames are among the input of every method, and the table averages per-scene means. Direct-agent comparisons use 101 frames across 30 scenes. At 8 novel cameras per scene, spaced evenly on a path around the scene (Supp. S12), DINOv3 similarity to the best-matching original frame measures content similarity, not geometric accuracy. Pairwise comparisons follow Sec. 3.6, using Claude Opus 5.5 judges; a pairwise win requires agreement across both display orders.

    Baselines. Direct-agent baselines are GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum reasoning effort, given access to the video and Blender without our harness, supplied measurements, fitting tools, or acceptance procedure. Each agent iterates on its scene until it considers the result complete. Video-based baselines use their released pipelines: Pi3-X [46], PGSR [5], COLMAP dense reconstruction and meshing [35, 36], and Video2Game [49] (Fig. 4 only). Gaussian reconstructions, including our Lyra 2 prior, are shown in Fig.  and Supp. S9. Single-image generators receive one video frame: MIDI-3D [15], SceneGen [26], Gen3DSR [1], and SAM 3D Objects [6] (Supp. S10).

    Output-token cost. On 40 Wikimedia Commons scenes (20 static and 20 with moving elements), owners, authors, and judges produce 0.9–5.6 million output tokens per run (median 2.4 million). At US $ 20 per million output tokens, this corresponds to $ 18–111 per scene (median $ 47). These figures exclude compute for vision models, fitting, and rendering (which can be run locally on the user’s compute hardware).

    4.2 Comparison with Other Methods

    Direct-agent reconstruction. On 30 scenes and 101 original-camera frames, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra obtain LPIPS 0.66 and 0.69 and DINOv3 similarity 0.55 and 0.52, compared with 0.51 and 0.76 for SceneAnything (lower LPIPS and higher DINOv3 similarity is better). Figure  illustrates errors in their layout, scale, lighting, and geometric detail. These results demonstrate the benefit of our complete reconstruction protocol and its supplied models and tools.

    Video-to-3D reconstruction. On the 10 jointly aligned scenes, SceneAnything has lower original-view LPIPS (0.50) than the compared methods (best baseline 0.56) and ties Pi3-X in DINOv3 similarity (0.74). At novel cameras, its content similarity to the input video is higher (0.53 versus at most 0.38; Table 1). Figure 4 compares video-based methods at an original camera; single-image results are in Supp. S10.

    4.3 Level-of-Detail Study

    Level of detail. Three garden beds, each filmed in one hand-held shot, test the policy at leaf scale; the densest contains about 150 weeds, shrubs, and ferns. The policy yields lower plant-region LPIPS than one generator instance per plant on all three beds and on every evaluated frame (Table 2; Fig. 3). For the city, building-pixel LPIPS drops from 0.53 to 0.49. Rendered plants cover 0.78 of the reference foliage pixels on the fence bed and 0.84 on the path bed. On the fence bed, revisions adding at least 300 observed leaves won their blind comparisons (8:0, 8:0, and 10:0).

    4.4 Author-Model Alternatives

    We test DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL authoring for the same 14 scenes, with the owner model, delivery requirements, and judges unchanged. While the overall quality is lower (on the 11 scenes that also have a run with the Claude Opus 5.5 author, mean LPIPS and DINOv3 similarity at the original cameras are 0.55 and 0.66 for DeepSeek and 0.58 and 0.60 for Nemotron, against 0.47 and 0.79), the resulting scenes retain separate mesh objects, fitted lighting, and qualitative coherence at novel views (Supp. S9). All 28 runs delivered a scene.

    4.5 Motion and Editing

    Moving objects are animated: the owner identifies the kind of motion and tools fit its parameters to the tracked masks. For example, a high-speed train, a harbor boat, a funicular car, an airliner, and a slewing crane follow the footage at median tracked-mask IoU 0.89–0.98 and median centroid error 2–13 px, measured over the frames in which each is tracked. Explicit animation allows the fitted motion to replay from novel cameras (Supp. S11).

    Separate meshes and explicit light sources also permit relighting (Fig. 5A) and removal and repositioning of objects (Fig. 5B). Surfaces revealed by an edit remain present, although their unseen geometry is inferred.

    4.6 Limitations

    Best results require commercial models; current open-source author agents produce lower quality scenes. Reconstruction of unseen regions is plausible but generally shows lower quality and detail than observed regions. Our method is built on top of imperfect camera, segmentation, depth, and material estimates. Each run reconstructs one continuous shot; unifying shots across cuts remains future work. Human reconstruction is a hard researcch problem and we do not attempt it; non-rigid motion other than water surfaces remains outside the current scope.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented SceneAnything, an automated system in which a software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools to turn real and generated videos into editable 3D scenes. The agents decide what to build and which revisions to try; the harness keeps a revision if it passes programmatic checks and separate judge agents prefer its renders. At novel views, our scenes agree better in content with the footage than those of three video-to-3D methods that produce geometry, and they remain coherent when smaller open-weight models author the components.

    LLM Usage Statement

    Claude (Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol) were used in code development and experiment execution, and to assist with manuscript editing. Language-model agents and generated input videos are part of the method and its evaluation (Secs. 3 and 4.1). The authors take full responsibility for the paper’s claims and results.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：从视频重建可编辑 3D 场景，既要对上可见结构，又要把看不见的表面合理地补出来。

要点：

  • 任务要求双向：从视频重建可编辑三维场景，既要**匹配可见结构**，又要**合理地补全不可见表面**
  • 已知问题：agent 能写「场景构建程序」，但直接照做常常在**布局、尺度与光照**上出错
  • SceneAnything 因此是一个自动化系统：从真实视频与生成视频重建网格场景，并支持**文本到场景**的构建流程

为什么值得看：「agent 写代码建场景」这条路最大的坑不是不会写，而是写错了没人发现。把它做成带验证的自动系统，才可能在资产管线里跑起来——这条与 11-18 的 RemeshingAgent（验证契约）是同一个方法论。

中文摘要：从一段视频重建可编辑的三维场景，需要同时做好两件事：匹配可见的结构，并合理地补全看不见的表面。已有方法让 agent 直接编写「场景构建程序」，但一次到位的重建尝试常常在布局、尺度与光照上出错。SceneAnything 因此把这一过程做成自动化系统，用于从真实视频与生成视频重建网格场景，并支持从文本到场景的构建流程。它的意义在于把「agent 会写代码」推进到「写出来的场景能被验证与使用」，这正是把 agentic 重建接入资产管线的必要条件。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video

Abstract

Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

1 Introduction

An editable 3D scene allows an environment to be explored, relit, and modified beyond a recorded or generated camera path. Recovering such a scene from video requires fitting visible structures and spatial relationships, separating materials from illumination, and completing unseen surfaces. Recent reconstruction and scene-generation models provide useful geometric estimates and priors [18, 37, 16, 22]. We build on these capabilities to reconstruct separate mesh objects, materials, and light sources from real and generated videos. Paired with text-to-video generation, the system also enables text-to-scene construction. Unseen surfaces are completed and marked as inferred.

Language and vision-language model agents can interpret structures, write Blender programs, and revise them from rendered feedback [11, 39, 54, 13]. Directly assigning the entire reconstruction task to an agent leaves it to establish cameras and scale, choose constructions, and assess its own result. In our zero-shot comparisons, two frontier agents produce recognizable content but simplified geometry and materials, with errors in layout, dimensions, and lighting (Fig. , columns 3 and 4). Some attempts project footage onto proxy surfaces, reproducing input views while exposing artifacts from new viewpoints. These failures motivate a process that grounds agent construction in geometric estimates and evaluates revisions in the assembled scene.

We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for coordinated component construction from video (Fig. 2). Pretrained vision models supply shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates. A scene-owner agent plans components and briefs author agents, which return parameterized Blender generators. Agents choose scene-specific constructions; the method specifies their shared inputs, authoring interfaces, level-of-detail policy, and revision procedure. The level-of-detail policy uses visibility and fit to select procedural recipes, fitted instances, or part-by-part construction. Components are assembled with fitted lighting and supported motion, then revisions undergo programmatic checks and render comparisons by separate judge agents. A software harness coordinates agents, models, and graphics tools and applies the acceptance rule. Accepted generators and curated lessons are reused in later runs. Section 3 details this structure and the decisions delegated to agents.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    An observation-grounded reconstruction framework that coordinates component authoring to produce editable scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation (Secs. 3.1–3.4).

  • •

    A level-of-detail policy and scene-level revision procedure that allocate individual modeling according to visibility and fit, and evaluate changes through programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6).

  • •

    An evaluation across 100 scenes, including direct-agent comparisons, a level-of-detail ablation, and open-weight author substitutions (Sec. 4), accompanied by a planned release of code, instructions, libraries, scenes, and evaluation records.

    • 2 Related Work

    Reconstruction from video. Structure from motion and multi-view stereo recover cameras and surfaces [35, 36, 30]; feed-forward models predict point maps, depth, and poses [45, 42, 46, 22, 14]. Neural radiance fields [28, 3] and Gaussian splatting [18, 17] represent appearance for view synthesis, with surface-oriented variants supporting mesh extraction [12, 5]. Dynamic methods recover time-varying scenes [25, 47, 44], while generative models synthesize explorable environments [37, 16, 24]. SceneAnything uses a video-to-3D model as a measurement prior, then constructs separate, named mesh components with explicit materials, lighting, and supported animation.

    Object-level reconstruction. Methods retrieve and align CAD models to scans [2], or generate objects using learned priors from an image [15, 26, 1, 6] or multiple views [29, 50, 48, 51, 34]. Video2Game reconstructs interactive mesh environments from video [49]. Our components are constructed by parameterized programs fitted to video observations, allowing their construction procedures and parameters to be revised and reused.

    Agentic scene construction. Language-model systems arrange assets [53, 10], write scene programs [39, 11], and coordinate generators with critics or verifiers [52, 9, 23]. Image-conditioned approaches predict structured scene descriptions [21], refine programs through rendering [54], orchestrate specialist agents [20, 40], or edit existing scenes [13]. SceneAnything grounds component authoring in shared video-derived measurements and evaluates revisions in a common assembled scene. Separate judges compare matched renders in both display orders, with identical-image controls and a prescribed acceptance rule. This procedure addresses the order sensitivity documented for language-model judges [56, 43].

    Procedural generation, reuse, and level of detail. Infinigen generates natural and indoor environments procedurally [31, 32]. Voyager stores reusable agent programs [41], and SceneCraft builds a scene-function library [11]. Our library retains generators fitted to video observations for adaptation to later scenes (Sec. 3.6). Rendering level-of-detail methods select representations according to viewing conditions [8, 19]. Our policy instead allocates construction detail according to visibility and achieved fit; unresolved detail and unseen surfaces are completed procedurally and recorded as inferred (Sec. 3.5).

    3 Method

    Given a captured or generated video, SceneAnything reconstructs an editable Blender scene containing separate mesh objects, materials, light sources, and animation data for supported moving objects.

    3.1 Overview and Terminology

    A reconstruction run (or simply run) is one complete attempt to reconstruct a scene; all agent sessions, vision model inferences and compute jobs for that attempt belong to the same run.

    Scene representation and agent roles. The current scene is the reconstruction state at a given stage of the run: its cameras and world coordinates, geometry, materials, lighting, and motion. A component is an authored portion of the scene, such as a building or terrain surface. A generator is a parameterized Blender program that constructs geometry and materials. A family groups objects or parts that share construction logic. A family may span several objects, such as windows on different buildings. An instance is one occurrence of an object or part in a family; different instances can have different generator parameters and poses.

    We use three types of agents. A scene owner agent coordinates the run, maintains the current scene, plans components, and assigns construction tasks to author agents. Authors write and revise generators for particular families or spatial regions. Separate judge agents compare candidate reconstructions with the current accepted scene and the observations. All three roles are language or vision-language model agents; our default owner uses Claude Opus 5.5, with alternative author models evaluated in Sec. 4.4.

    Figure 2 shows the stages of a run and Algorithm 1 summarizes it; the comment on each of its lines names who acts. Supp. S8 lists the responsibilities by stage.

    3.2 Video Processing and Geometric Initialization

    Frames and initial reconstruction. The harness extracts timestamped frames and detects shot boundaries; each run reconstructs one continuous shot. Lyra 2’s reconstruction branch [37] estimates cameras, depth, and a Gaussian representation, providing initial geometry for spatial measurements. These estimates serve as correctable priors rather than final scene geometry.

    Camera validation and world coordinates.Geometric diagnostic tools built with OpenCV and numerical routines, rather than large learned models, report reprojection error, trajectory discontinuities, vertical alignment, and near-object parallax (Supp. S1). The owner uses these diagnostics to accept, re-estimate, or correct the cameras before construction. It establishes a gravity-aligned coordinate system and estimates scale from two independent recognizable size references, checking their agreement. All components use these shared cameras and coordinates.

    3.3 Segmentation and 3D Association

    Segmentation and tracking. The owner names target classes and supplies text or box prompts. Mask2Former[7] provides semantic regions, SAM 3.1[4] segments prompted instances, and SAM 2.1[33] propagates instance masks through time. Each covers a case that the others handle poorly: Mask2Former labels continuous far regions that prompted instances miss, and SAM 2.1 keeps instance identities in dense scenes (Supp. S1). A track associates masks of the same instance across frames. Authors obtain masks for constituent parts using the same prompting procedure.

    Association with 3D geometry.Geometric tools project reconstructed points into the views, filter occluded points, and accumulate labels from overlapping masks. Plane fitting estimates supporting surfaces and facades; clustering provides approximate instance locations and extents (Supp. S1). This coarse 3D layout lets the owner plan the scene and assign authors, and lets assembly place each component at its estimated location instead of searching for its pose. These estimates inherit camera, depth, and segmentation errors and describe only observed geometry. For example, labeled building points constrain placement and visible dimensions; an author constructs coherent walls, a roof, and unseen sides.

    3.4 Scene Decomposition, Component Authoring

    Scene planning and briefs. The owner plans components, their relationships, and plausible completions of unseen parts, keeping continuous surfaces such as terrain within one component. Unseen sides and surroundings are built by the same generators as the observed parts and recorded as inferred (Supp. S13). It builds a coarse environment, then delegates families or large structures to parallel authors. Delegation separates the work into bounded tasks: a family’s author shares one generator and its lessons across all instances, and a smaller model can take such a task (Sec. 4.4; Supp. S9). Each author receives a brief specifying relevant observations, dimensions, coordinates, neighboring components, support constraints (what the component rests on or attaches to), and proposed level of detail (Sec. 3.5), together with current lighting, tools, and relevant generators and lessons.

    Parameterized construction and fitting.Authors write Blender generators with parameters for dimensions, placement, orientation, and counts. They choose construction procedures and revise code and parameters by comparing renders with the footage, optionally invoking inverse-rendering tools. Components must remain separate and movable, include unseen sides, and use materials without copied footage pixels (Supp. S5). Material parameters describe reflectance under the fitted illumination (Sec. 3.6).

    Author delivery. Authors deliver generator code, named closed mesh objects, an object-label manifest, declared supports, and records of measurements and inferred parts. The harness checks deliveries and compares rendered silhouettes with observation masks. Failed deliveries return for revision; passing permits assembly. Acceptance of changes to the assembled scene follows Sec. 3.6.

    3.5 Level of Detail

    The video supports different amounts of detail for different scene elements. Our level-of-detail policy chooses how each element is constructed from its own observations, and which detail is generated from regional statistics or structural assumptions. Components have a hierarchy of elements, such as a bed, its plants, and their leaves, or a district, its buildings, and their windows. A construction level describes how an element is built; it is distinct from its depth in this hierarchy. Part-by-part construction can be applied recursively at successive tiers.

    Construction levels. We use the following three levels, abbreviated L0, L1, and L2 in the author briefs:

  • •

    L0: Procedural recipe. Generate the element on its support using density, size, and color estimated for its region.

  • •

    L1: Fitted instance. Fit a generator instance’s position, scale, height, and orientation to the element’s own masks.

  • •

    L2: Part by part. Construct observed parts using their individual masks and spatial measurements, applying the policy recursively to those parts.

    • For example, a plant can be generated from regional statistics, fitted to its own outline, or built from individually observed leaves. The level is proposed during scene planning and reconsidered at each revision. Two visibility tests propose the construction level before building; a subsequent fit test checks a constructed part-by-part candidate.

    Visibility-based proposal. Let T(e) be the frames in which element e has an instance mask, and Mₜ(e) its mask in frame t. Its frame share is aₜ(e)=|Mₜ(e)|/(WH) for a W×H image, and ã(e) is the median share over T(e). Let m(e) count the masks of its parts over all frames of T(e), and let w(e) be the median diameter of the largest circle inscribed in each of these masks. Parts are not tracked at this stage, so a part visible in k frames contributes k masks.

    Tools compute these quantities. Before construction, the owner sets and records the visibility thresholds for each family, with a reason; defaults are in Supp. S3. The instance-visibility test S₁ requires enough views and sufficient median frame share. The part-visibility test S₂ additionally considers sustained image size, part width, and the number of part masks:

    S₁(e):|T(e)|≥n₁, ã(e)≥α₁,(1)
    S₂(e):ã(e)≥α₂, |{t∈T(e):aₜ(e)≥α₀}|≥n₂,
    w(e)≥w₀, m(e)≥m₀.(2)

    An element that passes both tests is proposed as a part-by-part candidate, one that passes only S₁ as a fitted instance, and any other as a procedural recipe. These tests use image measurements, not agent visual verdicts; their outputs depend on the supplied masks and recorded thresholds.

    Construction, fitting, and fallback. For a proposed L2 construction, the author obtains part masks with SAM 3.1 and constructs and refines a candidate Gₑ. Authors deliver a generator shared by the family and a parameter record for each element; fitting tools adjust parameters against the corresponding masks. At L1 this fits the whole instance, optionally using consistent depth for bounded deformation; at L2 the individual parts have their own masks and measurements.

    Let Rₜ(G) be the silhouette of a construction G in a render of the assembled scene at frame t, in which occluders hide the same pixels as in the observed mask Mₜ(e), and define IoUₜ(e,G)=|Rₜ(G)∩Mₜ(e)|/|Rₜ(G)∪Mₜ(e)|. The fit test requires median silhouette intersection-over-union of at least τ=0.6 over the element’s track:

    F(e): *med_t∈T(e)IoUₜ(e,Gₑ)≥τ.

    		(3)

    This is a silhouette-consistency check; agreement with the whole element’s outline alone does not establish the accuracy of its internal parts.

    Tools combine visibility and achieved fit into the level that the policy proposes for an element:

    ℓ(e)=\begincasespart by part&S₁(e)∧S₂(e)∧F(e), fitted instance&otherwise, ifS₁(e), procedural recipe&otherwise.\endcases

    		(4)

    A part-by-part candidate that fails F is thus proposed as a fitted instance. The same policy is applied recursively to retained parts, so instances of one family can have different construction levels. The author decides what is built: the instructions allow it to build individual parts wherever those parts have their own masks, also inside a fitted instance. The record for each element therefore holds the measurements, the proposed level, and the built level.

    The instructions emphasize separability as well as image size: a small, cleanly outlined dormer can be fitted individually, whereas unresolved house fronts are represented by their block’s estimated height, roof line, and window spacing. The visibility tests do not measure separability: the author judges it on the masks while building, and builds an element whose outline merges with its neighbors at a lower level than proposed. Detected elements remain represented even if their masks or tracks cannot support individual fitting.

    Completion and novel-view detail. Below the built level, procedural rules generate unresolved detail using estimated density, size, and color. Structural assumptions and the scene plan provide plausible completions of unseen parts. Generated detail and unseen completions are recorded as inferred. If an element’s placement is uncertain, it remains generated within its parent’s constraints rather than being dropped.

    After assembly, a tool compares each element’s maximum projected size over the delivered views with its size in the input frames. Where a novel view comes closer than any input view, the author generates one additional tier of finer elements. This tier is also inferred: a closer rendered view does not supply new observations of the scene.

    Figure 3 illustrates the policy at plant and city scales. In the city, whose original frame contains about 1,800 buildings, near landmarks are built individually and part by part, further houses are fitted to roof outlines, and unresolved blocks are generated inside their observed regions. On the embankment, theatre columns are built individually, the distant palace row uses fitted instances, and the city behind the frontage uses inferred recipes.

    3.6 Scene Assembly, Fitting, and Revision

    The owner assembles components in the shared coordinate system and fits lighting, materials, and supported motion. The initial assembly must pass the scene checks below. Thereafter, the parent is the current accepted scene and a candidate is a proposed revision, evaluated in the assembled environment to account for changes to shadows, occlusions, and neighboring components.

    Lighting and materials. The owner selects light sources and calibration regions for fitting their strengths. Outdoor scenes use sun and sky; indoor scenes use visible luminaires, with windows and doorways as sky portals. Fitting tools sweep sun directions against observed lit-and-shaded regions, initialized from date, time, and location when available. Authors choose material models; diffuse albedo is estimated under the fitted illumination and checked for consistency between lit and shaded pixels. Inconsistency triggers lighting refitting. Reflective and transmissive surfaces use corresponding material models.

    A fitted camera model maps scene-linear renders to displayed frames through exposure, white balance, and a bounded tone curve (Supp. S1). Its parameters are held fixed while lighting or material revisions are compared, preventing candidate-specific exposure adjustments from compensating for reconstruction errors.

    Motion fitting. The owner selects a rigid-body, mechanism, or water-surface representation; fitting tools estimate its parameters. Rigid poses are fitted to tracked silhouettes through the shared cameras, with trajectories constrained by supports. Mechanisms use axes, periods, and speeds estimated from the sequence; water uses a wave surface fitted to its extent, speed, and pattern. Animation uses the original timestamps, and shape changes trigger pose refitting.

    Candidate revisions and checks. The owner compares the current scene with the original frames, lists defects, and proposes or delegates a revision targeting the most severe defect. Each comparison evaluates one declared revision together with its necessary refits. Missing or inconsistent observations can trigger additional segmentation, measurement, or correction of derived estimates; the original frames remain the reference for image agreement.

    Before comparison, the level-of-detail policy is reconsidered for affected elements and lighting and supported motion are refitted as needed. The harness runs support and physical audits covering attachment relationships, interpenetration, emission from non-light materials, painted reflections, and implausible albedo; all but painted reflections, which the owner inspects, are tested by programs. Each audit counts findings on the assembled scene, and a candidate may not have more findings of a kind than its parent (Supp. S8). For every moving object, median tracked-mask IoU may decrease by at most 0.005. A candidate that fails these scene or motion checks is rejected before visual judging.

    Visual comparison and acceptance. Before judging, the owner declares the render pairs and the primary view group, a set of pairs for one kind of view, such as original or novel views. Candidate and parent use a common camera table, timestamps, observations, and rendering settings. Separate judges, without construction history or candidate identities, see a reference frame and two renders and choose the closer reconstruction or a tie. Judges are separate because agents accept their own work too readily, and the comparison controls two measured judge biases: judges pick a side even between identical images, and prefer the richer background (Supp. S2). Novel views use available reference frames to assess consistency and plausibility, not the correctness of unseen geometry.

    Each pair is evaluated in both display orders and counts as a win only when the same reconstruction wins both; a pair with a tie or with disagreeing orders is left out of the test. Identical-image controls test preferences unrelated to scene differences. The harness accepts a candidate when it wins the primary group under a two-sided sign test over pairs at significance level 0.05, controls tie, and no other evaluated group is lost, that is, won by the parent under the same test. Supp. S2 describes the judging and early-stopping procedure.

    Corrections that the owner declares, before judging, as required for physical validity undergo the same audits and motion checks but are retained unless the parent wins a view group under the same test. Accepted candidates replace the parent; rejected candidates leave it unchanged. A run returns its latest accepted scene when the owner has no further listed defects or the time budget expires; if no initial assembly passes the checks, it returns no scene (Algorithm 1).

    Reuse across runs. The generator library L_g stores accepted construction programs by family. A curation agent distills construction lessons into the experience library Lₑ, recording applicability conditions and supporting observations. Later owners and authors retrieve relevant generators and lessons and adapt them to the new video’s observations. Reused generators undergo the same fitting, checks, and acceptance process as new ones; reuse does not update model weights. Generators are written for a family rather than for one view, which also lets a scene be extended beyond the filmed region.

    4 Results

    4.1 Setup

    Scenes and evaluation subsets. We reconstruct 100 scenes: 39 static and 20 moving-element Wikimedia Commons videos, 17 generated videos, and 24 photo sets and our own captures, including Mip-NeRF 360 [3], LLFF [27]. The videos span indoor and outdoor scenes captured by handheld camera and by drone. Different experiments use subsets of this collection. Video-to-3D methods were run on 21 scenes (8 real, 13 generated). SceneAnything returns a scene on all 21; the reconstruction of a compared method can be registered to the original cameras on 19 scenes for Pi3-X, 15 for PGSR, and 12 for COLMAP (Supp. S12). Table 1 reports the 10 jointly aligned scenes (4 real, 6 generated). Direct-agent comparisons cover 30 scenes.

    Metrics. For video-to-3D comparisons, we report LPIPS [55] and DINOv3 feature similarity [38] against the input video at up to 8 original cameras per scene; these frames are among the input of every method, and the table averages per-scene means. Direct-agent comparisons use 101 frames across 30 scenes. At 8 novel cameras per scene, spaced evenly on a path around the scene (Supp. S12), DINOv3 similarity to the best-matching original frame measures content similarity, not geometric accuracy. Pairwise comparisons follow Sec. 3.6, using Claude Opus 5.5 judges; a pairwise win requires agreement across both display orders.

    Baselines. Direct-agent baselines are GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum reasoning effort, given access to the video and Blender without our harness, supplied measurements, fitting tools, or acceptance procedure. Each agent iterates on its scene until it considers the result complete. Video-based baselines use their released pipelines: Pi3-X [46], PGSR [5], COLMAP dense reconstruction and meshing [35, 36], and Video2Game [49] (Fig. 4 only). Gaussian reconstructions, including our Lyra 2 prior, are shown in Fig.  and Supp. S9. Single-image generators receive one video frame: MIDI-3D [15], SceneGen [26], Gen3DSR [1], and SAM 3D Objects [6] (Supp. S10).

    Output-token cost. On 40 Wikimedia Commons scenes (20 static and 20 with moving elements), owners, authors, and judges produce 0.9–5.6 million output tokens per run (median 2.4 million). At US $ 20 per million output tokens, this corresponds to $ 18–111 per scene (median $ 47). These figures exclude compute for vision models, fitting, and rendering (which can be run locally on the user’s compute hardware).

    4.2 Comparison with Other Methods

    Direct-agent reconstruction. On 30 scenes and 101 original-camera frames, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra obtain LPIPS 0.66 and 0.69 and DINOv3 similarity 0.55 and 0.52, compared with 0.51 and 0.76 for SceneAnything (lower LPIPS and higher DINOv3 similarity is better).
