Figure  illustrates errors in their layout, scale, lighting, and geometric detail. These results demonstrate the benefit of our complete reconstruction protocol and its supplied models and tools.

    Video-to-3D reconstruction. On the 10 jointly aligned scenes, SceneAnything has lower original-view LPIPS (0.50) than the compared methods (best baseline 0.56) and ties Pi3-X in DINOv3 similarity (0.74). At novel cameras, its content similarity to the input video is higher (0.53 versus at most 0.38; Table 1). Figure 4 compares video-based methods at an original camera; single-image results are in Supp. S10.

    4.3 Level-of-Detail Study

    Level of detail. Three garden beds, each filmed in one hand-held shot, test the policy at leaf scale; the densest contains about 150 weeds, shrubs, and ferns. The policy yields lower plant-region LPIPS than one generator instance per plant on all three beds and on every evaluated frame (Table 2; Fig. 3). For the city, building-pixel LPIPS drops from 0.53 to 0.49. Rendered plants cover 0.78 of the reference foliage pixels on the fence bed and 0.84 on the path bed. On the fence bed, revisions adding at least 300 observed leaves won their blind comparisons (8:0, 8:0, and 10:0).

    4.4 Author-Model Alternatives

    We test DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL authoring for the same 14 scenes, with the owner model, delivery requirements, and judges unchanged. While the overall quality is lower (on the 11 scenes that also have a run with the Claude Opus 5.5 author, mean LPIPS and DINOv3 similarity at the original cameras are 0.55 and 0.66 for DeepSeek and 0.58 and 0.60 for Nemotron, against 0.47 and 0.79), the resulting scenes retain separate mesh objects, fitted lighting, and qualitative coherence at novel views (Supp. S9). All 28 runs delivered a scene.

    4.5 Motion and Editing

    Moving objects are animated: the owner identifies the kind of motion and tools fit its parameters to the tracked masks. For example, a high-speed train, a harbor boat, a funicular car, an airliner, and a slewing crane follow the footage at median tracked-mask IoU 0.89–0.98 and median centroid error 2–13 px, measured over the frames in which each is tracked. Explicit animation allows the fitted motion to replay from novel cameras (Supp. S11).

    Separate meshes and explicit light sources also permit relighting (Fig. 5A) and removal and repositioning of objects (Fig. 5B). Surfaces revealed by an edit remain present, although their unseen geometry is inferred.

    4.6 Limitations

    Best results require commercial models; current open-source author agents produce lower quality scenes. Reconstruction of unseen regions is plausible but generally shows lower quality and detail than observed regions. Our method is built on top of imperfect camera, segmentation, depth, and material estimates. Each run reconstructs one continuous shot; unifying shots across cuts remains future work. Human reconstruction is a hard researcch problem and we do not attempt it; non-rigid motion other than water surfaces remains outside the current scope.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented SceneAnything, an automated system in which a software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools to turn real and generated videos into editable 3D scenes. The agents decide what to build and which revisions to try; the harness keeps a revision if it passes programmatic checks and separate judge agents prefer its renders. At novel views, our scenes agree better in content with the footage than those of three video-to-3D methods that produce geometry, and they remain coherent when smaller open-weight models author the components.

    LLM Usage Statement

    Claude (Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol) were used in code development and experiment execution, and to assist with manuscript editing. Language-model agents and generated input videos are part of the method and its evaluation (Secs. 3 and 4.1). The authors take full responsibility for the paper’s claims and results.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: LoopWAM：一个 checkpoint 循环 K 次核心块，就能覆盖从快到准的多档推理 ｜ LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
item.description:
一句话：每个专家存 12 个块、循环其中的 6 块核心 K 次；一份权重就能达到稠密模型的 30 层深度。

要点：

  • 结构：每个「专家」存储 **12 个块**，并把它共享的 **6 块核心循环 K 次**；因此**一个 checkpoint** 就能达到其稠密版本 30 层的深度，而参数量小得多（论文给出 2.4× 级别的收益）
  • 定位是「弹性推理」：不是训多个不同规模的模型，而是让同一份权重在不同循环次数下给出不同档位的质量与延迟
  • 这类循环结构此前在多视图重建里出现过（11-15 的 Déjà View 把 K 当算力旋钮），这里被搬到世界-动作模型上

为什么值得看：引擎最需要的就是「一套权重、多档预算」。弹性推理把 LOD 的思路搬到了模型层：同一 checkpoint 在低端设备少循环、高端设备多循环，而不必维护多套模型——这对端侧与云游戏同时存在的情况尤其划算。

中文摘要：LoopWAM 提出一种「弹性推理」的世界-动作模型结构：每个专家存储 12 个块，并将其共享的 6 块核心循环 K 次，因此单个 checkpoint 就能达到其稠密版本 30 层的深度，同时显著更小、更快。它的目标是让同一份权重在不同循环次数下提供不同的质量与延迟档位，而不是为每种预算训练一个模型。这种把「循环次数当作推理期算力旋钮」的思路此前出现在多视图重建中，如今被应用到世界-动作模型上——对既要在端侧、又要在云端部署同一能力的团队，这意味着模型维护成本可以显著下降。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference

LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models
for Elastic Inference

Anh DaoXinxin LiuHang YuJeffrey A Chan SantiagoYuzhang Shang

University of Central Florida

1  Introduction

A practical robot policy must satisfy two competing demands: producing accurate actions from visual observations and language instructions, while operating within the GPU memory and latency constraints of closed-loop control. Recent world action models (WAMs) have made remarkable progress on the former by leveraging pretrained video diffusion models to learn robotic actions, often through jointly training video and action experts [5, 29, 33, 60, 63]. Drawing on physical priors from web-scale video pretraining, WAMs have achieved competitive performance with vision-language-action models (VLAs) on benchmarks such as LIBERO [39], RoboTwin 2.0 [12], and RoboCasa [45], often without robot pretraining.

However, these gains come at a cost that conflicts with the latter demand. Most current WAMs carry 2B to 14B parameters and repeatedly execute a deep action expert across multiple denoising steps, whereas closed-loop control calls for a small memory footprint, low latency, and the flexibility to trade accuracy for speed without retraining. Two natural approaches address different aspects of this challenge, but neither is sufficient on its own. Sharing weights across depth reduces the number of stored parameters without reducing the sequential computation required at a fixed execution depth. Conversely, reducing the number of sampling steps lowers latency but may degrade action quality when the policy is not trained for fewer steps. A practical compact WAM must therefore answer two questions: how much capacity must it store, and how much computation must it execute to produce useful actions?

Answering these questions starts from where a WAM spends its computation. Fast-WAM [63] showed that a WAM need not generate future video at test time: the benefit of video modeling comes from joint training, allowing the video expert to encode the current observation once while the action expert generates an action chunk over N sampling steps. A query therefore requires one video-expert pass and N action-expert passes. At batch size one, for comparable block architectures, latency is primarily determined by the number of sequentially executed transformer blocks rather than parameter count alone (Section4.3, Figure3c). These observations suggest two complementary opportunities: reducing parameter storage through weight sharing and reducing execution cost by allocating computation differently between the two experts.

① For the first question, we turn to looped, or weight-shared, transformers [2, 15, 20, 22], which reach the depth of a deep network with the parameters of a shallow one by repeatedly applying a shared group of blocks. We bring this idea to world action models with LoopedWAM (Figure1a). Each expert stores 12 blocks organized into a 3-block prelude, a 6-block shared core, and a 3-block coda. Repeating the shared core four times recovers the 30-layer depth of its Wan2.1 donor [53]. The resulting policy has 0.58B parameters, 2.4× fewer than an equally deep dense model built from the same donor. Importantly, this makes execution depth a potential test-time choice without changing the stored parameters.

② For the second question, the asymmetric inference costs of the two experts suggest that their execution depths can be controlled independently. Given this asymmetry, LoopedWAM allows the two experts to use different loop counts, with late alignment enabling even a single action loop to access the deepest visual features. However, adjustable execution depth does not guarantee reliable inference at reduced depth: without elastic training, reducing the action expert to a single loop drops LIBERO success to 12.3% under our ablation training schedule (Figure3a). To address this, we introduce elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, to operate across action-loop counts Kₐ∈{1,2,4} and sampling steps N∈{2,5,10}, while keeping the video expert at full depth. By matching a frozen full-depth teacher starting from the student’s own intermediate states, the student learns to correct errors introduced by reduced computation.

With only 0.58B parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM is competitive with WAMs about ten times larger (Figure1b). It reaches 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, on par with Fast-WAM [63] and the best below 2B parameters, 96.1% on LIBERO, 0.5 points below Fast-WAM under the same protocol, and 52.2% on RoboCasa-GR1, ahead of StarVLA [13] and DiT4DiT [44], with 7.4× less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM. A single LoopedWAM-E checkpoint offers nine operating points over a 3.5× latency range (Figure1c): with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks, and with two action loops, it reaches 96.0% on LIBERO in 27.6 ms per query on one H100, 3.9× faster than Fast-WAM at its default ten steps. On a real robot arm, LoopedWAM matches the success of Fast-WAM with 3.4× less memory (Section4.6).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    LoopedWAM, a parameter-efficient two-expert WAM that decouples stored parameters from executed depth through weight-shared recurrence, with independently controlled video and action depths and late alignment.

  • •

    Elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint across action-depth and sampling-step budgets by distilling a frozen full-depth teacher from the student’s own intermediate states.

  • •

    A systematic evaluation with dense baselines matched in parameter count or execution depth, controlled ablations, and real-robot experiments, demonstrating the importance of preserving video depth and explicitly training for reduced-depth execution.

    • 2  Related Work

    2.1  World action models

    Early video-based policies predicted future frames and inferred actions from them [16, 55, 25] or diffused video and actions jointly [34, 66]. Recent WAMs adapt large pretrained video diffusion transformers [53]: Genie Envisioner [37] and Cosmos Policy [29] fine-tune a video model to produce actions, DreamZero [60] scales a 14B WAM, Motus [5] and LingBot-VA [33] couple video and action experts in a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) [36], DiT4DiT [44] conditions an action transformer on intermediate video features, and MemoryWAM [58] adds persistent memory. Fast-WAM [63] showed that the benefit of a WAM comes from video co-training rather than from imagining the future at test time, and several works now cut its cost: Light-WAM [35] freezes a 1.3B video backbone, LiLa-WAM [56] and LaWAM [11] predict compact latent dynamics instead of pixels, Efficient-WAM [32] and Faster-WAM [64] make future conditioning cheaper, AHA-WAM [9] runs video and action models at different rates, GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 [51] and SelfWAM [46] decode only actions at inference, and Flash-WAM [1] distills LingBot-VA to one denoising step per modality. These works shrink or remove components of the model. LoopedWAM keeps the full interface, a generative action expert as deep as the video expert, and instead shares depth across loops, which reduces stored parameters and makes the executed depth a test-time choice.

    2.2  Looped and weight-shared transformers

    Universal Transformers [15] and ALBERT [30] share weights across depth; looped transformers emulate iterative algorithms [22, 57, 48] and scale test-time compute [20]; relaxed recursive transformers [2] turn a pretrained model into a looped one, and Mixture-of-Recursions [3] routes tokens to different depths. Looped World Models [41] refine latent states with one shared block, and RD-VLA [52] iterates a weight-tied action head until convergence. Closest to us, ELT [23] distills intermediate loops from the full loop count for visual generation, and LoopFormer [27] conditions loops on their step size for elastic-depth language modeling. All of these loop a single network, and the elastic ones vary only its depth. LoopedWAM loops both experts of a video–action policy with separate loop counts, since the video expert runs once per query and the action expert once per sampler step. Late alignment lets any number of action loops read the last video loop, the shared cores start from a non-looped video model, and action depth is elastic jointly with the sampler steps.

    2.3  Fast sampling and elastic computation

    Flow-matching policies [38, 40, 7] need few integration steps, and step distillation reduces them further [47, 50, 19, 21, 1]. Slimmable and once-for-all networks [62, 8, 10] train one set of weights for many widths or depths, and early-exit and adaptive-computation models stop early [17, 18, 24, 4]. Elastic self-distillation conditions the student on its step size, as shortcut models do [19], but distills from the student’s own states and over recurrence depth and sampling steps at once, while the video expert, computed once per query, is left unchanged.

    3  Method

    LoopedWAM separates stored parameter capacity from executed computation depth (Figure2). Both the video and action experts reuse a compact weight-shared transformer core across depth while decoupling their recurrence counts to match their asymmetric inference rates. Elastic self-distillation then trains a single checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across joint action-depth and sampling-step budgets.

    3.1  Preliminaries: a world action model without test-time imagination

    A policy query receives camera images, the proprioceptive state s, and a language instruction ℓ, and returns a chunk of H future actions a∈ℝ^H×Dₐ, the first Hₓ of which are executed before the next query. As in Fast-WAM [63], a frozen video VAE encodes the images into latent tokens of the current frame x⁰ and, during training only, of future frames x^1:T. A Mixture-of-Transformers [36] with two experts processes the tokens: a video expert for video tokens and a narrower action expert for action tokens. The experts have separate projections, feed-forward layers, and modulation, but their tokens meet in one joint self-attention in every layer, and both cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of ℓ.

    Attention mask.  Tokens of the clean current frame attend only to each other, noisy future-frame tokens attend to the current frame and to themselves, and action tokens attend to the current frame and to themselves. The current frame therefore never depends on actions or future frames and always carries flow time 0, so at test time we drop the future frames, run the video expert once per query, and cache its keys and values for the action expert.

    Flow matching.  Both experts are trained with flow matching [38, 40]. For clean data x (actions or future latents), noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), and time τ∈[0,1], the model predicts the velocity of z_τ=(1-τ)x+τε:

    L_flow=𝔼[w(τ) ∥v_θ(z_τ,τ|x⁰,s,ℓ)-(ε-x)∥²],

    		(1)

    summed over the action and future-video branches, where w(τ) is a weighting of the flow time. At test time the action chunk is integrated from τ₀=1 to τ_N=0 with N Euler steps, zⱼ₊₁=zⱼ+(τⱼ₊₁-τⱼ) v_θ(zⱼ,τⱼ), without classifier-free guidance. A query thus runs the video expert once but the action expert N times, and its latency follows the number of executed layers while its memory follows the number of stored blocks. We therefore loop a shared core to keep depth with fewer stored blocks (Section3.2), let the two experts loop a different number of times (Section3.3), and train one checkpoint to run with fewer action loops and sampling steps (Section3.5).

    3.2  Looped experts

    Each expert stores L_P+L_C+L_E transformer blocks, split into a prelude P of L_P blocks, a shared core C of L_C blocks, and a coda E of L_E blocks. With K core loops, an expert maps its input tokens u to

    h⁽⁰⁾=P(u), h⁽ᵏ⁾=C(h⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾), k=1,…,K, y=E(h^(K)),

    		(2)

    so it executes L(K)=L_P+KL_C+L_E layers while storing L_P+L_C+L_E blocks: depth grows with K at no cost in parameters. We choose the partition and the default K so that the executed depth equals that of the donor network the expert is initialized from (Section3.4). We keep the loop minimal: there is no input injection, no loop-index embedding, and no outer residual around the core. At every executed layer the two experts share attention exactly as in a dense MoT.

    3.3  Decoupled video and action recurrence

    The two experts run at very different rates: the video expert once per query, the action expert once per sampling step. LoopedWAM therefore lets the number of video loops Kᵥ and action loops Kₐ differ (Figure2a). The video expert runs Kᵥ loops and caches keys and values at each of its L(Kᵥ) executed layers. The action expert runs Kₐ loops; its prelude and coda attend to the video prelude and coda, and for the core we use late alignment: block b of action loop r∈{1,…,Kₐ} attends to block b of video loop

    σ(r)=\max(1, Kᵥ-Kₐ+r),

    		(3)

    so the last action loop always reads the deepest visual features, and σ is the identity when Kₐ=Kᵥ. A query therefore costs

    T(Kᵥ,Kₐ,N)≈T₀+L(Kᵥ) tᵥ+N L(Kₐ) tₐ,

    		(4)

    where T₀ is the fixed cost of encoding and I/O, and tᵥ and tₐ are the per-block times of the two experts. Video depth is paid once per query, action depth N times. By default LoopedWAM trains and deploys Kᵥ=Kₐ=K.

    3.4  Initialization from a video diffusion transformer

    Both experts are initialized from a pretrained video diffusion transformer, the donor. The prelude and the coda copy the donor’s first L_P and last L_E blocks, and the core copies one contiguous group of L_C early-middle blocks (Section4.5 compares other choices). Where an expert’s feed-forward layers are narrower than the donor’s, we keep evenly spaced hidden units of the up- and down-projections. The narrower action expert is derived from the same blocks with the resizing rule of Fast-WAM [63].

    3.5  Elastic self-distillation

    Reducing our fixed-depth model to one action loop causes success to collapse (Section4.4), and fewer sampling steps add integration error. We therefore train one student, LoopedWAM-E, to run at every setting in a set S of action-loop counts Kₐ≤K and sampling steps N, with the video expert fixed at Kᵥ=K (Figure2b).

    Teacher and student.  The teacher is the trained LoopedWAM with its N_T-step Euler sampler, and it is frozen. The student starts as a copy of the teacher; its whole action expert is trainable, while the video expert, VAE, text encoder, and proprioceptive projection are frozen and shared with the teacher, so one video pass serves both. A small zero-initialized step-condition MLP adds an embedding of the step size d=1/N to the timestep modulation of the action expert, so the full-depth path initially preserves the teacher’s function.

    Targets from the student’s own states.  For a sampled (Kₐ,N), student and teacher start from the same noise. At macro step j the student moves from τⱼ to τⱼ₊₁=τⱼ-1/N, and its target is the teacher’s Euler map over the same interval started from the student’s current statezⱼ:

    L_local=1/N∑ⱼ₌₀^N-1∥ v̂ⱼ-sg[(Φ_T(zⱼ;τⱼ→τⱼ₊₁)-zⱼ)/(τⱼ₊₁-τⱼ)]∥²,

    		(5)

    where v̂ⱼ is the student’s velocity at zⱼ, sg stops the gradient, and Φ_T applies the teacher’s steps of size 1/N_T that lie in the interval (every macro step ends on the teacher’s grid because N divides N_T). Following the teacher from the student’s own states, rather than along the teacher’s trajectory, exposes the student to its own errors and trains it to correct them (Table8).

    Endpoint, gripper, and anchor terms.  An endpoint loss L_end (mean squared error) matches the Hₓ executed actions of the student’s final chunk to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise, L_grip applies a softplus margin to the gripper command of those actions, and L_anchor applies Eq.1 on real actions to the student at Kₐ=K and d=0, which keeps the full-depth path close to the data. The objective is

    L=L_local+λ_end L_end+λ_grip L_grip+λ_anchor L_anchor.

    		(6)

    Gradients flow through all loops of a step, but the state is detached at the start of steps j≤N-m, so only the last m steps are back-propagated end to end. Settings are drawn from a balanced sequence that visits each setting of S once per |S| updates. Algorithm1 summarizes one update: it draws the next setting from the balanced sequence, integrates the student from noise shared with the teacher, and evaluates the teacher at its fine steps for the local targets and the endpoint. At deployment, one set of weights serves every setting; an operating point is chosen by setting Kₐ and N.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Setup

    Benchmarks.  LIBERO [39] has four suites of ten tasks (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long). We train one model on all suites and evaluate every task on its 50 initial states with three evaluation seeds, i.e., 6,000 episodes per model. RoboTwin 2.0 [12] has 50 bimanual tasks; we train one model on 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task and report success over 100 episodes per task in the clean and the randomized setting. RoboCasa-GR1 [45, 6] has 24 tabletop tasks for a GR1 humanoid with 29-D actions, evaluated with 50 rollouts per task.

    Model.  Every model starts from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [53] (30 blocks of width 1536), whose VAE and text encoder stay frozen. Each expert stores L_P=3, L_C=6, and L_E=3 blocks, copied from donor blocks 1–3, 10–15, and 28–30, so with K=4 it executes 30 layers, the donor’s depth. The video expert keeps width 1536 with 6144 instead of 8960 feed-forward units, the action expert has width 512, and their joint attention has 12 heads of dimension 128. They hold 479.2M and 105.3M parameters, 584.5M in total (frozen VAE and text encoder excluded). LoopedWAM trains and deploys Kᵥ=Kₐ=4 with N=10 Euler steps, i.e., 300 action-block calls per query, and predicts H=32 actions per query. LoopedWAM-E covers S={1,2,4}×{2,5,10} for (Kₐ,N) with a teacher of N_T=10 steps; the gripper term L_grip is used only on LIBERO, whose gripper command is binary. Two dense controls use the same donor: Dense-12 executes the same 12 blocks once (equal parameters), and Dense-30 uses all 30 donor blocks (equal depth, 2.4× the parameters).

    Training.  No model uses robot pretraining, and all are trained on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. LoopedWAM is trained on the demonstrations of each benchmark, and LoopedWAM-E is then distilled from the trained LoopedWAM of that benchmark. Ablations use a shorter LIBERO schedule, half the length of the main one, under which LoopedWAM reaches 94.9%, and RoboTwin-10, ten RoboTwin tasks trained as on RoboTwin 2.0 (2,000 episodes per model). Detailed training recipes, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols will be released together with the code.

    Baselines and latency.  We re-evaluate Fast-WAM [63], Faster-WAM [64], and Light-WAM [35] on LIBERO with their released checkpoints; our runs land 0.3–1.4 points below their reported averages (TableA1), so we compare against our runs. Latency is measured on one H100 at batch size 1, from raw observation to actions, as the mean over 500 queries.

    4.2  Main results

    LIBERO (Table1).  LoopedWAM reaches 96.1%, 0.5 points below Fast-WAM∗ and 2.6 below Faster-WAM∗, which have 10–11× more parameters, and 0.3 points above Light-WAM∗, all under one protocol. Both gaps are concentrated in LIBERO-Long (90.1% vs. 93.5% and 98.1%), whereas on Object and Goal LoopedWAM is ahead of Fast-WAM∗. LoopedWAM-E keeps this accuracy with only two sampling steps: 95.6% at Kₐ=4, 96.0% at Kₐ=2.

    RoboTwin 2.0 (Table2).  LoopedWAM reaches 91.9%, with nearly equal success in the clean (92.1%) and randomized (91.7%) settings. This matches Fast-WAM (91.8%) with a tenth of its parameters and exceeds every model below 2B parameters as well as LaWAM (91.2%), which is 4× larger and pretrained on robot data; only LingBot-VA, Faster-WAM, and AHA-WAM, all above 5B parameters, are ahead, by 0.3, 0.7, and 0.9 points.

    RoboCasa-GR1 (Table3).  LoopedWAM reaches 52.2%, ahead of GR00T-N1.6 (47.6%), StarVLA-GR00T (47.8%), Being-H0.7 (49.2%), and DiT4DiT (50.8%); the latter three use the same 50-rollout protocol. LDA-1B (55.4%), VLAs on 4B backbones (VP-VLA 53.8%, TwinBrainVLA 54.6%, ABot-M0 58.3%), and ACE-Ego-0 (72.8%, pretrained on 6K hours of robot and human data) score higher, and RoboCasa-GR1 remains our hardest benchmark.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：每个专家存 12 个块、循环其中的 6 块核心 K 次；一份权重就能达到稠密模型的 30 层深度。

要点：

  • 结构：每个「专家」存储 **12 个块**，并把它共享的 **6 块核心循环 K 次**；因此**一个 checkpoint** 就能达到其稠密版本 30 层的深度，而参数量小得多（论文给出 2.4× 级别的收益）
  • 定位是「弹性推理」：不是训多个不同规模的模型，而是让同一份权重在不同循环次数下给出不同档位的质量与延迟
  • 这类循环结构此前在多视图重建里出现过（11-15 的 Déjà View 把 K 当算力旋钮），这里被搬到世界-动作模型上

为什么值得看：引擎最需要的就是「一套权重、多档预算」。弹性推理把 LOD 的思路搬到了模型层：同一 checkpoint 在低端设备少循环、高端设备多循环，而不必维护多套模型——这对端侧与云游戏同时存在的情况尤其划算。

中文摘要：LoopWAM 提出一种「弹性推理」的世界-动作模型结构：每个专家存储 12 个块，并将其共享的 6 块核心循环 K 次，因此单个 checkpoint 就能达到其稠密版本 30 层的深度，同时显著更小、更快。它的目标是让同一份权重在不同循环次数下提供不同的质量与延迟档位，而不是为每种预算训练一个模型。这种把「循环次数当作推理期算力旋钮」的思路此前出现在多视图重建中，如今被应用到世界-动作模型上——对既要在端侧、又要在云端部署同一能力的团队，这意味着模型维护成本可以显著下降。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference

LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models
for Elastic Inference

Anh DaoXinxin LiuHang YuJeffrey A Chan SantiagoYuzhang Shang

University of Central Florida

1  Introduction

A practical robot policy must satisfy two competing demands: producing accurate actions from visual observations and language instructions, while operating within the GPU memory and latency constraints of closed-loop control. Recent world action models (WAMs) have made remarkable progress on the former by leveraging pretrained video diffusion models to learn robotic actions, often through jointly training video and action experts [5, 29, 33, 60, 63]. Drawing on physical priors from web-scale video pretraining, WAMs have achieved competitive performance with vision-language-action models (VLAs) on benchmarks such as LIBERO [39], RoboTwin 2.0 [12], and RoboCasa [45], often without robot pretraining.

However, these gains come at a cost that conflicts with the latter demand. Most current WAMs carry 2B to 14B parameters and repeatedly execute a deep action expert across multiple denoising steps, whereas closed-loop control calls for a small memory footprint, low latency, and the flexibility to trade accuracy for speed without retraining. Two natural approaches address different aspects of this challenge, but neither is sufficient on its own. Sharing weights across depth reduces the number of stored parameters without reducing the sequential computation required at a fixed execution depth. Conversely, reducing the number of sampling steps lowers latency but may degrade action quality when the policy is not trained for fewer steps. A practical compact WAM must therefore answer two questions: how much capacity must it store, and how much computation must it execute to produce useful actions?

Answering these questions starts from where a WAM spends its computation. Fast-WAM [63] showed that a WAM need not generate future video at test time: the benefit of video modeling comes from joint training, allowing the video expert to encode the current observation once while the action expert generates an action chunk over N sampling steps. A query therefore requires one video-expert pass and N action-expert passes. At batch size one, for comparable block architectures, latency is primarily determined by the number of sequentially executed transformer blocks rather than parameter count alone (Section4.3, Figure3c). These observations suggest two complementary opportunities: reducing parameter storage through weight sharing and reducing execution cost by allocating computation differently between the two experts.

① For the first question, we turn to looped, or weight-shared, transformers [2, 15, 20, 22], which reach the depth of a deep network with the parameters of a shallow one by repeatedly applying a shared group of blocks. We bring this idea to world action models with LoopedWAM (Figure1a). Each expert stores 12 blocks organized into a 3-block prelude, a 6-block shared core, and a 3-block coda. Repeating the shared core four times recovers the 30-layer depth of its Wan2.1 donor [53]. The resulting policy has 0.58B parameters, 2.4× fewer than an equally deep dense model built from the same donor. Importantly, this makes execution depth a potential test-time choice without changing the stored parameters.

② For the second question, the asymmetric inference costs of the two experts suggest that their execution depths can be controlled independently. Given this asymmetry, LoopedWAM allows the two experts to use different loop counts, with late alignment enabling even a single action loop to access the deepest visual features. However, adjustable execution depth does not guarantee reliable inference at reduced depth: without elastic training, reducing the action expert to a single loop drops LIBERO success to 12.3% under our ablation training schedule (Figure3a). To address this, we introduce elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, to operate across action-loop counts Kₐ∈{1,2,4} and sampling steps N∈{2,5,10}, while keeping the video expert at full depth. By matching a frozen full-depth teacher starting from the student’s own intermediate states, the student learns to correct errors introduced by reduced computation.

With only 0.58B parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM is competitive with WAMs about ten times larger (Figure1b). It reaches 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, on par with Fast-WAM [63] and the best below 2B parameters, 96.1% on LIBERO, 0.5 points below Fast-WAM under the same protocol, and 52.2% on RoboCasa-GR1, ahead of StarVLA [13] and DiT4DiT [44], with 7.4× less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM. A single LoopedWAM-E checkpoint offers nine operating points over a 3.5× latency range (Figure1c): with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks, and with two action loops, it reaches 96.0% on LIBERO in 27.6 ms per query on one H100, 3.9× faster than Fast-WAM at its default ten steps. On a real robot arm, LoopedWAM matches the success of Fast-WAM with 3.4× less memory (Section4.6).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    LoopedWAM, a parameter-efficient two-expert WAM that decouples stored parameters from executed depth through weight-shared recurrence, with independently controlled video and action depths and late alignment.

  • •

    Elastic self-distillation, which trains a single checkpoint across action-depth and sampling-step budgets by distilling a frozen full-depth teacher from the student’s own intermediate states.

  • •

    A systematic evaluation with dense baselines matched in parameter count or execution depth, controlled ablations, and real-robot experiments, demonstrating the importance of preserving video depth and explicitly training for reduced-depth execution.

    • 2  Related Work

    2.1  World action models

    Early video-based policies predicted future frames and inferred actions from them [16, 55, 25] or diffused video and actions jointly [34, 66]. Recent WAMs adapt large pretrained video diffusion transformers [53]: Genie Envisioner [37] and Cosmos Policy [29] fine-tune a video model to produce actions, DreamZero [60] scales a 14B WAM, Motus [5] and LingBot-VA [33] couple video and action experts in a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) [36], DiT4DiT [44] conditions an action transformer on intermediate video features, and MemoryWAM [58] adds persistent memory. Fast-WAM [63] showed that the benefit of a WAM comes from video co-training rather than from imagining the future at test time, and several works now cut its cost: Light-WAM [35] freezes a 1.3B video backbone, LiLa-WAM [56] and LaWAM [11] predict compact latent dynamics instead of pixels, Efficient-WAM [32] and Faster-WAM [64] make future conditioning cheaper, AHA-WAM [9] runs video and action models at different rates, GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 [51] and SelfWAM [46] decode only actions at inference, and Flash-WAM [1] distills LingBot-VA to one denoising step per modality. These works shrink or remove components of the model. LoopedWAM keeps the full interface, a generative action expert as deep as the video expert, and instead shares depth across loops, which reduces stored parameters and makes the executed depth a test-time choice.

    2.2  Looped and weight-shared transformers

    Universal Transformers [15] and ALBERT [30] share weights across depth; looped transformers emulate iterative algorithms [22, 57, 48] and scale test-time compute [20]; relaxed recursive transformers [2] turn a pretrained model into a looped one, and Mixture-of-Recursions [3] routes tokens to different depths. Looped World Models [41] refine latent states with one shared block, and RD-VLA [52] iterates a weight-tied action head until convergence. Closest to us, ELT [23] distills intermediate loops from the full loop count for visual generation, and LoopFormer [27] conditions loops on their step size for elastic-depth language modeling. All of these loop a single network, and the elastic ones vary only its depth. LoopedWAM loops both experts of a video–action policy with separate loop counts, since the video expert runs once per query and the action expert once per sampler step. Late alignment lets any number of action loops read the last video loop, the shared cores start from a non-looped video model, and action depth is elastic jointly with the sampler steps.

    2.3  Fast sampling and elastic computation

    Flow-matching policies [38, 40, 7] need few integration steps, and step distillation reduces them further [47, 50, 19, 21, 1]. Slimmable and once-for-all networks [62, 8, 10] train one set of weights for many widths or depths, and early-exit and adaptive-computation models stop early [17, 18, 24, 4]. Elastic self-distillation conditions the student on its step size, as shortcut models do [19], but distills from the student’s own states and over recurrence depth and sampling steps at once, while the video expert, computed once per query, is left unchanged.

    3  Method

    LoopedWAM separates stored parameter capacity from executed computation depth (Figure2). Both the video and action experts reuse a compact weight-shared transformer core across depth while decoupling their recurrence counts to match their asymmetric inference rates. Elastic self-distillation then trains a single checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across joint action-depth and sampling-step budgets.

    3.1  Preliminaries: a world action model without test-time imagination

    A policy query receives camera images, the proprioceptive state s, and a language instruction ℓ, and returns a chunk of H future actions a∈ℝ^H×Dₐ, the first Hₓ of which are executed before the next query. As in Fast-WAM [63], a frozen video VAE encodes the images into latent tokens of the current frame x⁰ and, during training only, of future frames x^1:T. A Mixture-of-Transformers [36] with two experts processes the tokens: a video expert for video tokens and a narrower action expert for action tokens. The experts have separate projections, feed-forward layers, and modulation, but their tokens meet in one joint self-attention in every layer, and both cross-attend to frozen text embeddings of ℓ.

    Attention mask.  Tokens of the clean current frame attend only to each other, noisy future-frame tokens attend to the current frame and to themselves, and action tokens attend to the current frame and to themselves. The current frame therefore never depends on actions or future frames and always carries flow time 0, so at test time we drop the future frames, run the video expert once per query, and cache its keys and values for the action expert.

    Flow matching.  Both experts are trained with flow matching [38, 40]. For clean data x (actions or future latents), noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), and time τ∈[0,1], the model predicts the velocity of z_τ=(1-τ)x+τε:

    L_flow=𝔼[w(τ) ∥v_θ(z_τ,τ|x⁰,s,ℓ)-(ε-x)∥²],

    		(1)

    summed over the action and future-video branches, where w(τ) is a weighting of the flow time. At test time the action chunk is integrated from τ₀=1 to τ_N=0 with N Euler steps, zⱼ₊₁=zⱼ+(τⱼ₊₁-τⱼ) v_θ(zⱼ,τⱼ), without classifier-free guidance. A query thus runs the video expert once but the action expert N times, and its latency follows the number of executed layers while its memory follows the number of stored blocks. We therefore loop a shared core to keep depth with fewer stored blocks (Section3.2), let the two experts loop a different number of times (Section3.3), and train one checkpoint to run with fewer action loops and sampling steps (Section3.5).

    3.2  Looped experts

    Each expert stores L_P+L_C+L_E transformer blocks, split into a prelude P of L_P blocks, a shared core C of L_C blocks, and a coda E of L_E blocks. With K core loops, an expert maps its input tokens u to

    h⁽⁰⁾=P(u), h⁽ᵏ⁾=C(h⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾), k=1,…,K, y=E(h^(K)),

    		(2)

    so it executes L(K)=L_P+KL_C+L_E layers while storing L_P+L_C+L_E blocks: depth grows with K at no cost in parameters. We choose the partition and the default K so that the executed depth equals that of the donor network the expert is initialized from (Section3.4). We keep the loop minimal: there is no input injection, no loop-index embedding, and no outer residual around the core. At every executed layer the two experts share attention exactly as in a dense MoT.

    3.3  Decoupled video and action recurrence

    The two experts run at very different rates: the video expert once per query, the action expert once per sampling step. LoopedWAM therefore lets the number of video loops Kᵥ and action loops Kₐ differ (Figure2a). The video expert runs Kᵥ loops and caches keys and values at each of its L(Kᵥ) executed layers. The action expert runs Kₐ loops; its prelude and coda attend to the video prelude and coda, and for the core we use late alignment: block b of action loop r∈{1,…,Kₐ} attends to block b of video loop

    σ(r)=\max(1, Kᵥ-Kₐ+r),

    		(3)

    so the last action loop always reads the deepest visual features, and σ is the identity when Kₐ=Kᵥ. A query therefore costs

    T(Kᵥ,Kₐ,N)≈T₀+L(Kᵥ) tᵥ+N L(Kₐ) tₐ,

    		(4)

    where T₀ is the fixed cost of encoding and I/O, and tᵥ and tₐ are the per-block times of the two experts. Video depth is paid once per query, action depth N times. By default LoopedWAM trains and deploys Kᵥ=Kₐ=K.

    3.4  Initialization from a video diffusion transformer

    Both experts are initialized from a pretrained video diffusion transformer, the donor. The prelude and the coda copy the donor’s first L_P and last L_E blocks, and the core copies one contiguous group of L_C early-middle blocks (Section4.5 compares other choices). Where an expert’s feed-forward layers are narrower than the donor’s, we keep evenly spaced hidden units of the up- and down-projections. The narrower action expert is derived from the same blocks with the resizing rule of Fast-WAM [63].

    3.5  Elastic self-distillation

    Reducing our fixed-depth model to one action loop causes success to collapse (Section4.4), and fewer sampling steps add integration error. We therefore train one student, LoopedWAM-E, to run at every setting in a set S of action-loop counts Kₐ≤K and sampling steps N, with the video expert fixed at Kᵥ=K (Figure2b).

    Teacher and student.  The teacher is the trained LoopedWAM with its N_T-step Euler sampler, and it is frozen. The student starts as a copy of the teacher; its whole action expert is trainable, while the video expert, VAE, text encoder, and proprioceptive projection are frozen and shared with the teacher, so one video pass serves both. A small zero-initialized step-condition MLP adds an embedding of the step size d=1/N to the timestep modulation of the action expert, so the full-depth path initially preserves the teacher’s function.

    Targets from the student’s own states.  For a sampled (Kₐ,N), student and teacher start from the same noise. At macro step j the student moves from τⱼ to τⱼ₊₁=τⱼ-1/N, and its target is the teacher’s Euler map over the same interval started from the student’s current statezⱼ:

    L_local=1/N∑ⱼ₌₀^N-1∥ v̂ⱼ-sg[(Φ_T(zⱼ;τⱼ→τⱼ₊₁)-zⱼ)/(τⱼ₊₁-τⱼ)]∥²,

    		(5)

    where v̂ⱼ is the student’s velocity at zⱼ, sg stops the gradient, and Φ_T applies the teacher’s steps of size 1/N_T that lie in the interval (every macro step ends on the teacher’s grid because N divides N_T). Following the teacher from the student’s own states, rather than along the teacher’s trajectory, exposes the student to its own errors and trains it to correct them (Table8).

    Endpoint, gripper, and anchor terms.  An endpoint loss L_end (mean squared error) matches the Hₓ executed actions of the student’s final chunk to the teacher’s chunk from the same noise, L_grip applies a softplus margin to the gripper command of those actions, and L_anchor applies Eq.1 on real actions to the student at Kₐ=K and d=0, which keeps the full-depth path close to the data. The objective is

    L=L_local+λ_end L_end+λ_grip L_grip+λ_anchor L_anchor.

    		(6)

    Gradients flow through all loops of a step, but the state is detached at the start of steps j≤N-m, so only the last m steps are back-propagated end to end. Settings are drawn from a balanced sequence that visits each setting of S once per |S| updates. Algorithm1 summarizes one update: it draws the next setting from the balanced sequence, integrates the student from noise shared with the teacher, and evaluates the teacher at its fine steps for the local targets and the endpoint. At deployment, one set of weights serves every setting; an operating point is chosen by setting Kₐ and N.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Setup

    Benchmarks.  LIBERO [39] has four suites of ten tasks (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long). We train one model on all suites and evaluate every task on its 50 initial states with three evaluation seeds, i.e., 6,000 episodes per model. RoboTwin 2.0 [12] has 50 bimanual tasks; we train one model on 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task and report success over 100 episodes per task in the clean and the randomized setting. RoboCasa-GR1 [45, 6] has 24 tabletop tasks for a GR1 humanoid with 29-D actions, evaluated with 50 rollouts per task.

    Model.  Every model starts from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [53] (30 blocks of width 1536), whose VAE and text encoder stay frozen. Each expert stores L_P=3, L_C=6, and L_E=3 blocks, copied from donor blocks 1–3, 10–15, and 28–30, so with K=4 it executes 30 layers, the donor’s depth. The video expert keeps width 1536 with 6144 instead of 8960 feed-forward units, the action expert has width 512, and their joint attention has 12 heads of dimension 128. They hold 479.2M and 105.3M parameters, 584.5M in total (frozen VAE and text encoder excluded). LoopedWAM trains and deploys Kᵥ=Kₐ=4 with N=10 Euler steps, i.e., 300 action-block calls per query, and predicts H=32 actions per query. LoopedWAM-E covers S={1,2,4}×{2,5,10} for (Kₐ,N) with a teacher of N_T=10 steps; the gripper term L_grip is used only on LIBERO, whose gripper command is binary. Two dense controls use the same donor: Dense-12 executes the same 12 blocks once (equal parameters), and Dense-30 uses all 30 donor blocks (equal depth, 2.4× the parameters).

    Training.  No model uses robot pretraining, and all are trained on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. LoopedWAM is trained on the demonstrations of each benchmark, and LoopedWAM-E is then distilled from the trained LoopedWAM of that benchmark. Ablations use a shorter LIBERO schedule, half the length of the main one, under which LoopedWAM reaches 94.9%, and RoboTwin-10, ten RoboTwin tasks trained as on RoboTwin 2.0 (2,000 episodes per model). Detailed training recipes, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols will be released together with the code.

    Baselines and latency.  We re-evaluate Fast-WAM [63], Faster-WAM [64], and Light-WAM [35] on LIBERO with their released checkpoints; our runs land 0.3–1.4 points below their reported averages (TableA1), so we compare against our runs. Latency is measured on one H100 at batch size 1, from raw observation to actions, as the mean over 500 queries.

    4.2  Main results

    LIBERO (Table1).  LoopedWAM reaches 96.1%, 0.5 points below Fast-WAM∗ and 2.6 below Faster-WAM∗, which have 10–11× more parameters, and 0.3 points above Light-WAM∗, all under one protocol. Both gaps are concentrated in LIBERO-Long (90.1% vs. 93.5% and 98.1%), whereas on Object and Goal LoopedWAM is ahead of Fast-WAM∗. LoopedWAM-E keeps this accuracy with only two sampling steps: 95.6% at Kₐ=4, 96.0% at Kₐ=2.

    RoboTwin 2.0 (Table2).  LoopedWAM reaches 91.9%, with nearly equal success in the clean (92.1%) and randomized (91.7%) settings. This matches Fast-WAM (91.8%) with a tenth of its parameters and exceeds every model below 2B parameters as well as LaWAM (91.2%), which is 4× larger and pretrained on robot data; only LingBot-VA, Faster-WAM, and AHA-WAM, all above 5B parameters, are ahead, by 0.3, 0.7, and 0.9 points.

item.title: 原生 3D 生成不必先压进潜空间：Direct3D-V3 直接在体素域里跑扩散 transformer ｜ Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
item.description:
一句话：从 vecset、三平面到结构化稀疏体素，各家架构不同，但都共享「先压缩再建模」这个前提。

要点：

  • 现状梳理到位：原生 3D 生成基本建立在潜扩散之上，近期进展集中在**更强的 VAE** 与**越来越复杂的潜表示**（vecset、三平面、结构化稀疏体素）
  • 共同前提被点出来：这些方法**都先把几何压缩进潜空间**，再由扩散模型建模
  • Direct3D-V3 直接取消这一步，在**原生体素域**里运行扩散 transformer（latent-free）

为什么值得看：潜空间能降维，但也会带来解码损失与额外的解码开销——这正是 11-15 PixVid（视频）与 11-19 DWD（图像）在攻的问题，现在轮到 3D。三条放在一起看，「去掉潜空间」正在变成一条跨模态的路线。

中文摘要：原生三维生成目前基本建立在潜扩散之上：近期的进展集中在更强的变分自编码器，以及越来越精巧的潜表示——从 vecset、三平面一直到结构化的稀疏体素。Direct3D-V3 指出，尽管这些方法的架构各不相同，它们共享同一个前提：先把几何压缩到潜空间里，再由扩散模型建模。这篇因此取消这一前提，直接在原生体素域中运行扩散 transformer（latent-free）。这与视频与图像领域正在发生的「去掉潜空间」趋势相互呼应——代价是建模难度提高，收益则是绕开压缩与解码带来的信息损失与额外开销。

Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain

2026

Abstract.

Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. This paradigm carries two intrinsic limitations. First, VAE reconstruction removes fine geometric detail before the diffusion model ever sees the data. Second, the two-stage pipeline creates an objective mismatch, since the VAE is trained for reconstruction whereas the diffusion model is trained for distribution matching. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Extensive experiments show that Direct3D-V3 achieves competitive results to state-of-the-art latent-based methods, while producing finer geometry. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.
