PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] combines Gaussian appearance with spring-mass dynamics. PGND [zhang2025pgnd] and DeformMaster [li2026deformmaster] improve prediction through learned dynamics and residual corrections, while Boba [pang2026boba] accelerates simulation with compact models and batched execution. Yet accurate motion fitting and efficient rollout do not ensure physically meaningful, reusable material parameters. MorphTwin identifies interpretable material responses while keeping material calibration offline and online simulation explicit for efficient interactive rollout.

    Material representations and reuse across graphs. Spring parameters depend on graph geometry and connectivity [lloyd2008identification]. MatPhys [yang2026matphys] learns shared material embeddings, while NeuSpring [xu2026neuspring] models spring properties with neural fields. However, consistent parameter prediction does not guarantee consistent mechanical responses across graphs. Central springs also couple bulk and shear in unstressed, isotropic 3D networks under affine small strains. MorphTwin uses internally relaxable response carriers for separate bulk and shear control within standard central-force dynamics. Energy alignment maps shared response targets to graph-specific spring parameters for interpretable recovery, editing, and reuse across objects and discretizations. Appendix  compares the inputs, processing, and outputs of related methods, highlighting MorphTwin’s advantages.

    3 Problem Formulation

    Problem setting.

    Given an interaction video V and its reconstructed spring-mass graph G=(ℙ,S), where ℙ and S denote physical nodes and central-force spring connections, our goal is to identify physically meaningful material responses from limited deformation observations. The resulting twins should generalize to novel forces and manipulations and support material editing and reuse at interactive speeds. While FEM [zienkiewicz2013fem] and MPM [jiang2016mpm] offer expressive constitutive models, their costs can grow substantially at fine resolutions. We build on the spring-mass architecture of PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] to retain efficient explicit dynamics.

    Material parameters and graph discretization.

    Spring coefficients are defined on a specific graph, and their mechanical effect depends on its geometry and connectivity. Discretization and material identification are therefore coupled: under comparable geometry and loading, compliant objects with rich local deformations may require substantially more simulation nodes and spring connections than stiffer objects. For an unstressed graph, the affine elastic energy 𝔼^aff under a small-strain tensor ε is

    𝔼^aff(ε)=1/2∑_e∈SYₑLₑ(nₑ^⊤εnₑ)²,

    where Yₑ=kₑLₑ, kₑ is Hookean spring constant, and Lₑ,nₑ are edge’s reference length and unit direction. Because this energy also depends on graph geometry and connectivity, identical coefficients can produce different mechanical responses across discretizations. Material identification and reuse therefore require an explicit correspondence between physical responses and graph-specific spring parameters.

    Expressiveness of central-force networks.

    Material recovery also depends on which responses a graph can express. For an unstressed three-dimensional central-force network with an isotropic effective response under affine small strains, directional averaging gives

    W_\rmcentral=c/30[(trε)²+2ε:ε],(1)
    W_\rmiso=λ/2(trε)²+με:ε=λ/2 (= c/30)[(trε)²+2μ/λ (= 1)ε:ε].

    Here, c is the effective network stiffness scale, λ,μ are the Lamé parameters, μ is the shear modulus, and : denotes tensor double contraction. Matching the coefficients yields

    λ=μ=c/15, κ=λ+2/3μ=5/3μ, ν=3κ-2μ/2(3κ+μ)=1/4,

    		(2)

    where κ is the bulk modulus and ν is Poisson’s ratio. Topology and stiffness changes within this model class preserve the fixed ratio κ/μ=5/3, preventing independent control of volume and shape responses. Consequently, fitting axial stiffness alone cannot recover the correct transverse response of materials with ν≠1/4.

    These observations motivate MorphTwin’s response carriers and graph-specific energy calibration. Internally relaxable carriers enrich controllable local deformation modes, while offline calibration maps desired relative bulk and shear response changes to graph-specific stiffness updates. Together, they support material identification, editing, and reuse across different reconstructed graphs while retaining standard central-force springs and efficient explicit integration.

    4 Methodology

    Figure 2 provides an overview of our MorphTwin pipeline. We first initialize an explicit spring graph from geometry and motion cues extracted from sparse video observations (Sec. 4.1). We then introduce relaxable response carriers and calibrate the graph under volumetric and shear deformations (Secs. 4.2-4.3). The calibrated model is fitted to observed motion, followed by Gaussian appearance optimization with physics fixed. Material edits are expressed as shared relative response changes and mapped to spring stiffnesses for each graph, enabling material editing and reuse while retaining efficient explicit simulation. (Sec. 4.4).

    4.1 Video and Graph Initialization

    Given sparse video observations V, we follow PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] to obtain object masks with Grounded-SAM 2 [liu2024grounding, ravi2025sam2] and 2D point tracks with CoTracker3 [karaev2025cotracker3]. We lift these tracks to 3D using the corresponding depth maps and align a shape prior from TRELLIS [xiang2025trellis] to the initial observations.

    Spatial neighbor connections initialize the spring graph G₀=(ℙ₀,S₀), with physical nodes ℙ₀ and springs S₀. We denote the backbone stiffnesses by b. The interaction parameters η govern the stiffness of springs linking the hand to the object, as well as friction and restitution during contact. The recovered geometry and 3D tracks provide supervision for subsequent physics fitting.

    4.2 Relaxable Response Carriers

    As discussed in Sec. 3, conventional central-force spring networks couple volumetric and shear responses under affine deformation. Hybrid models [golec2020hybridMSS] introduce additional volumetric energy on regular lattices, but such structures poorly match the irregular graphs reconstructed from videos.

    MorphTwin instead introduces response freedom directly into the reconstructed graph G₀ by augmenting selected four-node cells with relaxable internal nodes, forming G=(ℙ,S) as illustrated in Fig. 3(A). A bulk carrier adds a centroid auxiliary node, while a paired shear carrier adds two symmetric auxiliary nodes on the circumsphere. These candidates are geometrically screened and jointly selected to match bulk and shear response targets while minimizing auxiliary mass, as detailed in Appendix . The original springs are retained, and all auxiliary nodes participate in the same explicit central-force dynamics, without requiring a regular volumetric mesh. Each edge has a base coefficient Yₑ(b,0), with carrier spokes following the local backbone scale. A fixed label wₑ∈{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)} distinguishes backbone, bulk carrier, and shear carrier edges. The controls u=(u_B,u_S)^⊤ adjust the corresponding spring families through logarithmic stiffness offsets:

    \logYₑ(b,u)=\logYₑ(b,0)+wₑ^⊤u,

    		(3)

    where b specifies backbone stiffnesses, while u_B and u_S independently scale corresponding carrier spring stiffnesses.

    The affine restriction λ=μ in Eq. (2) arises when all nodes follow the same imposed affine deformation. MorphTwin retains central-force springs but relaxes this assumption for auxiliary nodes. Under small strain E, physical nodes deform affinely (zᵢ=0), while auxiliary nodes undergo additional nonaffine displacements z. Minimizing over these displacements yields the reduced elastic energy:

    𝔼̄(E)=\min_z1/2∑_e=(i,j)∈SYₑLₑ[nₑ^⊤Enₑ+(nₑ^⊤(zⱼ-zᵢ))/(Lₑ)]².

    		(4)

    The bracket combines each spring’s affine strain with a nonaffine correction due to auxiliary motion. This relaxation can lower the energy by different amounts for volumetric and shear deformation, depending on carrier geometry. Hence, the effective bulk and shear responses need not satisfy the affine relation λ=μ, despite retaining central-force springs. The two carrier families provide distinct response sensitivities, enabling locally independent control when the response Jacobian has full rank. Minimization is used only for offline response evaluation, while online simulation advances all nodes explicitly, without per-step minimization.

    4.3 Energy Response Calibration

    To measure resistance to volume and shape changes, we evaluate 𝔼̄ under unit volumetric strain E_\rmvol=I/√3 and five orthonormal deviatoric strains {E_\rmdev⁽ᵃ⁾}ₐ₌₁⁵ spanning the volume-preserving strain modes in 3D:

    κ=2/3𝔼̄(E_\rmvol), μ=1/5∑ₐ₌₁⁵𝔼̄(E_\rmdev⁽ᵃ⁾), q=[\logκ,\logμ]^⊤.

    		(5)

    The prefactors normalize these energies. κ and μ are graph-integrated bulk and shear responses (dependence on (b,u) omitted). Their continuum moduli are κ/V and μ/V for reference volume V. Logarithmic differences encode relative response changes, canceling the fixed V within each graph.

    Although u_B and u_S scale distinct carrier families, each can affect both bulk and shear responses. Their effects also depend on graph geometry and connectivity. For each graph, let b⁰ denote the initial backbone stiffness parameters used for calibration. We define the reference response as q⁰=q(b⁰,0) and compute the sensitivity matrix:

    A=(∂q)/(∂u), Δq:=q(b⁰,u)-q⁰≃Au, u=A⁻¹Δq.

    		(6)

    For full-rank A, the inverse mapping enables independent local control of bulk and shear responses. Each graph converts a shared relative response change into its own spring controls. We compute A once and keep it fixed during fitting.

    4.4 Material Identification and Interaction

    Material identification.

    With masses fixed, we fit θ=(Δq,b,η) and retain the damping and contact distance from initialization. The carrier controls u=A⁻¹Δq determine the spring stiffnesses Y(b,u). Explicit simulation yields X̂(θ)=Simulate(G,Y,η), which collects the physical-node positions over time. We first fit physics with Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=L_geo+L_track as geometry and 3D correspondences supervision, then freeze θ and fit Gaussian appearance φ to RGB observations:

    \min_θL_\rmmotion(X̂(θ),V),(7)
    \min_φL_\rmRGB(Render(φ,X̂(θ)),V_\rmRGB).

    Material morphing and reuse.

    Edits adjust the overall elastic scale or change response coordinates through the local calibration. For cross-graph reuse, the target realizes the source response through its own offline calibration, preserving its reference geometry and canonical appearance.

    Interaction and fracture.

    Novel grasps drive the twin through force-limited control springs and explicit integration. Gaussian bindings are fixed on intact graphs, and when springs fail irreversibly under excessive strain, appearance support uses surviving local connections. Nonlinear response transfer and Gaussian binding are detailed in Appendices  and , respectively.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Benchmarks and baselines.

    We evaluate MorphTwin on the 20 PhysTwin scenes used by DeformMaster [li2026deformmaster], 14 synthetic Spring-Gaus [zhong2024springgaussian] development scenes with known material parameters, and our self-captured egocentric interaction benchmark comprising 15 spatiotemporally aligned sequences with stereo and external RGB-D observations (capture details in Appendix ). Real-world benchmarks assess reconstruction and future prediction, while Spring-Gaus evaluates material property identification. Baselines include PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin], DeformMaster, PGND [zhang2025pgnd], Boba [pang2026boba], GIC [cai2024gic] and MatPhys [yang2026matphys]. For DeformMaster, Boba and MatPhys, we use released checkpoints, Gaussian assets and code, while training PGND and GIC under matched settings.

    Evaluation.

    Following DeformMaster [li2026deformmaster], we report foreground-masked PSNR [hore2010psnr_ssim], SSIM [wang2004ssim], and LPIPS [zhang2018lpips]. We also report Chamfer distance [wu2021chamfer_distance], tracking error, relative Young’s modulus error, and absolute Poisson’s ratio error. All experiments use a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU. Further details are provided in Appendix .

    5.2 Quantitative Evaluation

    Reconstruction and future prediction.

    Table 1 reports reconstruction and future prediction results on the PhysTwin benchmark. With PhysTwin’s preprocessing unchanged, MorphTwin supports calibrated material control and achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM and the lowest LPIPS among the evaluated methods in both settings, with PSNR gains of 3.53 dB for reconstruction and 1.99 dB for future prediction over PhysTwin. LPIPS decreases by 22.5% for reconstruction and 24.8% for future prediction. Future prediction CD decreases from 12.00 to 11.30 mm, and tracking error decreases from 23.0 to 22.1 mm.

    Table 2 compares methods on our 15-sequence egocentric benchmark using three view modes: single RGB-D, egocentric stereo, and all views. With all views, MorphTwin reduces reconstruction and future-prediction LPIPS by 14.6% and 10.6% over PhysTwin, respectively. Moving from single RGB-D to all views increases reconstruction PSNR by 4.99 dB for MorphTwin versus 2.36 dB for PhysTwin. MorphTwin also outperforms PhysTwin on all metrics with egocentric stereo alone, demonstrating its advantage in real-world reconstruction and future interaction prediction.

    Efficient explicit simulation.

    MorphTwin calibrates volumetric and shape response targets into spring parameters for each graph offline. Online simulation directly advances the calibrated explicit graph, without per-step material identification, energy alignment, or an additional material-prediction network. Table 3 shows that MorphTwin achieves higher offline and same-node interactive throughput than PhysTwin and DeformMaster across all three dimensional groups. In addition, MorphTwin realizes material responses through an explicit spring graph, making it compatible with complementary acceleration strategies developed for PhysTwin.

    5.3 Qualitative Evaluation

    Figure 4 compares MorphTwin with PhysTwin, DeformMaster, and PGND on 1D curves, 2D surfaces, and 3D solids using semi-transparent GT overlays. Especially in the illustrated rope-lifting and sloth-lifting cases, MorphTwin more closely matches the reference contours and deformation in future frames than PhysTwin, suggesting better generalization beyond observed frames. Figure  in Appendix  extends the comparison to all 15 sequences of our benchmark.

    5.4 Downstream Applications

    Material property identification.

一句话：复现视频里的形变，并不能保证物体对新施加的力给出正确响应。

要点：

  • 观察很关键：**复现视频中的运动，并不能保证物体对新力给出正确响应**——当物理表示限制了物体可变形的方式时，就会出错
  • 具体机制：在基于弹簧的孪生表示中，**体积响应与形状响应之间的耦合**造成了这种限制
  • MorphTwin 因此丰富局部的形变能力（让表示本身不再限制响应方式），同时保持仿真的效率

为什么值得看：「看着像」与「推得动」是两件事，而视频驱动的物理孪生最容易在这里翻车：拟合了轨迹，却拟合不了力。做可交互柔性物体（旗子、布料、软体）时，这条点出的耦合问题是设计表示时必须处理的。

中文摘要：从视频重建可交互的物理孪生，需要既准确捕捉物体的形变方式，又保持仿真的效率。作者指出一个关键观察：复现视频中的运动，并不保证物体在面对新的外力时给出正确响应——当物理表示本身限制了物体可以如何形变时，这种错误就会出现。在基于弹簧的孪生表示中，体积响应与形状响应之间的耦合正是这类限制的来源。MorphTwin 因此着手丰富局部的形变能力，使表示不再束缚响应方式，同时维持可交互所需的仿真效率。对旗子、布料、软体这类可交互物体，这条点出的耦合问题在选表示时就必须处理。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-21

MorphTwin: Enriching Deformable Material Responses from Videos for Morphable and Interactive Physical Twins

Abstract

Reconstructing interactive physical twins from video requires accurately capturing how objects deform while maintaining efficient simulation. We observe that reproducing motion in a video does not guarantee correct responses to new forces when the physical representation restricts how an object can deform. In spring-based twins, coupling between volume and shape responses creates such a limitation. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes to capture and independently control these responses while retaining standard spring forces and explicit simulation. To support interpretable material editing and transfer, we use offline calibration to map shared relative response changes to stiffness updates on each reconstructed graph. Under identical inverse settings on synthetic scenes, MorphTwin reduces the mean absolute error of Poisson’s ratio by 75.8% and the mean relative error of Young’s modulus by 22.1% compared to PhysTwin. We introduce an egocentric stereo and RGB-D benchmark covering interactions with objects of varying stiffness. Real-world experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and up to 14.4% lower future tracking error than PhysTwin at interactive speeds.

1 Introduction

Reconstructing physical twins from videos turns observed objects into interactive assets that respond to novel forces and manipulations. Applications such as virtual reality and embodied AI require physically plausible responses at interactive speeds [ai2025robot_review_science_robotics, spielberg2023inverse_problem_reviews_nature_machine_intelligence, frisoli2024vr_review_nature_reviews]. Continuum methods such as PhysGaussian [xie2024physgaussian] and GIC [cai2024gic] use Material Point Methods (MPM) [jiang2016mpm] to model rich material behaviors, but detailed simulations can be costly for real-time interaction. PGND [zhang2025pgnd] learns particle motion but offers limited explicit control over material properties, while DeformMaster [li2026deformmaster] combines MPM simulator with neural corrections and faces a trade-off between simulation accuracy and interactive speed. Mass-spring systems [blickhan1989mss] provide a real-time foundation for explicit forward simulation, with simple local forces and directly adjustable mechanical parameters. PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin, zhong2024springgaussian] combines this structure with visual reconstruction, enabling physical twin reconstruction from sparse-view videos and real-time interaction, but the underlying spring representation can limit material expressiveness.

Our goal is to turn spring-based physical twins into physically faithful, reusable assets with interpretable material control. We further observe that these models can closely match observed motion yet respond incorrectly to novel interactions. This motivates an elastic-energy analysis of conventional central-force networks [golec2020hybridMSS]. As illustrated in Fig. (b), we identify a source of this discrepancy: their responses to volume and shape changes can be coupled. Consequently, a reconstructed model may capture how far an object stretches yet fail to reproduce how much it thins. Both responses govern shape and volume changes in deformable objects. This structural coupling can persist despite stiffness fitting. Overcoming it requires accommodating irregular geometry reconstructed from sparse views while retaining standard spring forces and efficient explicit simulation.

Accordingly, we introduce MorphTwin, a framework that enriches the deformation modes of reconstructed spring graphs to support independent estimation and control of volume and shape responses. We augment each graph with local structures whose internal nodes can move relative to surrounding nodes. These response carriers introduce additional deformation freedom while retaining standard central-force springs. All nodes evolve together through explicit forward simulation, preserving efficient interaction.

To support interpretable editing and transfer of material behavior, we account for how graph geometry and connectivity affect mechanical responses. We calibrate each graph using standardized volumetric and shear deformation tests, mapping shared relative response changes to graph-specific stiffness updates. This enables consistent material adjustments across objects relative to their respective reference states. Calibration is performed offline, and online interaction proceeds through explicit spring simulation.

Controlled experiments show that our method improves material recovery accuracy and better preserves relative material responses across different graph discretizations. Real-world experiments further demonstrate that MorphTwin improves both reconstruction and future prediction while maintaining efficient explicit simulation, and supports reconstructing physical twins from egocentric observations. Together, these results enable interactive physical twins with richer, editable material behaviors.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Reconstructing physical twins with richer material responses. We present MorphTwin, which enriches local deformation modes during video-based reconstruction to enable independent volume and shape control while retaining efficient explicit spring dynamics.

  • •

    Response carriers and calibration for material control. We design internally relaxable spring structures and energy-based calibration to support material identification and map shared relative response changes to graph-specific stiffness updates for interpretable editing and transfer.

  • •

    Controlled validation and an egocentric benchmark. We demonstrate improved material recovery, reconstruction, and future prediction through controlled experiments and real-world evaluations. We introduce a benchmark of temporally aligned egocentric stereo and RGB-D interaction sequences and demonstrate material editing and transfer in interactive physical twins.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video-based physical twins and interactive dynamics. Recent methods reconstruct deformable physical twins from visual observations [li2023pac, cai2024gic, jiang2025phystwin, rho2026monophysics, kim2026egophys, lee2026physhandi, hong2026pidg]. PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] combines Gaussian appearance with spring-mass dynamics. PGND [zhang2025pgnd] and DeformMaster [li2026deformmaster] improve prediction through learned dynamics and residual corrections, while Boba [pang2026boba] accelerates simulation with compact models and batched execution. Yet accurate motion fitting and efficient rollout do not ensure physically meaningful, reusable material parameters. MorphTwin identifies interpretable material responses while keeping material calibration offline and online simulation explicit for efficient interactive rollout.

    Material representations and reuse across graphs. Spring parameters depend on graph geometry and connectivity [lloyd2008identification]. MatPhys [yang2026matphys] learns shared material embeddings, while NeuSpring [xu2026neuspring] models spring properties with neural fields. However, consistent parameter prediction does not guarantee consistent mechanical responses across graphs. Central springs also couple bulk and shear in unstressed, isotropic 3D networks under affine small strains. MorphTwin uses internally relaxable response carriers for separate bulk and shear control within standard central-force dynamics. Energy alignment maps shared response targets to graph-specific spring parameters for interpretable recovery, editing, and reuse across objects and discretizations. Appendix  compares the inputs, processing, and outputs of related methods, highlighting MorphTwin’s advantages.

    3 Problem Formulation

    Problem setting.

    Given an interaction video V and its reconstructed spring-mass graph G=(ℙ,S), where ℙ and S denote physical nodes and central-force spring connections, our goal is to identify physically meaningful material responses from limited deformation observations. The resulting twins should generalize to novel forces and manipulations and support material editing and reuse at interactive speeds. While FEM [zienkiewicz2013fem] and MPM [jiang2016mpm] offer expressive constitutive models, their costs can grow substantially at fine resolutions. We build on the spring-mass architecture of PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] to retain efficient explicit dynamics.

    Material parameters and graph discretization.

    Spring coefficients are defined on a specific graph, and their mechanical effect depends on its geometry and connectivity. Discretization and material identification are therefore coupled: under comparable geometry and loading, compliant objects with rich local deformations may require substantially more simulation nodes and spring connections than stiffer objects. For an unstressed graph, the affine elastic energy 𝔼^aff under a small-strain tensor ε is

    𝔼^aff(ε)=1/2∑_e∈SYₑLₑ(nₑ^⊤εnₑ)²,

    where Yₑ=kₑLₑ, kₑ is Hookean spring constant, and Lₑ,nₑ are edge’s reference length and unit direction. Because this energy also depends on graph geometry and connectivity, identical coefficients can produce different mechanical responses across discretizations. Material identification and reuse therefore require an explicit correspondence between physical responses and graph-specific spring parameters.

    Expressiveness of central-force networks.

    Material recovery also depends on which responses a graph can express. For an unstressed three-dimensional central-force network with an isotropic effective response under affine small strains, directional averaging gives

    W_\rmcentral=c/30[(trε)²+2ε:ε],(1)
    W_\rmiso=λ/2(trε)²+με:ε=λ/2 (= c/30)[(trε)²+2μ/λ (= 1)ε:ε].

    Here, c is the effective network stiffness scale, λ,μ are the Lamé parameters, μ is the shear modulus, and : denotes tensor double contraction. Matching the coefficients yields

    λ=μ=c/15, κ=λ+2/3μ=5/3μ, ν=3κ-2μ/2(3κ+μ)=1/4,

    		(2)

    where κ is the bulk modulus and ν is Poisson’s ratio. Topology and stiffness changes within this model class preserve the fixed ratio κ/μ=5/3, preventing independent control of volume and shape responses. Consequently, fitting axial stiffness alone cannot recover the correct transverse response of materials with ν≠1/4.

    These observations motivate MorphTwin’s response carriers and graph-specific energy calibration. Internally relaxable carriers enrich controllable local deformation modes, while offline calibration maps desired relative bulk and shear response changes to graph-specific stiffness updates. Together, they support material identification, editing, and reuse across different reconstructed graphs while retaining standard central-force springs and efficient explicit integration.

    4 Methodology

    Figure 2 provides an overview of our MorphTwin pipeline. We first initialize an explicit spring graph from geometry and motion cues extracted from sparse video observations (Sec. 4.1). We then introduce relaxable response carriers and calibrate the graph under volumetric and shear deformations (Secs. 4.2-4.3). The calibrated model is fitted to observed motion, followed by Gaussian appearance optimization with physics fixed. Material edits are expressed as shared relative response changes and mapped to spring stiffnesses for each graph, enabling material editing and reuse while retaining efficient explicit simulation. (Sec. 4.4).

    4.1 Video and Graph Initialization

    Given sparse video observations V, we follow PhysTwin [jiang2025phystwin] to obtain object masks with Grounded-SAM 2 [liu2024grounding, ravi2025sam2] and 2D point tracks with CoTracker3 [karaev2025cotracker3]. We lift these tracks to 3D using the corresponding depth maps and align a shape prior from TRELLIS [xiang2025trellis] to the initial observations.

    Spatial neighbor connections initialize the spring graph G₀=(ℙ₀,S₀), with physical nodes ℙ₀ and springs S₀. We denote the backbone stiffnesses by b. The interaction parameters η govern the stiffness of springs linking the hand to the object, as well as friction and restitution during contact. The recovered geometry and 3D tracks provide supervision for subsequent physics fitting.

    4.2 Relaxable Response Carriers

    As discussed in Sec. 3, conventional central-force spring networks couple volumetric and shear responses under affine deformation. Hybrid models [golec2020hybridMSS] introduce additional volumetric energy on regular lattices, but such structures poorly match the irregular graphs reconstructed from videos.

    MorphTwin instead introduces response freedom directly into the reconstructed graph G₀ by augmenting selected four-node cells with relaxable internal nodes, forming G=(ℙ,S) as illustrated in Fig. 3(A). A bulk carrier adds a centroid auxiliary node, while a paired shear carrier adds two symmetric auxiliary nodes on the circumsphere. These candidates are geometrically screened and jointly selected to match bulk and shear response targets while minimizing auxiliary mass, as detailed in Appendix . The original springs are retained, and all auxiliary nodes participate in the same explicit central-force dynamics, without requiring a regular volumetric mesh. Each edge has a base coefficient Yₑ(b,0), with carrier spokes following the local backbone scale. A fixed label wₑ∈{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)} distinguishes backbone, bulk carrier, and shear carrier edges. The controls u=(u_B,u_S)^⊤ adjust the corresponding spring families through logarithmic stiffness offsets:

    \logYₑ(b,u)=\logYₑ(b,0)+wₑ^⊤u,

    		(3)

    The affine restriction λ=μ in Eq. (2) arises when all nodes follow the same imposed affine deformation. MorphTwin retains central-force springs but relaxes this assumption for auxiliary nodes. Under small strain E, physical nodes deform affinely (zᵢ=0), while auxiliary nodes undergo additional nonaffine displacements z. Minimizing over these displacements yields the reduced elastic energy:

    𝔼̄(E)=\min_z1/2∑_e=(i,j)∈SYₑLₑ[nₑ^⊤Enₑ+(nₑ^⊤(zⱼ-zᵢ))/(Lₑ)]².

    		(4)

    The bracket combines each spring’s affine strain with a nonaffine correction due to auxiliary motion. This relaxation can lower the energy by different amounts for volumetric and shear deformation, depending on carrier geometry. Hence, the effective bulk and shear responses need not satisfy the affine relation λ=μ, despite retaining central-force springs. The two carrier families provide distinct response sensitivities, enabling locally independent control when the response Jacobian has full rank. Minimization is used only for offline response evaluation, while online simulation advances all nodes explicitly, without per-step minimization.

    4.3 Energy Response Calibration

    To measure resistance to volume and shape changes, we evaluate 𝔼̄ under unit volumetric strain E_\rmvol=I/√3 and five orthonormal deviatoric strains {E_\rmdev⁽ᵃ⁾}ₐ₌₁⁵ spanning the volume-preserving strain modes in 3D:

    		(5)

    The prefactors normalize these energies. κ and μ are graph-integrated bulk and shear responses (dependence on (b,u) omitted). Their continuum moduli are κ/V and μ/V for reference volume V. Logarithmic differences encode relative response changes, canceling the fixed V within each graph.

    Although u_B and u_S scale distinct carrier families, each can affect both bulk and shear responses. Their effects also depend on graph geometry and connectivity. For each graph, let b⁰ denote the initial backbone stiffness parameters used for calibration. We define the reference response as q⁰=q(b⁰,0) and compute the sensitivity matrix:

    A=(∂q)/(∂u), Δq:=q(b⁰,u)-q⁰≃Au, u=A⁻¹Δq.

    		(6)

    For full-rank A, the inverse mapping enables independent local control of bulk and shear responses. Each graph converts a shared relative response change into its own spring controls. We compute A once and keep it fixed during fitting.

We first fit physics with Lₘₒₜᵢₒₙ=L_geo+L_track as geometry and 3D correspondences supervision, then freeze θ and fit Gaussian appearance φ to RGB observations:
